              # only expressible form. It is a read of alarm configuration and
              # state; there is nothing sensitive in it that the account owner
              # does not already share with the platform.
              - Effect: Allow
                Action: 'cloudwatch:DescribeAlarms'
                Resource: '*'
              # Scoped to the exception group specifically. The digest reports
              # what could not be instrumented; it has no business reading
              # application logs, which is where regulated data would be.
              - Effect: Allow
                Action:
                  - 'logs:FilterLogEvents'
                  - 'logs:GetLogEvents'
                Resource:
                  - !Sub '${ExceptionLogGroup.Arn}'
                  - !Sub '${ExceptionLogGroup.Arn}:*'
      Tags:
        - { Key: platform-managed, Value: 'true' }

  # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # EventBridge delivery role
  # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # A CloudWatch alarm publishes to the cross-account alerting topic as the
  # service principal cloudwatch.amazonaws.com, which the topic policy admits
  # by aws:SourceOrgID. An EventBridge RULE cannot do that: targeting a topic
  # in another account requires a RoleArn, and PutTargets fails outright
  # without one —
  #
  #   ValidationException: RoleArn is required for target
  #   arn:aws:sns:us-east-2:...:platform-alerts-low
  #
  # So the account-level event rules publish as this role instead. It exists
  # only to relay events to the two alerting topics and can do nothing else.
  #
  # The name is load-bearing. The topic policy admits publishers by
  # aws:PrincipalArn matching */role/PlatformEventBridgeDelivery, which is far
  # tighter than admitting every principal in the Organization — that would let
  # any compromised workload in any member account flood the channel every page
  # travels through.
  EventDeliveryRole:
    Type: AWS::IAM::Role
    Condition: HasAlerting
    Properties:
      RoleName: PlatformEventBridgeDelivery
      AssumeRolePolicyDocument:
        Version: '2012-10-17'
        Statement:
          - Effect: Allow
            Principal: { Service: events.amazonaws.com }
            Action: sts:AssumeRole
            Condition:
              StringEquals:
                'aws:SourceAccount': !Ref AWS::AccountId
      Policies:
        - PolicyName: PublishToAlerting
          PolicyDocument:
            Version: '2012-10-17'
            Statement:
              - Effect: Allow
                Action: 'sns:Publish'
                Resource: !If
                  - MetaAlarmsLowUrgency
                  - [!Ref AlertTopicArn, !Ref LowUrgencyTopicArn]
                  - [!Ref AlertTopicArn]
              # The alerting topics are ENCRYPTED, so publishing needs KMS as
              # well as SNS — on both sides. This was missing from the moment
              # the event rules were built and stayed invisible because the
              # rules had targets attached and had never delivered an event.
              # Wiring that looks complete and fails on first use.
              #
              # Found while debugging the response engine's identical gap, not
              # by testing the event rules.
              - Effect: Allow
                Action: ['kms:GenerateDataKey*', 'kms:Decrypt']
                Resource: '*'
                Condition:
                  StringEquals:
                    'kms:ViaService': !Sub 'sns.${AWS::Region}.amazonaws.com'
      Tags:
        - { Key: platform-managed, Value: 'true' }

  # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # Drift detection
  # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # Prompt 4.2. Everything the instrumentation Lambda creates can be removed by
  # one console click, and nothing would notice until an incident went
  # unalarmed.
  #
  # Same package, second handler. drift.py imports handler.py and calls
  # plan_alarms, so both derive the expected alarm from one code path. A second
  # definition would let drift "correct" alarms toward whichever copy was
  # edited last, silently, on a schedule, across every account.
  DriftLogGroup:
    Type: AWS::Logs::LogGroup
    # Retained. A drift record says monitoring that existed was removed or
    # changed, which is a security-relevant statement about someone's action
    # rather than an operational log line.
    DeletionPolicy: Retain
    UpdateReplacePolicy: Retain
    Properties:
      LogGroupName: /aws/platform/alarm-drift
      RetentionInDays: !Ref ExceptionRetentionDays
      KmsKeyId: !If
        - UseDefaultLogsKey
        - !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:kms:${AWS::Region}:${AWS::AccountId}:alias/platform-logs'
        - !Ref LogsKeyArn

  DriftMetricFilter:
    Type: AWS::Logs::MetricFilter
    Properties:
      LogGroupName: !Ref DriftLogGroup
      FilterName: PlatformAlarmDrift
      # Matches recreate and correct events, NOT orphan reports or sweep
      # failures. An orphan is usually a decommissioned resource, and alarming
      # on it would make the signal routine.
      FilterPattern: '{ $.event = "recreated-deleted-alarm" || $.event = "corrected-modified-alarm" }'
      MetricTransformations:
        - MetricNamespace: AltDigital/Platform
          MetricName: AlarmDriftCorrected
          MetricValue: '1'
          DefaultValue: 0

  DriftAlarm:
    Type: AWS::CloudWatch::Alarm
    Properties:
      AlarmName: platform-alarm-drift
      AlarmDescription: >-
        A platform-managed alarm was deleted or modified and has been put back.
        The alarm is fine now; what needs explaining is why it changed.
        Read /aws/platform/alarm-drift — a corrected-modified-alarm record
        carries the previous values. A threshold raised far enough leaves an
        alarm that exists, evaluates, shows green and can never fire, which is
        indistinguishable from healthy unless someone compares it to the
        specification.
        If the change was deliberate it belongs in
        design/06a-alarm-specification.yaml, not in the console. This sweep
        will revert it again otherwise.
      Namespace: AltDigital/Platform
      MetricName: AlarmDriftCorrected
      Statistic: Sum
      Period: 300
      EvaluationPeriods: 1
      Threshold: 1
      ComparisonOperator: GreaterThanOrEqualToThreshold
      TreatMissingData: notBreaching
      AlarmActions: !If
        - MetaAlarmsLowUrgency
        - [!Ref LowUrgencyTopicArn]
        - !If [HasAlerting, [!Ref AlertTopicArn], !Ref 'AWS::NoValue']

  DriftFunction:
    Type: AWS::Lambda::Function
    Properties:
      FunctionName: platform-alarm-drift
      Runtime: python3.13
      Handler: drift.handler
      Role: !GetAtt InstrumentationRole.Arn
      # A full sweep walks every in-scope resource type through Config and
      # re-derives every alarm. Minutes rather than seconds once an account
      # holds real workloads, and a timeout mid-sweep leaves the remaining
      # types unchecked with no record — the one outcome worth paying to avoid.
      Timeout: 600
      MemorySize: 512
      Code:
        S3Bucket: !Ref ArtifactBucket
        S3Key: !Ref ArtifactKey
      Environment:
        Variables:
          EXCEPTION_LOG_GROUP: !Ref ExceptionLogGroup
          DRIFT_LOG_GROUP: !Ref DriftLogGroup
          ENVIRONMENT_TIER: !Ref EnvironmentTier
          ALERT_TOPIC_ARN: !Ref AlertTopicArn
          LOW_URGENCY_TOPIC_ARN: !Ref LowUrgencyTopicArn
          ALARM_PREFIX: platform-auto
          CENTRAL_BUS_ARN: !Ref CentralBusArn
          EVENT_FORWARDING_ROLE_ARN: !If
            - HasCentralBus
            - !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:iam::${AWS::AccountId}:role/PlatformEventForwarding'
            - ''
          EVENT_RULE_PREFIX: platform-event
          EVENT_DELIVERY_ROLE_ARN: !If
            - HasAlerting
            - !GetAtt EventDeliveryRole.Arn
            - ''
      Tags:
        - { Key: platform-managed, Value: 'true' }

  DriftLambdaLogGroup:
    Type: AWS::Logs::LogGroup
    DeletionPolicy: Delete
    UpdateReplacePolicy: Delete
    Properties:
      LogGroupName: /aws/lambda/platform-alarm-drift
      RetentionInDays: 30
      KmsKeyId: !If
        - UseDefaultLogsKey
        - !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:kms:${AWS::Region}:${AWS::AccountId}:alias/platform-logs'
        - !Ref LogsKeyArn

  # Scheduled sweep. Catches deletions the event rule missed, modifications
  # (which emit no distinctive event worth matching), and alarms never created
  # because an earlier invocation failed.
  DriftScheduleRule:
    Type: AWS::Events::Rule
    Properties:
      Name: platform-alarm-drift-schedule
      Description: Hourly sweep comparing live alarms against the specification.
      ScheduleExpression: 'rate(1 hour)'
      State: ENABLED
      Targets:
        - Id: drift
          Arn: !GetAtt DriftFunction.Arn

  # Immediate response to a deletion. The schedule alone would leave up to an
  # hour with monitoring removed, and an hour is long enough to cover the
  # window someone deleted the alarm to create.
  DriftDeleteRule:
    Type: AWS::Events::Rule
    Properties:
      Name: platform-alarm-drift-on-delete
      Description: >-
        CloudWatch DeleteAlarms via CloudTrail. Fires a full sweep rather than
        parsing the deleted names: an alarm name is
        platform-auto-RESOURCEID-ALARMID and both halves may contain dashes, so
        parsing is ambiguous and would fail on exactly the resources with
        awkward identifiers.
      EventPattern:
        source:
          - aws.monitoring
        detail-type:
          - 'AWS API Call via CloudTrail'
        detail:
          eventSource:
            - monitoring.amazonaws.com
          eventName:
            - DeleteAlarms
      State: ENABLED
      Targets:
        - Id: drift
          Arn: !GetAtt DriftFunction.Arn

  DriftSchedulePermission:
    Type: AWS::Lambda::Permission
    Properties:
      FunctionName: !GetAtt DriftFunction.Arn
      Action: lambda:InvokeFunction
      Principal: events.amazonaws.com
      SourceArn: !GetAtt DriftScheduleRule.Arn

  DriftDeletePermission:
    Type: AWS::Lambda::Permission
    Properties:
      FunctionName: !GetAtt DriftFunction.Arn
      Action: lambda:InvokeFunction
      Principal: events.amazonaws.com
      SourceArn: !GetAtt DriftDeleteRule.Arn

  # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # CloudWatch agent
  # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # Prompt 4.1: "Include the SSM association that installs the CloudWatch
  # agent on new instances, since memory and disk alarms are useless without
  # it."
  #
  # Worth being precise about why. EC2 publishes CPU, network and disk I/O from
  # the hypervisor, which cannot see inside the guest. Memory used and
  # filesystem used are guest-internal and are not published at all without an
  # agent. An alarm on mem_used_percent with no agent does not error — it sits
  # in INSUFFICIENT_DATA indefinitely, which in a console full of green looks
  # near enough to healthy that nobody investigates.
  #
  # Targeted by tag rather than by instance id, so an instance created after
  # this association picks it up. Instances must carry
  # platform-managed=true; anything that does not is out of scope by
  # construction, which is a decision the baseline makes rather than this
  # template.
  CloudWatchAgentAssociation:
    Type: AWS::SSM::Association
    Properties:
      AssociationName: platform-install-cloudwatch-agent
      Name: AWS-ConfigureAWSPackage
      Targets:
        - Key: tag:platform-managed
          Values: ['true']
      Parameters:
        action: ['Install']
        name: ['AmazonCloudWatchAgent']
      # Re-applies on a schedule so a replaced or manually removed agent comes
      # back. Without this the association is a one-time install and the agent
      # is only as present as nobody having touched it.
      ScheduleExpression: 'rate(1 day)'
      ComplianceSeverity: HIGH
      MaxConcurrency: '10%'
      MaxErrors: '10%'

Outputs:

  DriftFunctionName:
    Description: Alarm drift detection, hourly sweep and on-delete
    Value: !Ref DriftFunction

  DriftLogGroupName:
    Description: Where drift events are recorded
    Value: !Ref DriftLogGroup

  FunctionName:
    Description: Auto-instrumentation function
    Value: !Ref InstrumentationFunction

  ExceptionLogGroupName:
    Description: Where instrumentation exceptions are recorded
    Value: !Ref ExceptionLogGroup

  ExceptionAlarmName:
    Description: Fires when a resource comes up uninstrumented
    Value: !Ref ExceptionAlarm

  EnvironmentTierApplied:
    Description: Tier the alarm thresholds were resolved at
    Value: !Ref EnvironmentTier
files.baseline/60-response.yaml:
AWSTemplateFormatVersion: '2010-09-09'

Description: >-
  AltDigital Managed Platform — Tier 1 automated response. The four-stage
  runbook framework, its safety rails, and the state they depend on. Part of
  the member baseline StackSet.

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# This is the first stack permitted to stop anything
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Everything before it creates, reads or alarms. This one can stop an ECS task
# and restart a process, so the interesting part is not what it does — it is
# what it is unable to do.
#
# The refusals recorded in runbooks/catalog.yaml on 2026-09-18 are enforced
# HERE, in IAM, not only in code. A future catalog entry naming
# drain_and_replace would fail at the API rather than succeeding because
# somebody added a function to actions.py. Code says what the platform intends;
# IAM says what it can do, and only the second survives a mistake.
#
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Automation runs ALONGSIDE paging, not in front of it
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Doc 07 implies automation first and a page only on escalation. That would
# mean removing AlarmActions from every alarm and letting the engine page — and
# it would make this Lambda a single point of failure for every page the
# platform sends. A bug here would be silent, because the symptom is the
# absence of an alert.
#
# So alarms keep their existing actions and the engine is triggered in parallel
# by an EventBridge rule on alarm state change. The cost is duplication: an
# alarm the automation fixes has already paged. That is the right way round for
# now — recorded as B-030, to revisit once the engine has a track record.

Parameters:

  ArtifactBucket:
    Type: String
    Description: Artifact bucket in Platform Tooling holding the response package.

  ArtifactKey:
    Type: String
    Description: Content-addressed package key.

  EnvironmentTier:
    Type: String
    Default: dev
    AllowedValues: [dev, test, uat, prod]

  EscalationViaBus:
    Type: String
    AllowedValues: ['true', 'false']
    Default: 'false'
    Description: >-
      When true the engine puts its dossier on the account's default event bus
      and baseline/70-event-forwarding.yaml carries it to the router, which
      pages with the dossier attached under the same dedup key as the raw
      alarm. When false it publishes to SNS as before.

      Either/or, never both: the two paths reach PagerDuty through different
      integrations, so doing both raises two unrelated incidents for one
      outage. Set to true only in accounts where 70-event-forwarding is
      deployed with a bus.

  AlertTopicArn:
    Type: String
    Default: ''
    Description: Where stage 4 publishes the dossier.

  LowUrgencyTopicArn:
    Type: String
    Default: ''

  LogsKeyArn:
    Type: String
    Default: ''
    Description: >-
      Empty falls back to alias/platform-logs, created by
      baseline/20-log-data-protection.yaml.

  ResponseEnabled:
    Type: String
    Default: 'disabled'
    AllowedValues: ['enabled', 'disabled']
    Description: >-
      Initial value of the kill switch.

      DEFAULTS TO DISABLED. An account does not begin taking automated action
      because a stack was deployed to it — somebody turns it on deliberately,
      per account, after looking at what the catalog would do there. The
      parameter is then changed OUT OF BAND by scripts/response-kill-switch.sh,
      because 06a requires the switch usable without a deployment and the
      moment you want it is the moment you least want to run one.

      Note this template does not manage the value after creation: the SSM
      parameter is created here and then owned by the operator. A stack update
      would otherwise revert a deliberate emergency stop.

Conditions:
  HasAlerting: !Not [!Equals [!Ref AlertTopicArn, '']]
  UseDefaultLogsKey: !Equals [!Ref LogsKeyArn, '']
  MetaLowUrgency: !And
    - !Not [!Equals [!Ref LowUrgencyTopicArn, '']]
    - !Or
      - !Equals [!Ref EnvironmentTier, dev]
      - !Equals [!Ref EnvironmentTier, test]

Resources:

  # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # Kill switch
  # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # An SSM parameter because 06a requires it usable without a deployment, which
  # rules out a stack parameter and an environment variable alike.
  #
  # rails.check_kill_switch FAILS CLOSED: absent, unreadable or anything other
  # than 'enabled' all block. A switch that defaults to go when it cannot be
  # consulted works only when nothing is wrong.
  ResponseKillSwitch:
    Type: AWS::SSM::Parameter
    Properties:
      Name: /platform/response/enabled
      Type: String
      Value: !Ref ResponseEnabled
      Description: >-
        Tier 1 automated response. 'enabled' or anything else. Changed out of
        band by scripts/response-kill-switch.sh; do not edit via the stack.
      Tags:
        platform-managed: 'true'

  # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # Rail state
  # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  RemediationHistory:
    Type: AWS::DynamoDB::Table
    # Retained. The circuit breaker and the failed-attempt limit are only as
    # good as their memory, and a stack replacement that emptied this table
    # would silently reset every count — handing the automation a clean slate
    # on exactly the resource it had already given up on.
    DeletionPolicy: Retain
    UpdateReplacePolicy: Retain
    Properties:
      TableName: platform-remediation-history
      BillingMode: PAY_PER_REQUEST
      AttributeDefinitions:
        - { AttributeName: resource_action,  AttributeType: S }
        - { AttributeName: attempted_at,     AttributeType: S }
        - { AttributeName: pending,          AttributeType: S }
        - { AttributeName: revalidate_after, AttributeType: S }
      KeySchema:
        # Partitioned by (resource, action) so the circuit breaker's question —
        # "how often has THIS action run on THIS resource" — is a single query
        # rather than a scan. The rate limit's question is account-wide and does
        # scan, which is acceptable because the TTL below bounds the table.
        - { AttributeName: resource_action, KeyType: HASH }
        - { AttributeName: attempted_at,    KeyType: RANGE }
      GlobalSecondaryIndexes:
        # SPARSE, deliberately. Only an item parked for revalidation carries
        # `pending`, so this index contains outstanding work and nothing else:
        # the sweep's query returns exactly what is due and costs nothing on the
        # overwhelming majority of runs where nothing is.
        #
        # A constant partition key is normally a mistake — it is one hot
        # partition. It is right here because the index is bounded by the number
        # of remediations in flight in a single account, which is capped at 20
        # per hour by the rate limit.
        - IndexName: pending-revalidation
          KeySchema:
            - { AttributeName: pending,          KeyType: HASH }
            - { AttributeName: revalidate_after, KeyType: RANGE }
          Projection:
            ProjectionType: ALL
      TimeToLiveSpecification:
        AttributeName: expires_at
        Enabled: true
      PointInTimeRecoverySpecification:
        PointInTimeRecoveryEnabled: true
      SSESpecification:
        SSEEnabled: true
      Tags:
        - { Key: platform-managed, Value: 'true' }

  ChangeRecordLogGroup:
    Type: AWS::Logs::LogGroup
    # Retained, and the retention is long. 06a requires a change record for
    # every automated action, and doc 07 explains why: automation must not
    # become a route around change management. That record is only worth
    # anything if it outlives the incident.
    DeletionPolicy: Retain
    UpdateReplacePolicy: Retain
    Properties:
      LogGroupName: /aws/platform/change-records
      RetentionInDays: 2557
      KmsKeyId: !If
        - UseDefaultLogsKey
        - !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:kms:${AWS::Region}:${AWS::AccountId}:alias/platform-logs'
        - !Ref LogsKeyArn

  DossierLogGroup:
    Type: AWS::Logs::LogGroup
    DeletionPolicy: Retain
    UpdateReplacePolicy: Retain
    Properties:
      LogGroupName: /aws/platform/incident-dossiers
      RetentionInDays: 365
      KmsKeyId: !If
        - UseDefaultLogsKey
        - !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:kms:${AWS::Region}:${AWS::AccountId}:alias/platform-logs'
        - !Ref LogsKeyArn

  # A gap is a finding. An alarm with no runbook means somebody answered a page
  # from a blank console, which is the situation this whole phase exists to
  # remove — so it is counted rather than left in a log nobody reads.
  ResponseGapFilter:
    Type: AWS::Logs::MetricFilter
    Properties:
      LogGroupName: !Ref DossierLogGroup
      FilterName: PlatformResponseGap
      FilterPattern: '{ $.record_type = "response-gap" }'
      MetricTransformations:
        - MetricNamespace: AltDigital/Platform
          MetricName: ResponseGaps
          MetricValue: '1'
          DefaultValue: 0

  ResponseGapAlarm:
    Type: AWS::CloudWatch::Alarm
    Properties:
      AlarmName: platform-response-gap
      AlarmDescription: >-
        An alarm fired with no runbook for its (alarm x resource) pair. The
        alarm paged on its own, so the incident was seen — but nothing was
        gathered, so whoever answered started from a blank console.
        Read /aws/platform/incident-dossiers for which pair. The fix is an
        entry in runbooks/catalog.yaml, and an entry that only GATHERS is worth
        having: most incidents are resolved by the gather stage naming a recent
        deployment, not by a remediation.
        Low urgency by design — this is a coverage gap to review, not an
        incident. The incident already paged.
      Namespace: AltDigital/Platform
      MetricName: ResponseGaps
      Statistic: Sum
      # A day, not five minutes. This counts catalog coverage, which is a thing
      # you review over a week — alarming on it every five minutes would make a
      # backlog look like an emergency.
      Period: 86400
      EvaluationPeriods: 1
      Threshold: 1
      ComparisonOperator: GreaterThanOrEqualToThreshold
      TreatMissingData: notBreaching
      AlarmActions: !If
        - MetaLowUrgency
        - [!Ref LowUrgencyTopicArn]
        - !If [HasAlerting, [!Ref AlertTopicArn], !Ref 'AWS::NoValue']

  # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # Execution role — the interesting part is the absences
  # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  ResponseRole:
    Type: AWS::IAM::Role
    Properties:
      RoleName: PlatformResponseAutomation
      AssumeRolePolicyDocument:
        Version: '2012-10-17'
        Statement:
          - Effect: Allow
            Principal: { Service: [lambda.amazonaws.com, ssm.amazonaws.com] }
            Action: sts:AssumeRole
      Policies:
        - PolicyName: GatherReadOnly
          PolicyDocument:
            Version: '2012-10-17'
            Statement:
              # Stage 1 is read-only and runs on every alarm, so these are the
              # permissions the role uses almost all the time.
              - Effect: Allow
                Action:
                  - 'cloudwatch:DescribeAlarms'
                  - 'cloudwatch:DescribeAlarmHistory'
                  - 'cloudwatch:GetMetricStatistics'
                  - 'cloudwatch:ListMetrics'
                  - 'cloudtrail:LookupEvents'
                  - 'config:GetResourceConfigHistory'
                  - 'ecs:DescribeServices'
                  - 'ecs:DescribeTasks'
                  - 'ecs:ListTasks'
                  - 'elasticloadbalancing:DescribeTargetGroups'
                  - 'elasticloadbalancing:DescribeTargetHealth'
                  - 'application-autoscaling:DescribeScalingPolicies'
                  - 'ec2:DescribeInstances'
                  - 'ssm:DescribeInstanceInformation'
                  - 'ssm:GetCommandInvocation'
                Resource: '*'

        - PolicyName: RailState
          PolicyDocument:
            Version: '2012-10-17'
            Statement:
              - Effect: Allow
                # DeleteItem is scoped to this table and is used only to clear a
                # pending-revalidation marker once the sweep has reached a
                # verdict. It removes the engine's own bookkeeping, never a
                # managed resource — the CLAUDE.md prohibition on deletion is
                # about the things automation acts on. The attempt record that
                # proves what was DONE is a separate item and is not touched.
                Action:
                  - 'dynamodb:PutItem'
                  - 'dynamodb:Query'
                  - 'dynamodb:Scan'
                  - 'dynamodb:DeleteItem'
                Resource:
                  - !GetAtt RemediationHistory.Arn
                  - !Sub '${RemediationHistory.Arn}/index/pending-revalidation'
              - Effect: Allow
                Action: 'ssm:GetParameter'
                Resource: !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:ssm:${AWS::Region}:${AWS::AccountId}:parameter/platform/response/*'
              - Effect: Allow
                # The account's own default bus, and only that. The engine
                # publishes the dossier there; the forwarding rule carries it
                # cross-account, which is a permission held by the forwarding
                # role rather than by this one. The engine cannot reach another
                # account's bus even if the code asked it to.
                Action: 'events:PutEvents'
                Resource: !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:events:${AWS::Region}:${AWS::AccountId}:event-bus/default'
              - Effect: Allow
                Action: ['logs:CreateLogStream', 'logs:PutLogEvents']
                Resource:
                  - !Sub '${ChangeRecordLogGroup.Arn}'
                  - !Sub '${ChangeRecordLogGroup.Arn}:*'
                  - !Sub '${DossierLogGroup.Arn}'
                  - !Sub '${DossierLogGroup.Arn}:*'
              - Effect: Allow
                Action: ['logs:CreateLogGroup', 'logs:CreateLogStream', 'logs:PutLogEvents']
                Resource: !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:logs:${AWS::Region}:${AWS::AccountId}:log-group:/aws/lambda/platform-response*'
              - !If
                - HasAlerting
                - Effect: Allow
                  Action: 'sns:Publish'
                  Resource: !If
                    - MetaLowUrgency
                    - [!Ref AlertTopicArn, !Ref LowUrgencyTopicArn]
                    - [!Ref AlertTopicArn]
                - !Ref AWS::NoValue
              # Publishing to an ENCRYPTED cross-account topic needs KMS on
              # BOTH sides: the key policy must admit this role, and this role
              # must be allowed to call KMS. Having only the first produces
              # KMSAccessDenied with a key policy that visibly contains the
              # role — which reads as though the policy is wrong when it is
              # complete.
              #
              # Scoped by kms:ViaService rather than by key ARN. The alerting
              # key lives in another account and its id is not known here, and
              # ViaService is tighter than a wildcard anyway: it permits KMS
              # calls made THROUGH SNS and nothing else, so this grant cannot
              # be used to decrypt anything the role reaches directly.
              - Effect: Allow
                Action: ['kms:GenerateDataKey*', 'kms:Decrypt']
                Resource: '*'
                Condition:
                  StringEquals:
                    'kms:ViaService': !Sub 'sns.${AWS::Region}.amazonaws.com'

        - PolicyName: PermittedRemediations
          PolicyDocument:
            Version: '2012-10-17'
            Statement:
              # The four permitted actions, and only those.
              #
              # ecs:StopTask is task cycling. ecs:UpdateService is scale-out —
              # which can also scale IN, and that is deliberate: a policy that
              # let the automation only increase capacity would prevent it ever
              # undoing its own change.
              - Effect: Allow
                Action: ['ecs:StopTask', 'ecs:UpdateService']
                Resource: '*'
                Condition:
                  StringEquals:
                    'aws:ResourceTag/platform-managed': 'true'
              # SendCommand is clear_log_files and restart_service. Scoped to
              # the one AWS document those use, so the role cannot run an
              # arbitrary SSM document — which would otherwise be a general
              # remote-execution grant wearing a remediation costume.
              - Effect: Allow
                Action: 'ssm:SendCommand'
                Resource:
                  - !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:ssm:${AWS::Region}::document/AWS-RunShellScript'
              - Effect: Allow
                Action: 'ssm:SendCommand'
                Resource: !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:ec2:${AWS::Region}:${AWS::AccountId}:instance/*'
                Condition:
                  StringEquals:
                    'aws:ResourceTag/platform-managed': 'true'

        - PolicyName: RefusalsEnforcedInIam
          PolicyDocument:
            Version: '2012-10-17'
            Statement:
              # Explicit denies for everything refused on 2026-09-18.
              #
              # Redundant against the Allow statements above, which do not grant
              # these — and that redundancy is the point. An explicit Deny cannot
              # be overridden by a later Allow, so adding a permission to this
              # role by mistake does not silently enable a refused action. The
              # decision survives the next person editing this file.
              - Sid: NeverTerminateOrDeregister
                Effect: Deny
                Action:
                  - 'ec2:TerminateInstances'
                  - 'ec2:StopInstances'
                  - 'elasticloadbalancing:DeregisterTargets'
                  - 'autoscaling:TerminateInstanceInAutoScalingGroup'
                  - 'autoscaling:DetachInstances'
                Resource: '*'
              - Sid: NeverTouchDatabases
                Effect: Deny
                Action:
                  # RDS failover was refused on duration, not on destruction.
                  # Storage expansion was refused because AWS does not permit
                  # shrinking allocated storage — the one genuinely
                  # irreversible action on the list.
                  - 'rds:RebootDBInstance'
                  - 'rds:FailoverDBCluster'
                  - 'rds:ModifyDBInstance'
                  - 'rds:PromoteReadReplica'
                  - 'rds:DeleteDBInstance'
                Resource: '*'
              - Sid: NeverDeleteMonitoring
                Effect: Deny
                Action:
                  - 'cloudwatch:DeleteAlarms'
                  - 'logs:DeleteLogGroup'
                  - 'config:DeleteConfigurationRecorder'
                Resource: '*'
      Tags:
        - { Key: platform-managed, Value: 'true' }

  # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # The engine
  # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  ResponseFunction:
    Type: AWS::Lambda::Function
    Properties:
      FunctionName: platform-response
      Runtime: python3.13
      Handler: engine.handler
      Role: !GetAtt ResponseRole.Arn
      # Long enough to gather, act, and sleep through a short settle period.
      # MAX_INLINE_SETTLE below caps how much of that is sleeping — anything
      # longer returns awaiting-settle rather than risking a timeout, because a
      # timeout mid-incident produces no dossier at all.
      Timeout: 300
      MemorySize: 512
      Code:
        S3Bucket: !Ref ArtifactBucket
        S3Key: !Ref ArtifactKey
      Environment:
        Variables:
          ENVIRONMENT_TIER: !Ref EnvironmentTier
          ACCOUNT_ID: !Ref AWS::AccountId
          HISTORY_TABLE: !Ref RemediationHistory
          KILL_SWITCH_PARAM: !Ref ResponseKillSwitch
          CHANGE_LOG_GROUP: !Ref ChangeRecordLogGroup
          DOSSIER_LOG_GROUP: !Ref DossierLogGroup
          # Stage 4 publishes the dossier to the tier-appropriate topic, the
          # same rule the workload alarms follow. A dev incident that
          # automation could not fix is worth reading; it is not worth a phone
          # call, and routing every engine escalation to the paging topic would
          # quietly undo the tier separation everywhere else in the platform.
          ALERT_TOPIC_ARN: !If
            - MetaLowUrgency
            - !Ref LowUrgencyTopicArn
            - !Ref AlertTopicArn
          # Always the low-urgency topic, regardless of tier. Used for the two
          # states that report a PLATFORM gap rather than an unhandled
          # incident: no-runbook (the alarm paged on its own) and
          # awaiting-settle (the sweep is about to revalidate). Paging twice for
          # one incident is how a notification rule gets written that then
          # swallows the real pages too.
          LOW_URGENCY_TOPIC_ARN: !Ref LowUrgencyTopicArn
          ESCALATION_VIA_BUS: !Ref EscalationViaBus
          MAX_INLINE_SETTLE: '120'
          REVALIDATION_ATTEMPTS: '3'
      Tags:
        - { Key: platform-managed, Value: 'true' }

  ResponseLogGroup:
    Type: AWS::Logs::LogGroup
    DeletionPolicy: Delete
    UpdateReplacePolicy: Delete
    Properties:
      LogGroupName: /aws/lambda/platform-response
      RetentionInDays: 90
      KmsKeyId: !If
        - UseDefaultLogsKey
        - !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:kms:${AWS::Region}:${AWS::AccountId}:alias/platform-logs'
        - !Ref LogsKeyArn

  # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # Trigger
  # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # Alarm state change, filtered to platform-auto alarms entering ALARM.
  #
  # The engine needs alarm_id, resource_type and resource_id, which this event
  # does not carry — it has the alarm NAME. The engine refuses to guess rather
  # than parsing them out, because the name is
  # platform-auto-RESOURCEID-ALARMID and both halves may contain dashes. A
  # small input transformer would be the obvious fix and would be the same
  # ambiguous parse in a different language.
  #
  # So the alarm TAGS carry them — the instrumentation Lambda already writes
  # platform-alarm-id — and B-031 covers wiring that lookup. Until then the
  # engine is invoked manually and by test, which is the right state for
  # something that can stop a container.
  AlarmStateChangeRule:
    Type: AWS::Events::Rule
    Properties:
      Name: platform-response-on-alarm
      Description: >-
        Platform alarms entering ALARM. DISABLED until B-031 wires the
        alarm-name-to-resource lookup — an enabled rule that invokes an engine
        which then refuses every event would fill the logs with exceptions and
        teach everyone to ignore them.
      EventPattern:
        source: ['aws.cloudwatch']
        detail-type: ['CloudWatch Alarm State Change']
        detail:
          state:
            value: ['ALARM']
      State: DISABLED
      Targets:
        - Id: response
          Arn: !GetAtt ResponseFunction.Arn

  # Revalidation sweep.
  #
  # ENABLED, while the alarm trigger above is disabled — which looks backwards
  # and is not. The settle table is clear_log_files 120s, restart_service 180s,
  # cycle_ecs_task 300s, scale_out 600s, default 300s, against an inline cap of
  # 120s. Every action but one settles above the cap, so "the engine acted and
  # cannot yet tell whether it worked" is the ordinary outcome of a remediation.
  #
  # Before this rule existed, that outcome was terminal: the engine parked
  # nothing, nothing revalidated, and nothing paged. The platform's normal
  # behaviour was to change something on a customer's resource and then never
  # look again or mention it. Disabling this would restore exactly that, and it
  # would do so silently, so it is enabled from the start and the engine is
  # gated by the kill switch and the trigger rule instead.
  #
  # Two minutes rather than five: the sweep only reads until something is due,
  # and the wait it adds lands on an incident that is already open.
  RevalidationSweepRule:
    Type: AWS::Events::Rule
    Properties:
      Name: platform-response-sweep
      Description: >-
        Revalidates remediations whose settle period has elapsed. Without it,
        every action that settles above MAX_INLINE_SETTLE — which is all but
        one — is never re-checked and never escalated.
      ScheduleExpression: 'rate(2 minutes)'
      State: ENABLED
      Targets:
        - Id: sweep
          Arn: !GetAtt ResponseFunction.Arn
          Input: '{"mode":"sweep"}'

  SweepInvokePermission:
    Type: AWS::Lambda::Permission
    Properties:
      FunctionName: !GetAtt ResponseFunction.Arn
      Action: lambda:InvokeFunction
      Principal: events.amazonaws.com
      SourceArn: !GetAtt RevalidationSweepRule.Arn

  # The sweep is now load-bearing: if it stops running, remediations park and
  # are never revalidated, and the failure is silent — which is the property
  # that makes it worth an alarm of its own rather than relying on the
  # function's Errors alarm.
  SweepStalledAlarm:
    Type: AWS::CloudWatch::Alarm
    Properties:
      AlarmName: platform-response-sweep-stalled
      AlarmDescription: >-
        The revalidation sweep has not invoked successfully for 15 minutes. Any
        remediation taken in that window has not been re-checked and will not
        page on its own. Check the platform-response-sweep rule and the
        platform-response function.
      Namespace: AWS/Events
      MetricName: Invocations
      Dimensions:
        - Name: RuleName
          Value: !Ref RevalidationSweepRule
      Statistic: Sum
      Period: 900
      EvaluationPeriods: 1
      Threshold: 1
      ComparisonOperator: LessThanThreshold
      # A rule that has stopped emitting reports no data at all, so missing
      # data must breach. The default would treat silence as health, which is
      # the precise failure this alarm exists to catch.
      TreatMissingData: breaching
      # Same shape as ResponseGapAlarm: AlertTopicArn is optional, and an
      # empty action list is rejected at create rather than ignored.
      AlarmActions: !If
        - MetaLowUrgency
        - [!Ref LowUrgencyTopicArn]
        - !If [HasAlerting, [!Ref AlertTopicArn], !Ref 'AWS::NoValue']
      # OK actions too, unusually. A stalled sweep is a condition somebody has
      # to go and fix, so the "it is running again" signal is the one that says
      # whether the fix worked.
      OKActions: !If
        - MetaLowUrgency
        - [!Ref LowUrgencyTopicArn]
        - !If [HasAlerting, [!Ref AlertTopicArn], !Ref 'AWS::NoValue']

  AlarmInvokePermission:
    Type: AWS::Lambda::Permission
    Properties:
      FunctionName: !GetAtt ResponseFunction.Arn
      Action: lambda:InvokeFunction
      Principal: events.amazonaws.com
      SourceArn: !GetAtt AlarmStateChangeRule.Arn

  # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # Automation document
  # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # Prompt 5.1 asks for the framework "as SSM Automation documents". ONE
  # document, driven by the catalog — not one per runbook, which is the
  # arrangement the data-driven design exists to avoid.
  #
  # It is a thin wrapper over the Lambda rather than the logic itself. The
  # staging, rails and dossier assembly are a few hundred lines of Python with
  # tests; expressing them as aws:executeScript steps would put untested code
  # in a document nobody can run locally, to satisfy the letter of "as SSM
  # Automation documents" while losing what makes it reviewable.
  #
  # The document earns its place regardless: it gives an operator a way to
  # invoke a runbook by hand, with the same rails, and it is what a future
  # OpsItem or Incident Manager response plan will target.
  ResponseAutomationDocument:
    Type: AWS::SSM::Document
    Properties:
      Name: PlatformRunbook
      DocumentType: Automation
      DocumentFormat: YAML
      TargetType: /
      Content:
        schemaVersion: '0.3'
        description: >-
          AltDigital four-stage runbook. Gathers, applies permitted
          remediations with every safety rail, revalidates between stages, and
          assembles the incident dossier. What it does for a given alarm is in
          runbooks/catalog.yaml, not in this document.
        assumeRole: !GetAtt ResponseRole.Arn
        parameters:
          AlarmName:
            type: String
            description: CloudWatch alarm that fired.
          AlarmId:
            type: String
            description: 06a alarm id, e.g. ec2-disk-high.
          ResourceType:
            type: String
            description: e.g. AWS::EC2::Instance
          ResourceId:
            type: String
            description: The resource the alarm is about.
        mainSteps:
          - name: runFourStageRunbook
            action: 'aws:invokeLambdaFunction'
            maxAttempts: 1
            # No retries, deliberately. Re-invoking the engine would re-run the
            # remediations, and "the fix did not fix, so try it again" is
            # precisely the behaviour the failed-attempt rail exists to stop.
            # The rails would catch it — this makes sure it never gets that far.
            timeoutSeconds: 300
            inputs:
              FunctionName: !Ref ResponseFunction
              Payload: |
                {
                  "alarm_name": "{{ AlarmName }}",
                  "alarm_id": "{{ AlarmId }}",
                  "resource_type": "{{ ResourceType }}",
                  "resource_id": "{{ ResourceId }}"
                }
            outputs:
              - Name: result
                Selector: $.Payload
                Type: String
      Tags:
        - { Key: platform-managed, Value: 'true' }

Outputs:

  FunctionName:
    Value: !Ref ResponseFunction

  KillSwitchParameter:
    Description: Change with scripts/response-kill-switch.sh, never via the stack
    Value: !Ref ResponseKillSwitch

  AutomationDocument:
    Value: !Ref ResponseAutomationDocument

  HistoryTable:
    Description: Circuit breaker and failed-attempt state
    Value: !Ref RemediationHistory

  TriggerState:
    Description: Alarm trigger is disabled until B-031
    Value: DISABLED
files.baseline/70-event-forwarding.yaml:
AWSTemplateFormatVersion: '2010-09-09'

Description: >-
  AltDigital Managed Platform — forwards everything that wants attention to the
  central routing bus in the Audit account. Part of the member baseline
  StackSet.

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# What this replaces
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Until now an alarm's destination was decided when the alarm was CREATED: the
# instrumentation Lambda put the paging ones on the alerts topic and everything
# else on the low-urgency topic, and recorded `pending_destination` for the
# three routing classes that had nowhere to go — jira_and_commercial,
# digest_and_jira and review_queue.
#
# Those alarms were real, evaluating, and heard by a topic that does not page
# and has no consumer. This is the other half: the events reach a router that
# knows what each class means.
#
# The alarm ACTIONS are unchanged and stay in place. The SNS path is the
# fallback for a broken router, and it is the reason a routing outage degrades
# the alert rather than silencing it.
#
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Forwarding a rule's own events back to itself
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# A rule that forwards to another bus can, if its pattern is wide enough, match
# the events it generates. None of the patterns below are wide — each names its
# detail-type — but the failure is worth stating because it is a loop that
# bills by the event and looks like a traffic spike rather than a bug.

Parameters:

  CentralBusArn:
    Type: String
    Description: >-
      The platform-alerts bus in the Audit account. An empty value disables
      forwarding entirely, which is the correct behaviour before the routing
      layer is deployed — see the Condition below.
    Default: ''

# No EnvironmentTier parameter, deliberately. Forwarding is tier-independent:
# every account sends everything, and the ROUTER decides what each tier does
# with it, reading the tier off the alarm's own platform-tier tag. Filtering
# here as well would put the same decision in two places — one of them in a
# template deployed per account, free to drift — and the failure mode of that
# is an account quietly forwarding nothing.

Conditions:
  # No bus, no rules. The alternative is rules that exist, show ENABLED and
  # deliver nothing, which is the state that taught us to write this Condition
  # — see the EventBridge notes in CLAUDE.md.
  HasBus: !Not [!Equals [!Ref CentralBusArn, '']]

Resources:

  # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # Delivery role
  # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # EventBridge cannot put events on another account's bus as a service
  # principal — it needs a role, and it needs iam:PassRole to use it.
  # Omitting the role does not fail at PutRule; it fails at PutTargets, leaving
  # a rule that shows ENABLED with no targets attached. That has already cost
  # an afternoon on this platform once.
  ForwardingRole:
    Type: AWS::IAM::Role
    Condition: HasBus
    Properties:
      RoleName: PlatformEventForwarding
      AssumeRolePolicyDocument:
        Version: '2012-10-17'
        Statement:
          - Effect: Allow
            Principal: { Service: events.amazonaws.com }
            Action: sts:AssumeRole
      Policies:
        - PolicyName: ForwardToCentralBus
          PolicyDocument:
            Version: '2012-10-17'
            Statement:
              - Effect: Allow
                Action: 'events:PutEvents'
                # Exactly one bus. A wildcard here would let anything that can
                # assume this role raise an incident on any bus in the
                # organization.
                Resource: !Ref CentralBusArn

  # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # Sources
  # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # design/06's diagram, one rule each. Separate rather than combined so that a
  # source producing nothing is visibly a rule with no invocations, rather than
  # a share of one rule's traffic that nobody can pick apart.

  AlarmForwarding:
    Type: AWS::Events::Rule
    Condition: HasBus
    Properties:
      Name: platform-forward-alarms
      Description: >-
        Platform-managed alarms changing state. The router reads the routing
        class off the alarm's own tags, so it needs no filtering here beyond
        excluding alarms the platform did not create.
      EventPattern:
        source: ['aws.cloudwatch']
        detail-type: ['CloudWatch Alarm State Change']
        detail:
          state:
            # OK as well as ALARM. Without it PagerDuty incidents raised by the
            # router never auto-resolve, and an on-call engineer closes by hand
            # every incident the platform recovered from on its own — which is
            # how people stop trusting auto-resolution and start closing
            # incidents without reading them.
            value: ['ALARM', 'OK']
      State: ENABLED
      Targets:
        - Id: central
          Arn: !Ref CentralBusArn
          RoleArn: !GetAtt ForwardingRole.Arn

  SecurityHubForwarding:
    Type: AWS::Events::Rule
    Condition: HasBus
    Properties:
      Name: platform-forward-securityhub
      EventPattern:
        source: ['aws.securityhub']
        detail-type: ['Security Hub Findings - Imported']
        detail:
          findings:
            Severity:
              # INFORMATIONAL and LOW are excluded at source rather than at the
              # router. They are the overwhelming majority of Security Hub
              # volume and they route to review in every tier, so forwarding
              # them buys a cross-account PutEvents charge per finding and a
              # review queue nobody can read.
              Label: ['CRITICAL', 'HIGH', 'MEDIUM']
      State: ENABLED
      Targets:
        - Id: central
          Arn: !Ref CentralBusArn
          RoleArn: !GetAtt ForwardingRole.Arn

  GuardDutyForwarding:
    Type: AWS::Events::Rule
    Condition: HasBus
    Properties:
      Name: platform-forward-guardduty
      EventPattern:
        source: ['aws.guardduty']
        detail-type: ['GuardDuty Finding']
        detail:
          severity:
            # Numeric, and a RANGE rather than a list: GuardDuty severities are
            # decimals (4.0, 5.3, 7.8) and a list of integers matches almost
            # nothing. Getting this wrong produces a rule that matches zero
            # events and looks exactly like an account with no findings.
            - numeric: ['>=', 4]
      State: ENABLED
      Targets:
        - Id: central
          Arn: !Ref CentralBusArn
          RoleArn: !GetAtt ForwardingRole.Arn

  ConfigForwarding:
    Type: AWS::Events::Rule
    Condition: HasBus
    Properties:
      Name: platform-forward-config
      EventPattern:
        source: ['aws.config']
        detail-type: ['Config Rules Compliance Change']
        detail:
          messageType: ['ComplianceChangeNotification']
          newEvaluationResult:
            complianceType: ['NON_COMPLIANT']
      State: ENABLED
      Targets:
        - Id: central
          Arn: !Ref CentralBusArn
          RoleArn: !GetAtt ForwardingRole.Arn

  # The response engine's dossier. Not an AWS source — the engine puts this on
  # the member account's default bus itself, and this forwards it on.
  #
  # It is the reason prompt 5.3 says the payload must carry "the full dossier,
  # not just the alarm name": the raw alarm above pages immediately with
  # nothing, and this arrives minutes later with everything the engine learned.
  # The router gives both the same dedup key, so the second updates the first
  # rather than paging again.
  # design 08's six deployment event types, forwarded for reconciliation
  # (prompt 8.2). CloudTrail management events reach the account's default bus
  # already; this carries the deployment-shaped ones to the central bus where
  # the reconciliation engine stores them.
  #
  # The eventName list is narrow ON PURPOSE, and is the same list the capture
  # rule in change/10-reconciliation.yaml matches. Two filters for one decision
  # looks redundant and is not: this one decides what crosses an account
  # boundary and bills per event, and that one decides what is worth storing
  # for seven years. Widening either alone is visible; widening both by
  # accident is not.
  #
  # Volume is worth knowing before a busy tenant arrives. A team deploying
  # several times a day produces tens of events a day, which is nothing. A team
  # running CloudFormation in a loop, or an autoscaling group churning launch
  # template versions, could produce thousands — at which point the right
  # answer is a narrower list, not a bigger table.
  # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # Protected actions
  # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # design/03-identity-and-access.md, on the quorum-controlled actions:
  #
  #     Any attempt against these actions -- successful or denied -- pages
  #     immediately. A denied attempt is either confusion or something worse;
  #     both warrant knowing within minutes.
  #
  # containment/10-containment.yaml has the rule that declares them, listening
  # on the organization bus in Audit. Nothing put these events on that bus.
  #
  # So the control was inert for every member account in the estate. It could
  # only ever have fired for an action taken inside Audit itself -- which is
  # not where tenant keys, vaults or trails live. Found when a key deletion in
  # the sandbox produced no declaration, while the quorum reverse sweep caught
  # it. B-087.
  #
  # A SEPARATE rule from DeploymentForwarding rather than more event names in
  # that one. They answer to different designs (08 and 03), they page
  # differently, and a single pattern means every future edit to one is an edit
  # to the other -- which is how the deployment list quietly acquires a
  # security event, or how a narrowing for cost quietly drops a page.
  ProtectedActionForwarding:
    Type: AWS::Events::Rule
    Condition: HasBus
    Properties:
      Name: platform-forward-protected-actions
      Description: >-
        Quorum-controlled and audit-tampering actions. design 03's four, plus
        the reversible siblings design 07 wants declared. Successful or denied.
      EventPattern:
        source: ['aws.kms', 'aws.cloudtrail', 'aws.backup', 'aws.config',
                 'aws.organizations']
        detail-type: ['AWS API Call via CloudTrail']
        detail:
          eventName:
            # design 03's four quorum-controlled actions
            - ScheduleKeyDeletion
            - DeleteBackupVault
            - PutBackupVaultLockConfiguration
            - DeleteBackupVaultLockConfiguration
            - RemoveAccountFromOrganization
            - StopLogging
            - DeleteTrail
            - StopConfigurationRecorder
            - DeleteConfigurationRecorder
            # Reversible, and declared anyway. design 07 lists these alongside
            # the destructive ones: disabling a key or editing a trail is how
            # somebody tests whether anyone is watching before doing the
            # irreversible version.
            - DisableKey
            - UpdateTrail
            - DeleteRecoveryPoint
      State: ENABLED
      Targets:
        - Id: central
          Arn: !Ref CentralBusArn
          RoleArn: !GetAtt ForwardingRole.Arn

  DeploymentForwarding:
    Type: AWS::Events::Rule
    Condition: HasBus
    Properties:
      Name: platform-forward-deployments
      Description: >-
        Deployment events for change reconciliation. design 08, "What is
        captured as a deployment event".
      EventPattern:
        source: ['aws.sts', 'aws.ecs', 'aws.lambda', 'aws.cloudformation',
                 'aws.ec2', 'aws.rds']
        detail-type: ['AWS API Call via CloudTrail']
        detail:
          eventName:
            - AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity
            - RegisterTaskDefinition
            - UpdateService
            - CreateService
            - UpdateFunctionCode
            - UpdateFunctionConfiguration
            - PublishVersion
            - CreateStack
            - UpdateStack
            - ExecuteChangeSet
            - CreateLaunchTemplate
            - CreateLaunchTemplateVersion
            - ModifyLaunchTemplate
            - ModifyDBParameterGroup
            - ModifyDBInstance
            - ModifyDBCluster
      State: ENABLED
      Targets:
        - Id: central
          Arn: !Ref CentralBusArn
          RoleArn: !GetAtt ForwardingRole.Arn

  DossierForwarding:
    Type: AWS::Events::Rule
    Condition: HasBus
    Properties:
      Name: platform-forward-dossiers
      EventPattern:
        # platform.recovery is the restore workflow (prompt 6.1), which emits
        # the same dossier shape so that it needs no destination of its own.
        # Must stay in step with DossierRule in alerting/20-router.yaml: a
        # source forwarded here and not matched there lands in the review
        # queue, which has no consumer.
        source: ['platform.response', 'platform.recovery']
        detail-type: ['Platform Incident Dossier']
      State: ENABLED
      Targets:
        - Id: central
          Arn: !Ref CentralBusArn
          RoleArn: !GetAtt ForwardingRole.Arn

Outputs:
  ForwardingState:
    Value: !If [HasBus, 'forwarding', 'disabled-no-bus-configured']
  ForwardingRoleArn:
    Condition: HasBus
    Value: !GetAtt ForwardingRole.Arn
files.baseline/80-developer-boundary.yaml:
AWSTemplateFormatVersion: '2010-09-09'

Description: >-
  AltDigital Managed Platform — the permissions boundary every developer-created
  role must carry (prompt 10.1). Part of the member baseline. design 11's Layer 2.

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# "The layer most often forgotten"
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# design/11-developer-access.md calls it that, and explains why it is not
# optional:
#
#     A developer able to create IAM roles — which in dev they should be — can
#     otherwise create a role more privileged than themselves and pass it to a
#     service.
#
# That is the whole attack, and it needs no malice. A developer who cannot read
# a secret writes a Lambda that can, attaches AdministratorAccess to it because
# that is what the tutorial said, and invokes it. Every individual step is
# something they are permitted to do. The result is a principal that ignores
# every restriction on the person who created it.
#
# The permission set restricts the HUMAN. The boundary restricts what the human
# can BUILD. Without it, Layer 3 is a suggestion.
#
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# A boundary is a ceiling, not a grant
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# This policy gives nobody anything. A role's effective permissions are the
# INTERSECTION of its policies and its boundary, so `Allow *` here means "this
# boundary does not itself narrow anything" — the role still only has what its
# own policies grant.
#
# That is why the allow is broad and the denies are the content. Writing a
# careful allow-list here would be a second permission model to maintain
# alongside the permission sets, drifting quietly, and the first symptom would
# be a developer's legitimate role mysteriously failing.
#
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# It carries the same denies as Layer 1, and that duplication is deliberate
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# design 11: "The boundary carries the same denies as Layer 1."
#
# An SCP already denies these to every principal in the account, so repeating
# them looks redundant. It is not: an SCP applies to the ACCOUNT, and if the
# account is ever moved between OUs, or a policy is detached during an
# incident, the boundary is what still holds. Two independent statements of the
# same rule fail independently.

Resources:

  DeveloperBoundary:
    Type: AWS::IAM::ManagedPolicy
    # Retain. Roles reference a boundary by ARN, and deleting it while roles
    # still carry it leaves those roles unusable with an error that names a
    # policy nobody can find. An orphaned boundary costs nothing.
    DeletionPolicy: Retain
    UpdateReplacePolicy: Retain
    Properties:
      # A LITERAL, not a parameter, for two reasons.
      #
      # policies/scp/05-require-boundary.json names this exact ARN, so a
      # parameter was false flexibility: changing it would silently break the
      # SCP's requirement rather than reconfigure it.
      #
      # And cfn-guard evaluates statically. With !Ref here it sees
      # {"Ref": "BoundaryName"}, cannot resolve it, and the rule exempting
      # boundaries from IAM_NO_WILDCARD_ACTION_AND_RESOURCE never matches --
      # so the template would fail the guard for being unreadable rather than
      # pass it for being correct. Same reasoning as the session duration in
      # identity/00-commercial-readonly.yaml.
      ManagedPolicyName: PlatformDeveloperBoundary
      Description: >-
        Maximum permissions for any role a developer creates. Not a grant —
        effective permissions are the intersection of this and the role's own
        policies.
      PolicyDocument:
        Version: '2012-10-17'
        Statement:

          # The ceiling. See the header: this is what makes the boundary a
          # boundary rather than a second permission model.
          - Sid: CeilingNotGrant
            Effect: Allow
            Action: '*'
            Resource: '*'

          # design 11 Layer 1's list, repeated here so it survives the SCP
          # being detached or the account being re-parented.
          - Sid: NeverTheDetectiveControls
            Effect: Deny
            Action:
              - 'config:Delete*'
              - 'config:Stop*'
              - 'config:Put*'
              - 'cloudtrail:Stop*'
              - 'cloudtrail:Delete*'
              - 'cloudtrail:Update*'
              - 'cloudtrail:Put*'
              - 'guardduty:Delete*'
              - 'guardduty:Disassociate*'
              - 'guardduty:Update*'
              - 'securityhub:Delete*'
              - 'securityhub:Disable*'
              - 'securityhub:Update*'
              - 'ec2:DeleteFlowLogs'
            Resource: '*'

          - Sid: NeverTheDataProtection
            Effect: Deny
            Action:
              - 'kms:ScheduleKeyDeletion'
              - 'kms:DisableKey'
              - 'kms:PutKeyPolicy'
              - 'kms:DisableKeyRotation'
              - 'backup:Delete*'
              - 'backup:Put*'
              - 'backup:Update*'
              - 'logs:DeleteLogGroup'
              - 'logs:DeleteRetentionPolicy'
              - 'logs:DeleteDataProtectionPolicy'
              - 'logs:PutDataProtectionPolicy'
            Resource: '*'

          # A role created by a developer must not be able to touch the
          # platform's own identities -- including, recursively, this boundary
          # and the roles that enforce it.
          - Sid: NeverThePlatformIdentities
            Effect: Deny
            Action:
              - 'iam:*'
            Resource:
              - !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:iam::${AWS::AccountId}:role/Platform*'
              - !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:iam::${AWS::AccountId}:role/OrganizationAccountAccessRole'
              - !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:iam::${AWS::AccountId}:role/stacksets-exec-*'
              - !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:iam::${AWS::AccountId}:policy/PlatformDeveloperBoundary'

          # THE recursion guard, and the reason the boundary is not merely a
          # copy of the SCP.
          #
          # Without this, a role created with the boundary can create ANOTHER
          # role without one -- or with a boundary it wrote itself -- and the
          # ceiling is escaped in one hop. The SCP denies unbounded creation
          # account-wide, so this is the second independent statement of it;
          # if the SCP is ever detached, this is what still holds.
          - Sid: BoundedRolesMayOnlyCreateBoundedRoles
            Effect: Deny
            Action:
              - 'iam:CreateRole'
              - 'iam:PutRolePolicy'
              - 'iam:AttachRolePolicy'
            Resource: '*'
            Condition:
              StringNotEquals:
                'iam:PermissionsBoundary': !Sub
                  'arn:${AWS::Partition}:iam::${AWS::AccountId}:policy/PlatformDeveloperBoundary'

          # Removing your own ceiling is the other one-hop escape.
          - Sid: NeverRemoveABoundary
            Effect: Deny
            Action:
              - 'iam:DeleteRolePermissionsBoundary'
              - 'iam:DeleteUserPermissionsBoundary'
            Resource: '*'

          - Sid: NeverLeaveTheOrganization
            Effect: Deny
            Action:
              - 'organizations:LeaveOrganization'
            Resource: '*'

Outputs:

  BoundaryArn:
    Description: >-
      Pass to developer role creation. The SCP denies iam:CreateRole without it.
    Value: !Ref DeveloperBoundary
    Export:
      Name: !Sub '${AWS::StackName}-DeveloperBoundaryArn'

  BoundaryName:
    Description: Must match policies/scp/05-require-boundary.json.
    Value: PlatformDeveloperBoundary
files.baseline/90-verification-reader.yaml:
AWSTemplateFormatVersion: '2010-09-09'

Description: >-
  AltDigital Managed Platform — a read-only role the verification sweep can
  assume to answer two of design 13's nine checks from inside a member account.
  Part of the member baseline StackSet. B-112.

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Why this exists
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Three of design 13's verification checks need to read state INSIDE a tenant's
# accounts. `provisioning/src/verify.py` runs outside them, holds no role in a
# member account, and reported all three as `undeterminable` — which blocks
# go-live. Correct, and useless: the sweep could never clear for any tenant no
# matter how healthy, so the gate was permanently shut rather than selective.
#
# Two of the three are genuine reads and this role serves them:
#
#   canary running and passing        synthetics, last run result
#   backup policy and recovery point  backup, plans and recovery points
#
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The third check is NOT served by this role, deliberately
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Decided with Jamie, 2026-09-22.
#
# B-112 originally asked this role to also carry "the guardrail harness against
# these accounts". It cannot, and it should not.
#
# `scripts/test-guardrails.sh` proves SCPs work by ATTEMPTING DENIED ACTIONS
# with an administrator. It creates IAM roles, KMS keys, backup vaults and EBS
# volumes, and its own header says it requires credentials in the management
# account. A read-only role cannot run it, and giving the sweep what it needs
# would mean a scheduled job holding admin in every tenant account in the
# estate — the exact thing B-112 said it wanted to avoid.
#
# It would also mean creating test IAM roles and KMS keys inside a client's
# account as a condition of their go-live.
#
# The deeper objection is that it is the wrong check. SCPs attach to OUs, not
# to accounts. Running the harness for forty accounts in one OU tests the same
# policy forty times and learns nothing after the first. What is true PER
# ACCOUNT is narrower and is a genuine read: is this account under the OU we
# believe it is, and are the expected policies attached to that OU?
#
# So the harness stays the per-OU exercise it already is, and the per-tenant
# check became an inheritance assertion in `verify.py`, which reads
# Organizations and needs nothing in the member account at all.
#
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Why not OrganizationAccountAccessRole
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# It exists in every member account and would work today. It is also
# administrative. A sweep that runs on a schedule should not hold admin in
# every tenant account in the estate in order to find out whether a canary
# passed, and a role that can do anything gives an auditor no way to bound what
# a scheduled job did.

Parameters:

  ToolingAccountId:
    Type: String
    Default: ''
    AllowedPattern: '^$|^[0-9]{12}$'
    Description: >-
      The Platform Tooling account, which is where the verification sweep
      runs.

      Empty creates nothing. That is the correct state before the provisioning
      stack exists — B-110 records that `provisioning/` has no CloudFormation
      at all and the saga has only ever run locally, so there is currently no
      principal to trust. A role trusting an account with no caller in it is a
      standing grant nobody is using, which is worse than its absence because
      it reads as deliberate.

Conditions:
  # No tooling account, no role. Same shape as the CentralBusArn condition in
  # 70-event-forwarding: an empty parameter disables the resource rather than
  # creating one that exists, reads as configured, and serves nobody.
  HasTooling: !Not [!Equals [!Ref ToolingAccountId, '']]

Resources:

  VerificationReaderRole:
    Type: AWS::IAM::Role
    Condition: HasTooling
    Properties:
      RoleName: PlatformVerificationReader
      Description: >-
        Read-only. Assumed by the provisioning verification sweep in the
        Platform Tooling account to answer two of design 13's checks. B-112.
      MaxSessionDuration: 3600
      AssumeRolePolicyDocument:
        Version: '2012-10-17'
        Statement:
          - Effect: Allow
            Principal:
              AWS: !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:iam::${ToolingAccountId}:root'
            Action: sts:AssumeRole
            Condition:
              # Naming the account alone would let ANY principal in tooling
              # assume this, which is most of the tooling account's own
              # automation. The sweep is the only legitimate caller.
              #
              # A pattern rather than an exact role ARN because the
              # verification function is not deployed yet (B-110), so there is
              # no ARN to name. The pattern is still narrow: SCP 03 governs
              # who may create a role named Platform*, so the set of principals
              # that can ever match this is controlled rather than open.
              #
              # Replace with the exact function role ARN once the provisioning
              # stack exists. A pattern that could have been an ARN is a
              # standing exception nobody revisits.
              ArnLike:
                'aws:PrincipalArn': !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:iam::${ToolingAccountId}:role/PlatformVerification*'
      Policies:
        - PolicyName: VerificationReads
          PolicyDocument:
            Version: '2012-10-17'
            Statement:

              # --- check 3: the canary is running and passing ---------------
              #
              # DescribeCanariesLastRun is the check almost exactly: it returns
              # each canary's most recent run and its state. GetCanaryRuns is
              # here because "passing" is a question about a RUN OF RUNS — one
              # green run after four red ones is not a passing canary, and the
              # sweep should be able to see that rather than reading the last
              # result and calling it health.
              - Sid: ReadCanaryState
                Effect: Allow
                Action:
                  - synthetics:DescribeCanaries
                  - synthetics:DescribeCanariesLastRun
                Resource: '*'
                # Both are list operations and admit no resource ARN. The
                # actions are enumerated, which is what the guard rule asks
                # for, and neither can mutate or read anything beyond canary
                # metadata.

              - Sid: ReadCanaryRuns
                Effect: Allow
                Action: synthetics:GetCanaryRuns
                Resource: !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:synthetics:*:${AWS::AccountId}:canary:*'

              # --- check 5: backup policy attached, first recovery point ----
              #
              # Two halves, and the check is only satisfied by both. A plan
              # with no recovery point is a policy that has never run, which
              # looks identical to a healthy one in every console view that
              # shows configuration rather than outcome.
              - Sid: ReadBackupConfiguration
                Effect: Allow
                Action:
                  - backup:ListBackupPlans
                  - backup:ListBackupVaults
                  - backup:GetBackupPlan
                  - backup:ListBackupSelections
                Resource: '*'

              - Sid: ReadRecoveryPoints
                Effect: Allow
                Action: backup:ListRecoveryPointsByBackupVault
                Resource: !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:backup:*:${AWS::AccountId}:backup-vault:platform-backup-*'
                # Scoped to the platform's own vault naming
                # (recovery/30-backup-policy.yaml creates
                # platform-backup-<tier>). A tenant's own vaults are not the
                # platform's business and the sweep has no reason to enumerate
                # what is in them.

      Tags:
        # CLAUDE.md hard rule, Jamie 2026-09-22: everything the platform builds
        # carries this. It is what tells the router at alarm time that a
        # resource is AltDigital's to answer for rather than the application
        # team's. B-127.
        - Key: platform-layer
          Value: infrastructure
        - Key: platform-managed
          Value: 'true'

Outputs:

  VerificationReaderRoleArn:
    Condition: HasTooling
    Description: >-
      The ARN the verification sweep assumes. Read by provisioning/src/verify.py
      once the provisioning stack exists.
    Value: !GetAtt VerificationReaderRole.Arn
    Export:
      Name: !Sub '${AWS::StackName}-VerificationReaderRoleArn'
files.canaries/00-canary-artifacts.yaml:
AWSTemplateFormatVersion: '2010-09-09'

Description: >-
  AltDigital Managed Platform — one canary artifacts bucket per account, shared
  by every canary deployed into it. Deploy once per account, before any canary.

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Why this is a separate stack, and separate from the canaries themselves
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# It was a resource inside canaries/10-canary.yaml until 2026-09-18, when the
# first deployment failed on the canary runtime version and could not then be
# retried. The sequence is worth recording because it applies to any bucket a
# template creates:
#
#   1. Stack create fails on an unrelated resource.
#   2. Rollback runs. The bucket carries DeletionPolicy: Retain, so it stays.
#   3. Every retry fails AWS::EarlyValidation::ResourceExistenceCheck, because
#      the bucket it wants to create already exists.
#
# The stack is now unretryable and the error names neither the bucket nor the
# retain policy — it says "Validation failed with 1 error(s)", with no resource
# events at all, because the failure happens before provisioning starts. Across
# a StackSet that is one poisoned account per failed rollout, each needing a
# manual bucket deletion before it can be retried.
#
# Dropping Retain is not the fix. CloudFormation cannot delete a non-empty
# bucket, so the stack would then fail on DELETE instead of on CREATE — the same
# trap moved to the other end.
#
# The fix is that the bucket outlives the canaries. One per account, created
# once, shared by every canary through a prefix. Canary stacks come and go as
# tenant services come and go; the bucket does not, so its lifecycle stops
# interacting with theirs.
#
# It is also just better: an account with six monitored services had six buckets
# under the old arrangement, for no reason anybody could state.

Parameters:
  LogsKeyArn:
    Type: String
    Default: ''
    Description: >-
      Defaults to the platform storage key alias in this account.

Conditions:
  UseDefaultKey: !Equals [!Ref LogsKeyArn, '']

Resources:

  CanaryArtifacts:
    Type: AWS::S3::Bucket
    # Retain is correct HERE, where it was wrong in the canary stack. This stack
    # holds one resource and will not fail partway through creating it, so the
    # retry trap above cannot arise; and on deliberate teardown the run
    # artifacts of a service being decommissioned are the thing most likely to
    # be wanted afterwards.
    DeletionPolicy: Retain
    UpdateReplacePolicy: Retain
    Properties:
      BucketName: !Sub 'altdig-canary-artifacts-${AWS::AccountId}-${AWS::Region}'
      PublicAccessBlockConfiguration:
        BlockPublicAcls: true
        BlockPublicPolicy: true
        IgnorePublicAcls: true
        RestrictPublicBuckets: true
      BucketEncryption:
        ServerSideEncryptionConfiguration:
          - ServerSideEncryptionByDefault:
              SSEAlgorithm: aws:kms
              KMSMasterKeyID: !If
                - UseDefaultKey
                - !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:kms:${AWS::Region}:${AWS::AccountId}:alias/platform-storage'
                - !Ref LogsKeyArn
            BucketKeyEnabled: true
      VersioningConfiguration:
        Status: Enabled
      LifecycleConfiguration:
        Rules:
          # Screenshots and HAR files are a copy of whatever the canary saw,
          # including any authenticated page it reached. Useful for triage for
          # about as long as an incident stays open; a liability indefinitely.
          - Id: expire-run-artifacts
            Status: Enabled
            ExpirationInDays: 30
            NoncurrentVersionExpirationInDays: 7
            AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload:
              DaysAfterInitiation: 7

  CanaryArtifactsPolicy:
    Type: AWS::S3::BucketPolicy
    Properties:
      Bucket: !Ref CanaryArtifacts
      PolicyDocument:
        Version: '2012-10-17'
        Statement:
          - Sid: DenyInsecureTransport
            Effect: Deny
            Principal: '*'
            Action: 's3:*'
            Resource:
              - !GetAtt CanaryArtifacts.Arn
              - !Sub '${CanaryArtifacts.Arn}/*'
            Condition:
              Bool: { 'aws:SecureTransport': 'false' }

Outputs:
  BucketName:
    Description: 'Pass to canaries/10-canary.yaml as ArtifactsBucketName.'
    Value: !Ref CanaryArtifacts
    Export:
      Name: !Sub '${AWS::StackName}-BucketName'
files.canaries/10-canary.yaml:
AWSTemplateFormatVersion: '2010-09-09'

Description: >-
  AltDigital Managed Platform — synthetic monitoring. One canary per tenant
  service, run either by CloudWatch Synthetics or by a Fargate task wrapping an
  existing Playwright suite. Both publish the same metrics, so the alarms below
  are defined once and apply to either.

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Why one template with a runner switch, rather than two templates
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Prompt 4.3 requires the Fargate runner to publish "on the same metric names,
