                {
                  "And": [
                    { "Variable": "$.mode", "IsPresent": true },
                    { "Variable": "$.mode", "StringEquals": "test" }
                  ],
                  "Next": "Teardown"
                }
              ],
              "Default": "Done"
            },

            "Teardown": {
              "Type": "Task",
              "Comment": "Removes only what this execution created, proven by a tag this workflow applied and enforced again by the role's condition key. Anything it cannot prove it created is reported as an orphan and left alone.",
              "Resource": "${TeardownArn}",
              "Parameters": {
                "execution_id.$": "$$.Execution.Name",
                "state.$": "$"
              },
              "ResultPath": "$.teardown",
              "Retry": [
                {
                  "ErrorEquals": ["Lambda.ServiceException", "Lambda.AWSLambdaException", "Lambda.SdkClientException", "Lambda.TooManyRequestsException"],
                  "IntervalSeconds": 5, "MaxAttempts": 3, "BackoffRate": 2
                }
              ],
              "Catch": [
                { "ErrorEquals": ["States.ALL"], "ResultPath": "$.teardownError", "Next": "TeardownFailed" }
              ],
              "Next": "Done"
            },

            "TeardownFailed": {
              "Type": "Fail",
              "Comment": "teardown.py handles its own expected failures and returns an orphan report, so reaching here means something unhandled. A restored copy of tenant data may still be running; that needs a human, and a failed execution is how it becomes visible in the console alongside the record.",
              "Error": "TeardownFailed",
              "Cause": "Test-mode teardown failed unexpectedly. A restored resource may still exist; it carries platform-restore-execution with this execution's id."
            },

            "Done": {
              "Type": "Succeed",
              "Comment": "The RECORD carries the verdict, not the execution status. A restore that failed still succeeded at reporting that it failed, and the dossier is what routes to a human. Marking the execution failed as well would raise a second, unrelated signal about one event - the shape of B-041."
            }
          }
        }

Outputs:
  StateMachineArn:
    Description: 'Pass to recovery/20-restore-schedule.yaml.'
    Value: !Ref RestoreStateMachine
    Export:
      Name: !Sub '${AWS::StackName}-StateMachineArn'
  RestoreExecutionRoleArn:
    Value: !GetAtt RestoreExecutionRole.Arn
  HasSource:
    Description: >-
      Whether this account has anything to restore. "none" is expected until
      backup plans exist — B-043.
    Value: !Ref SourceResourceArn
files.recovery/20-restore-schedule.yaml:
AWSTemplateFormatVersion: '2010-09-09'

Description: >-
  AltDigital Managed Platform — monthly restore test scheduling (prompt 6.2).
  Starts recovery/10-restore-workflow.yaml's state machine in TEST mode once a
  month. The duration thresholds and the trend warning are evaluated by the
  workflow itself and live with it; see the notes below.

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Where the two threshold tiers actually live
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Prompt 6.2 asks for "two-tier threshold alerting on restore duration —
# warning: Jira ticket with owner and due date, email, no page; breach:
# PagerDuty page."
#
# Those thresholds are NOT in this template. They are parameters of
# 10-restore-workflow.yaml, because the thing that evaluates them is the record
# step inside the workflow, and a threshold configured in one stack and consumed
# by a Lambda in another is a value that drifts silently the first time only one
# of the two is updated.
#
# What evaluates them, and how they reach a human:
#
#   warning  ->  the run declares routing class `digest_and_jira`, so the
#                router raises a ticket intent and includes the run in the
#                digest email. No page. That IS 6.2's warning tier.
#   breach   ->  the run declares NOTHING, so the router applies the account's
#                tier default from design/06a — which pages in prod. That is
#                6.2's breach tier, reached through the one routing layer.
#
# Prompt 6.2 says "DO NOT build a second routing path", and this template
# builds none. There is no SNS topic here, no PagerDuty client, no Jira client
# and — after the rewrite described below — no CloudWatch alarm either. This
# template schedules; the workflow decides and reports.
#
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Why the duration TREND is not a CloudWatch alarm
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# It was, and CloudWatch refused it. An alarm whose period is an hour or more
# must satisfy EvaluationPeriods x Period <= 604800 seconds, so the longest
# window any such alarm can examine is ONE WEEK. The restore test runs MONTHLY,
# so every alarm over its metrics would look at an empty window three weeks in
# four — permanently breaching or permanently blind depending on
# TreatMissingData, and both of those are worse than not having the alarm.
#
# Found by deploying. The stack rolled back with "Metrics cannot be checked
# across more than a week (EvaluationPeriods * Period must be <= 604800)",
# which names the constraint but not the reason it bites here. B-050.
#
# So the trend warning is raised by the workflow itself, at the moment it
# records, where the projection is already in hand: a run that is trending at
# the RTO declares `digest_and_jira` instead of `digest`, and the router turns
# that into a dated ticket and a digest line. The threshold lives with its
# consumer in 10-restore-workflow.yaml as TrendWarningMonths, for the same
# reason the duration percentages do.
#
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Why breach does not simply say "pagerduty"
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# It would be one word and it would be wrong. B-041: two places reduced 06a's
# five routing classes to a boolean, picked the wrong half, and produced five
# false pages that took a day to trace. The lesson recorded there is that a
# component deciding for itself whether something pages is a component that can
# be quietly wrong about it.
#
# So the workflow may DOWNGRADE (declare a non-paging class, with its reason
# recorded) and may never ESCALATE. Escalation stays with the tier table in
# design/06a, in the router, where it is decided once. alerting/src/router.py
# enforces this — a declared paging class is refused and logged.
#
# The visible consequence, stated plainly: in a UAT account the tier default is
# not PagerDuty, so a duration BREACH in UAT tickets rather than pages.
# design/14-environment-tiers.md line 84 is explicit that UAT has "no page
# routing", and where 6.2 and 14 disagree the tier wins. Recorded as a
# deviation in docs/deviations.md.

Parameters:

  StateMachineArn:
    Type: String
    Description: >-
      From 10-restore-workflow.yaml's StateMachineArn output. Passed rather
      than imported: an Export cannot be changed while anything imports it,
      which would freeze the workflow template against this one.

  EnvironmentTier:
    Type: String
    Default: uat
    AllowedValues: [dev, test, uat, prod]
    Description: >-
      design/14-environment-tiers.md line 85: restore testing is Yes for uat
      and prod, No for dev and test. This template should not be deployed to a
      dev or test account — there is nothing wrong with the workflow being
      there, but a schedule there tests nothing and bills for it.

      The default is uat rather than dev, unlike every other template in this
      repository, because uat is the lowest tier where this belongs at all.

  ScheduleExpression:
    Type: String
    Default: 'cron(0 15 ? * 2#2 *)'
    Description: >-
      Monthly. Default is the second Tuesday at 15:00 UTC — 10:00 US Central.

      The time of day is the interesting part. design/14-environment-tiers.md
      line 211 requires restore testing to fall INSIDE the HOOP: "Must not
      collide with a turndown window; schedule inside the HOOP". A restore test
      scheduled at 03:00 into a UAT account whose HOOP is business hours runs
      against a turned-down environment, and the obvious out-of-hours default
      would have walked straight into that.

      15:00 UTC is inside a weekday business-hours HOOP for a US tenant. It is
      NOT validated against the tenant's actual HOOP, because HOOPs do not
      exist yet — they are phase 13 (prompt 13.x), and open-items.md V11 tracks
      the validation. Until then this is a sensible default, not a checked one.
      B-046.

      Second Tuesday rather than the 1st: month-end and month-start are when
      finance and reporting jobs run, and a restore test competing with them
      measures the contention rather than the restore.

  FlexibleWindowMinutes:
    Type: Number
    Default: 60
    MinValue: 1
    MaxValue: 1440
    Description: >-
      Jitter. Every account restoring at the same instant contends on the same
      regional Backup and EBS APIs, and the resulting slowdown shows up as
      every account's restore getting slower at once — which is
      indistinguishable from the creep this phase exists to detect, and would
      be read as real.

  ScheduleEnabled:
    Type: String
    Default: 'ENABLED'
    AllowedValues: ['ENABLED', 'DISABLED']
    Description: >-
      A restore test creates a resource and costs money. This is the switch that
      stops it per account without a stack delete.

Resources:

  # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # The schedule
  # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  SchedulerRole:
    Type: AWS::IAM::Role
    Properties:
      RoleName: PlatformRestoreScheduler
      AssumeRolePolicyDocument:
        Version: '2012-10-17'
        Statement:
          - Effect: Allow
            Principal: { Service: scheduler.amazonaws.com }
            Action: sts:AssumeRole
            Condition:
              StringEquals:
                # Without this, any EventBridge Scheduler in any AWS account
                # that can name this role's ARN can assume it — the confused
                # deputy the service-principal trust policy invites.
                'aws:SourceAccount': !Ref AWS::AccountId
      Policies:
        - PolicyName: StartRestoreTest
          PolicyDocument:
            Version: '2012-10-17'
            Statement:
              - Effect: Allow
                Action: 'states:StartExecution'
                # Exactly one state machine. This role can start a restore
                # test and can do nothing else at all.
                Resource: !Ref StateMachineArn

  MonthlyRestoreTest:
    Type: AWS::Scheduler::Schedule
    Properties:
      Name: platform-restore-test-monthly
      Description: !Sub >-
        Prompt 6.2 — monthly restore test in TEST mode, ${EnvironmentTier} tier.
        Starts the same state machine a real recovery uses (P4). Duration
        thresholds and the trend warning are evaluated by the workflow, not
        here.
      State: !Ref ScheduleEnabled
      ScheduleExpression: !Ref ScheduleExpression
      # The account's own clock, not UTC, so that a HOOP expressed in local
      # business hours and a schedule expressed against it do not drift apart
      # twice a year when daylight saving moves one and not the other.
      ScheduleExpressionTimezone: America/Chicago
      FlexibleTimeWindow:
        Mode: FLEXIBLE
        MaximumWindowInMinutes: !Ref FlexibleWindowMinutes
      Target:
        Arn: !Ref StateMachineArn
        RoleArn: !GetAtt SchedulerRole.Arn
        # mode is the whole of P4's parameterisation. A real recovery starts
        # the SAME state machine with mode: recovery, by hand, from the runbook.
        Input: '{"mode": "test"}'
        RetryPolicy:
          # One retry. A restore test that could not be STARTED is worth trying
          # again; one that started and failed must not be started a second
          # time, because the second run would restore from the same recovery
          # point into the same target while the first attempt's resource may
          # still exist.
          MaximumRetryAttempts: 1
          MaximumEventAgeInSeconds: 3600

Outputs:
  ScheduleName:
    Value: !Ref MonthlyRestoreTest
  ScheduleState:
    Value: !Ref ScheduleEnabled
  ThresholdNote:
    Description: >-
      Where the duration thresholds stand.
    Value: >-
      Warning 50% / breach 80% of RTO - decided 2026-09-18, open-items.md B3.
      The TREND notice period was not part of B3 and is still unset; records
      flag it separately as warn_months_is_placeholder.
files.recovery/30-backup-policy.yaml:
AWSTemplateFormatVersion: '2010-09-09'

Description: >-
  AltDigital Managed Platform — the backup vault a member account writes to,
  and the plans that fill it. design 05. Deploys to each member account.

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# What design 05 specifies, and what this is
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 05 "Backup architecture":
#
#   AWS Backup, driven centrally from the Organization via backup policies
#   pushed down to the Members OU. Coverage is enforced by policy, not by
#   hoping each account configured it correctly.
#
# That sentence describes TWO things, and conflating them is the mistake this
# template exists to avoid. The Organization backup POLICY (in org/) decides
# which resources are selected and on what schedule, and it is pushed down so
# that a member account cannot opt out. This template creates what that policy
# needs to exist in the account: a local vault, and the copy destination.
#
# Splitting them this way is not tidiness. An Organization policy that selects
# resources in an account with no vault produces backup jobs that fail, one per
# resource per schedule, forever -- and the failure is per-job rather than
# per-account, so it reads as a resource problem rather than a missing vault.
#
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The 2-hour RPO is the sharper constraint
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 05: "Standard daily snapshots do not meet this."
#
#   RDS / Aurora   continuous backup with point-in-time recovery
#   DynamoDB       point-in-time recovery
#   S3             versioning + cross-region replication
#   EBS / EC2      snapshot every 2 hours, or replication
#   EFS            AWS Backup continuous where supported
#
# Continuous backup is a PROPERTY OF THE RULE (`EnableContinuousBackup`), not a
# frequency, and it is what actually delivers a 2-hour RPO for the database
# types. The 2-hourly schedule below covers the types where continuous backup
# is unavailable, which is EBS and EC2.
#
# A single 2-hourly snapshot plan applied to everything would cost twelve times
# a daily plan on resources that gain nothing from it, which is how a
# reasonable RPO turns into an unreasonable bill.
#
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Vault Lock, and why the delay matters
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 05: "Vault Lock enabled — a compromised member account cannot destroy its own
# backups. This is the ransomware answer, and auditors ask about it directly."
#
# Vault Lock in COMPLIANCE mode is irreversible. Not difficult to reverse --
# irreversible, by AWS, including by AWS support, for the life of the vault.
# A wrong retention value locked in compliance mode is permanent.
#
# So `ChangeableForDays` is set and non-zero. During that grace period the lock
# is in governance mode and can be corrected; after it, compliance. 05 asks for
# the protection and does not specify the grace period, and three days is short
# enough to be meaningfully locked and long enough that a mistake discovered on
# the Monday after a Friday deploy is still fixable.
#
# The vault itself is never deleted by automation. CLAUDE.md, and 05 puts vault
# deletion under quorum control (design 03) rather than under any schedule.

Parameters:

  BackupAccountId:
    Type: String
    Description: >-
      The separate backup account copies land in. design 05: "Backup copies
      land in a separate backup account." A copy in the same account as the
      resource is not a backup against account compromise, which is the threat
      Vault Lock exists for.

  EnvironmentTier:
    Type: String
    AllowedValues: [dev, test, uat, prod]
    Description: >-
      Drives retention and frequency. design 05 and design 14 split these
      across two axes: the POLICY follows the data (uat gets production's
      policy because its data is real) and the FREQUENCY follows resilience
      (uat is reduced because its infrastructure is not).

  RetentionDays:
    Type: Number
    Default: 35
    Description: >-
      Retention for the daily rule, in days. The full/reduced split comes from
      config/tiers.yaml (`backup_policy`), resolved by the deploy script rather
      than recomputed here.

  ContinuousRetentionDays:
    Type: Number
    Default: 35
    MaxValue: 35
    Description: >-
      Point-in-time recovery window. AWS caps continuous backup at 35 days and
      rejects anything higher, which is worth failing on at deploy time rather
      than in a backup job.

  CopyRetentionDays:
    Type: Number
    Default: 35
    Description: >-
      Retention for the CROSS-ACCOUNT COPY, which is a different number from
      local retention and must not be derived from it.

      The destination vault is under Vault Lock with its own
      `MinRetentionDays`, and a copy job specifying less is REJECTED. Found by
      deploying: a dev account keeping 7 days locally produced copy jobs that
      failed with "the retention specified in the job is not within the range
      specified for the target Backup Vault" -- one per resource per schedule,
      indefinitely, and per-job rather than per-account so it reads as a
      resource problem.

      Local retention is a cost decision the tier makes. Copy retention is a
      floor the locked destination sets, and the destination wins because it
      cannot be argued with after the lock hardens.

  SnapshotIntervalHours:
    Type: Number
    Default: 2
    Description: >-
      For resource types with no continuous backup — EBS and EC2. design 05's
      2-hour RPO. Raised for non-production tiers, where 05 permits "relaxed
      frequency".

  VaultLockChangeableDays:
    Type: Number
    Default: 3
    MinValue: 3
    Description: >-
      Grace period before the lock becomes irreversible. AWS enforces a
      three-day minimum. See the header: compliance mode cannot be undone by
      anyone, including AWS.

  KmsKeyArn:
    Type: String
    Default: ''
    Description: >-
      Customer-managed key for the LOCAL vault. Left empty uses the AWS Backup
      service-managed key, which is adequate for local recovery points and
      CANNOT participate in a cross-account copy -- the service key has no
      editable policy, so no other account can be granted its use.

      Supply a CMK in any account whose copies must reach the backup account.

Conditions:

  UseDefaultKey: !Equals [!Ref KmsKeyArn, '']
  IsProduction: !Equals [!Ref EnvironmentTier, prod]

Resources:

  BackupVault:
    Type: AWS::Backup::BackupVault
    # Retained on stack deletion, deliberately and non-negotiably. A vault
    # removed with its stack takes every recovery point with it, and the moment
    # somebody deletes a stack is not the moment to discover that.
    DeletionPolicy: Retain
    UpdateReplacePolicy: Retain
    Properties:
      BackupVaultName: !Sub 'platform-backup-${EnvironmentTier}'
      # Omitted when no CMK is supplied, rather than pointing at the default
      # key's alias. AWS Backup rejects an ALIAS arn here -- "Key Aliases are
      # not supported for this operation" -- and applies the AWS-managed key
      # itself when the property is absent. Found by deploying; the template
      # validated and the alias looked like every other key reference in this
      # repository.
      EncryptionKeyArn: !If
        - UseDefaultKey
        - !Ref 'AWS::NoValue'
        - !Ref KmsKeyArn
      LockConfiguration:
        MinRetentionDays: !Ref RetentionDays
        ChangeableForDays: !Ref VaultLockChangeableDays
      AccessPolicy:
        Version: '2012-10-17'
        Statement:
          # The ransomware answer, stated as a policy rather than assumed from
          # the lock. Vault Lock stops recovery points being deleted early;
          # this stops the vault's contents being tampered with by the local
          # account at all. design 05 is explicit that "a compromised member
          # account cannot destroy its own backups".
          - Sid: DenyLocalDeletion
            Effect: Deny
            Principal: '*'
            Action:
              - backup:DeleteRecoveryPoint
              - backup:UpdateRecoveryPointLifecycle
              - backup:PutBackupVaultAccessPolicy
              - backup:DeleteBackupVault
              - backup:DeleteBackupVaultAccessPolicy
              - backup:DeleteBackupVaultLockConfiguration
            Resource: '*'
            Condition:
              # Everything except the platform's own quorum-controlled role.
              # design 05 puts vault deletion and lock modification under
              # quorum (design 03), and PlatformQuorumExecutor is the only
              # principal that path produces.
              ArnNotLike:
                aws:PrincipalArn: !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:iam::${AWS::AccountId}:role/PlatformQuorumExecutor'

  BackupRole:
    Type: AWS::IAM::Role
    Properties:
      RoleName: PlatformBackupService
      AssumeRolePolicyDocument:
        Version: '2012-10-17'
        Statement:
          - Effect: Allow
            Principal: { Service: backup.amazonaws.com }
            Action: sts:AssumeRole
      ManagedPolicyArns:
        - !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:iam::aws:policy/service-role/AWSBackupServiceRolePolicyForBackup'
        # Restore is granted here because design 05's monthly test restores
        # into this same account. Withholding it would mean the restore
        # workflow could find a recovery point and not use it.
        - !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:iam::aws:policy/service-role/AWSBackupServiceRolePolicyForRestores'

  # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # Continuous — the types that can actually meet a 2-hour RPO
  # -------------------------------------------------------------------------

  ContinuousPlan:
    Type: AWS::Backup::BackupPlan
    Properties:
      BackupPlan:
        BackupPlanName: !Sub 'platform-continuous-${EnvironmentTier}'
        BackupPlanRule:
          - RuleName: continuous-pitr
            TargetBackupVault: !Ref BackupVault
            # Daily as the snapshot cadence; the RPO comes from
            # EnableContinuousBackup, which gives point-in-time recovery to
            # any second in the window rather than to the last snapshot.
            ScheduleExpression: 'cron(0 5 * * ? *)'
            EnableContinuousBackup: true
            StartWindowMinutes: 60
            CompletionWindowMinutes: 180
            Lifecycle:
              DeleteAfterDays: !Ref ContinuousRetentionDays
            # design 05: copies land in a separate backup account, because a
            # copy beside the original survives neither account compromise nor
            # a region event.
            CopyActions:
              - DestinationBackupVaultArn: !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:backup:${AWS::Region}:${BackupAccountId}:backup-vault:platform-backup-copies'
                Lifecycle:
                  # NOT RetentionDays. See CopyRetentionDays.
                  DeleteAfterDays: !Ref CopyRetentionDays

  ContinuousSelection:
    Type: AWS::Backup::BackupSelection
    Properties:
      BackupPlanId: !Ref ContinuousPlan
      BackupSelection:
        SelectionName: continuous-capable
        IamRoleArn: !GetAtt BackupRole.Arn
        # RDS, Aurora, DynamoDB and EFS. Selected by TYPE rather than by tag,
        # because design 05 says coverage is "enforced by policy, not by
        # hoping each account configured it correctly" -- and a tag is a thing
        # an account can forget to apply.
        Resources:
          - !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:rds:*:${AWS::AccountId}:db:*'
          - !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:rds:*:${AWS::AccountId}:cluster:*'
          - !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:dynamodb:*:${AWS::AccountId}:table/*'
          - !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:elasticfilesystem:*:${AWS::AccountId}:file-system/*'

  # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # Frequent snapshots — the types with no continuous option
  # -------------------------------------------------------------------------

  SnapshotPlan:
    Type: AWS::Backup::BackupPlan
    Properties:
      BackupPlan:
        BackupPlanName: !Sub 'platform-snapshot-${EnvironmentTier}'
        BackupPlanRule:
          - RuleName: frequent-snapshot
            TargetBackupVault: !Ref BackupVault
            ScheduleExpression: !Sub 'cron(0 0/${SnapshotIntervalHours} * * ? *)'
            # A start window shorter than the interval, so a job that has not
            # started by the time the next one is due is abandoned rather than
            # queued. Two overlapping snapshot jobs on one volume is how a
            # 2-hourly schedule becomes a backlog.
            StartWindowMinutes: 60
            CompletionWindowMinutes: 120
            Lifecycle:
              DeleteAfterDays: !Ref RetentionDays
            CopyActions:
              - DestinationBackupVaultArn: !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:backup:${AWS::Region}:${BackupAccountId}:backup-vault:platform-backup-copies'
                Lifecycle:
                  DeleteAfterDays: !Ref CopyRetentionDays

  SnapshotSelection:
    Type: AWS::Backup::BackupSelection
    Properties:
      BackupPlanId: !Ref SnapshotPlan
      BackupSelection:
        SelectionName: snapshot-only
        IamRoleArn: !GetAtt BackupRole.Arn
        Resources:
          - !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:ec2:*:${AWS::AccountId}:volume/*'
          - !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:ec2:*:${AWS::AccountId}:instance/*'

  # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # The two things design 05 says are "load-bearing and quietly breakable"
  # -------------------------------------------------------------------------

  BackupJobFailedAlarm:
    Type: AWS::CloudWatch::Alarm
    Condition: IsProduction
    Properties:
      AlarmName: platform-backup-job-failed
      AlarmDescription: >-
        A backup job failed. With a 2-hour RPO the window to notice is small,
        and a failed job is not retried into the next window - that window has
        its own job and its own resources.

        Most likely: a resource created without the tags or in a region the
        selection does not cover, or a vault access policy change. Check AWS
        Backup, Jobs, filtered to Failed.
      Namespace: AWS/Backup
      MetricName: NumberOfBackupJobsFailed
      Statistic: Sum
      Period: 3600
      EvaluationPeriods: 1
      Threshold: 0
      ComparisonOperator: GreaterThanThreshold
      # A period with no failures publishes nothing. Treating that as breaching
      # would alarm on a quiet account.
      TreatMissingData: notBreaching

Outputs:

  VaultName:
    Description: Where this account's recovery points land.
    Value: !Ref BackupVault

  VaultArn:
    Description: For the restore workflow's recovery point lookup.
    Value: !GetAtt BackupVault.BackupVaultArn

  LockChangeableUntilDays:
    Description: >-
      Days during which the Vault Lock can still be corrected. After this it is
      compliance mode and irreversible by anyone, including AWS.
    Value: !Ref VaultLockChangeableDays
files.recovery/40-backup-vault.yaml:
AWSTemplateFormatVersion: '2010-09-09'

Description: >-
  AltDigital Managed Platform — the copy destination. design 05: "Backup copies
  land in a separate backup account." Deploys ONLY to altdig-security-backup.

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Why a separate account at all
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# design 05: "Vault Lock enabled — a compromised member account cannot destroy
# its own backups. This is the ransomware answer, and auditors ask about it
# directly."
#
# Vault Lock alone does not answer that. A locked vault in the SAME account as
# the resource stops early deletion of recovery points, and leaves everything
# else about that account in the attacker's hands: the KMS key, the account's
# own quotas, the ability to fill the vault with garbage until it is useless.
# The separation is what makes the lock mean something.
#
# So this vault lives in an account whose only job is holding copies, whose
# only inbound permission is `backup:CopyIntoBackupVault`, and which no member
# account can reach in any other way.
#
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Compliance mode is irreversible, including by AWS
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Once `ChangeableForDays` elapses, the lock cannot be removed, shortened or
# altered by anyone -- not by this account's root, not by the Organization
# management account, not by AWS Support. The vault cannot be deleted until
# every recovery point in it has aged out under the retention it was locked
# with.
#
# That is the property that makes it worth having and the reason the grace
# period is not zero. Three days is AWS's minimum and is what is set: long
# enough that a wrong value deployed on a Friday is still correctable on the
# Monday, short enough that the window is not the answer to "is it locked".
#
# MinRetentionDays is the value that becomes permanent. It is deliberately set
# from a parameter with a conservative default rather than computed, because a
# computed retention is a retention somebody can change without noticing that
# this particular one cannot be changed back.

Parameters:

  MembersOrgPath:
    Type: String
    Description: >-
      Organization ID. Copy permission is granted to the ORGANIZATION rather
      than to a list of account ids, so a newly vested member can copy on the
      day it is created rather than after somebody remembers to add it here.
      The permission granted is narrow enough that org-wide is the right scope.

  MinRetentionDays:
    Type: Number
    Default: 35
    MinValue: 1
    Description: >-
      Becomes PERMANENT when the lock hardens. Copies cannot be deleted before
      this many days, by anyone, for the life of the vault.

  MaxRetentionDays:
    Type: Number
    Default: 2555
    Description: >-
      Seven years, matching the evidence retention elsewhere in the platform.
      An upper bound is required by Vault Lock and is the less dangerous half:
      it caps how long a copy may be kept, not how soon it may be destroyed.

  VaultLockChangeableDays:
    Type: Number
    Default: 3
    MinValue: 3
    Description: Grace period before the lock becomes irreversible. AWS minimum is 3.

Resources:

  # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # A customer-managed key, because cross-account copy requires one
  # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # Found by deploying. A vault encrypted with the default AWS Backup
  # service-managed key cannot participate in a cross-account copy at all:
  #
  #   "Copy job failed because the destination Backup vault is encrypted with
  #    the default Backup service managed key. The contents of this vault
  #    cannot be copied."
  #
  # The service-managed key has no key policy anybody can edit, so there is no
  # way to grant another account the use of it -- which is precisely what a
  # cross-account copy needs. design 05 asks for copies into a separate
  # account; a CMK is the mechanism that makes that possible rather than an
  # optional hardening.
  #
  # The key policy grants USE to the organization and ADMINISTRATION to nobody
  # but this account. A member account can encrypt a copy under this key and
  # cannot schedule its deletion.

  CopyVaultKey:
    Type: AWS::KMS::Key
    DeletionPolicy: Retain
    UpdateReplacePolicy: Retain
    Properties:
      Description: Encrypts cross-account backup copies. Required for copy to work at all.
      EnableKeyRotation: true
      # design 04 specifies 30 days, not KMS's 7-day default. Missed when this
      # template was written and caught by cfn-guard afterwards, which means
      # B-043 was committed with a template that did not pass the gate
      # CLAUDE.md requires. The consequence was real rather than cosmetic: this
      # key encrypts every cross-account backup copy, and scheduling its
      # deletion destroys the copies with it. Seven days is not enough notice
      # for the one key whose loss is unrecoverable by design.
      PendingWindowInDays: 30
      KeyPolicy:
        Version: '2012-10-17'
        Statement:
          - Sid: AccountRoot
            Effect: Allow
            Principal: { AWS: !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:iam::${AWS::AccountId}:root' }
            Action: 'kms:*'
            Resource: '*'
          - Sid: MembersMayEncryptCopies
            Effect: Allow
            Principal: '*'
            Action:
              - kms:Decrypt
              - kms:DescribeKey
              - kms:Encrypt
              - kms:GenerateDataKey
              - kms:GenerateDataKeyWithoutPlaintext
              - kms:ReEncryptFrom
              - kms:ReEncryptTo
              # AWS Backup creates grants on the caller's behalf during a copy.
              - kms:CreateGrant
            Resource: '*'
            Condition:
              StringEquals:
                aws:PrincipalOrgID: !Ref MembersOrgPath
          - Sid: NobodySchedulesDeletion
            Effect: Deny
            Principal: '*'
            # A key deletion destroys every copy encrypted under it, which is
            # a faster route to the same outcome Vault Lock exists to prevent.
            Action:
              - kms:ScheduleKeyDeletion
              - kms:DisableKey
            Resource: '*'
            Condition:
              ArnNotLike:
                aws:PrincipalArn: !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:iam::${AWS::AccountId}:role/PlatformQuorumExecutor'

  CopyVaultKeyAlias:
    Type: AWS::KMS::Alias
    Properties:
      AliasName: alias/platform-backup-copies
      TargetKeyId: !Ref CopyVaultKey

  CopyVault:
    Type: AWS::Backup::BackupVault
    # Retained, always. The stack that created it must never be the thing that
    # removes it -- and after the lock hardens, CloudFormation could not delete
    # it anyway, which would leave a stack that cannot be rolled back.
    DeletionPolicy: Retain
    UpdateReplacePolicy: Retain
    Properties:
      # Named exactly as recovery/30-backup-policy.yaml's CopyActions expect.
      # A mismatch here produces copy jobs that fail one per resource per
      # schedule, which reads as a resource problem rather than a naming one.
      BackupVaultName: platform-backup-copies
      # The key ARN, never the alias. AWS Backup rejects an alias here with
      # "Key Aliases are not supported for this operation".
      EncryptionKeyArn: !GetAtt CopyVaultKey.Arn
      LockConfiguration:
        MinRetentionDays: !Ref MinRetentionDays
        MaxRetentionDays: !Ref MaxRetentionDays
        ChangeableForDays: !Ref VaultLockChangeableDays
      AccessPolicy:
        Version: '2012-10-17'
        Statement:
          # Inbound: copy, and nothing else. A member account can put a copy
          # here and cannot list, read, restore or delete what is here --
          # including its own copies. That asymmetry is the whole design: the
          # account that gets compromised is the account that cannot reach
          # the backups.
          - Sid: MembersMayCopyIn
            Effect: Allow
            Principal: '*'
            Action: backup:CopyIntoBackupVault
            Resource: '*'
            Condition:
              StringEquals:
                aws:PrincipalOrgID: !Ref MembersOrgPath

          - Sid: NobodyDeletes
            Effect: Deny
            Principal: '*'
            Action:
              - backup:DeleteRecoveryPoint
              - backup:UpdateRecoveryPointLifecycle
              - backup:DeleteBackupVault
              - backup:DeleteBackupVaultAccessPolicy
              - backup:PutBackupVaultAccessPolicy
            Resource: '*'
            Condition:
              # design 05 puts vault deletion and lock modification under
              # quorum control (design 03). This is that, expressed where it
              # is enforced rather than where it is documented.
              ArnNotLike:
                aws:PrincipalArn: !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:iam::${AWS::AccountId}:role/PlatformQuorumExecutor'

  # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # design 05: "periodically verify that a member account with full local admin
  # genuinely cannot delete or alter its own backups"
  # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # The alarm, not the exercise. The exercise is a scheduled attempt from a
  # member account and belongs with the other guardrail exercises; this is the
  # detection that fires if a delete ever SUCCEEDS.
  #
  # A successful DeleteRecoveryPoint in this vault means the access policy, the
  # lock, or both have stopped working, and it is the single most serious
  # finding the backup layer can produce -- it is the ransomware answer having
  # quietly stopped being an answer.

  CopyVaultDeletionAlarm:
    Type: AWS::CloudWatch::Alarm
    Properties:
      AlarmName: platform-backup-copy-deleted
      AlarmDescription: >-
        A recovery point was deleted from the cross-account copy vault. This
        vault denies deletion to every principal except the quorum executor and
        is under Vault Lock, so a successful deletion means one of those two
        controls is not working.

        This is the ransomware answer having stopped being an answer. Treat it
        as a security incident, not a backup problem.

        CHECK: CloudTrail in the backup account for DeleteRecoveryPoint, then
        the vault access policy and the lock configuration.
      Namespace: AWS/Backup
      MetricName: NumberOfRecoveryPointsDeleted
      Statistic: Sum
      Period: 300
      EvaluationPeriods: 1
      Threshold: 0
      ComparisonOperator: GreaterThanThreshold
      TreatMissingData: notBreaching

Outputs:

  CopyVaultArn:
    Description: Copy destination for every member account's backup plans.
    Value: !GetAtt CopyVault.BackupVaultArn

  LockHardensAfterDays:
    Description: >-
      Days during which MinRetentionDays can still be corrected. After this the
      lock is irreversible by anyone, including AWS.
    Value: !Ref VaultLockChangeableDays
files.registry/10-registry-table.yaml:
AWSTemplateFormatVersion: '2010-09-09'

Description: >-
  AltDigital Managed Platform — the platform registry. The authoritative record
  of every partner, client and member account, and the parameters each was
  provisioned with. Deployed to the Platform Tooling account.

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# "The registry is the spine"
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Design doc 13's phrase, and it sets the durability bar. Every other system is
# provisioned FROM a registry record and writes back to it: AWS accounts, Jira,
# PagerDuty, Truveon, billing. A member account is de-vested and re-vested from
# the same record.
#
# So losing this table does not lose "some metadata". It loses the only
# statement of what each account was SUPPOSED to be — which is the half of
# drift detection that cannot be recovered by looking at AWS, because AWS can
# only tell you what things ARE.
#
# That is why point-in-time recovery, a stream, and DeletionPolicy: Retain are
# all on, for a table that will hold a few hundred small items.
#
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Why Platform Tooling and not Audit
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Audit is a read-mostly aggregation account whose trustworthiness rests on
# having very few writers. The registry is a provisioning control plane written
# on every onboarding, every baseline bump and every declared override. Putting
# it there would have traded a clean separation for one fewer account.
#
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Single table, and the key design
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# One table rather than four, because every access pattern here is "give me
# this partner and everything under it" or "give me all records of one type".
# Both are single queries in this layout and would be joins across four tables.
#
#   PK                    SK                  Record
#   --------------------  ------------------  ----------------------------
#   CONFIG                BASELINE            current global baseline version
#   PARTNER#<slug>        META                partner: state, BAA, windows
#   PARTNER#<slug>        CLIENT#<slug>       client under that partner
#   ACCOUNT#<id>          META                member account + parameters
#   ACCOUNT#<id>          OVERRIDE#<name>     a declared local override
#
# An override is a CHILD of the account rather than a field on it, so that each
# one carries its own reason, owner and review date, and so that adding one is
# a write that cannot accidentally overwrite the others.

Parameters:

  TableName:
    Type: String
    Default: platform-registry
    Description: Registry table name. Referenced by scripts/registry.sh.

Resources:

  RegistryKey:
    Type: AWS::KMS::Key
    DeletionPolicy: Retain
    UpdateReplacePolicy: Retain
    Properties:
      Description: Encrypts the platform registry
      EnableKeyRotation: true
      PendingWindowInDays: 30
      KeyPolicy:
        Version: '2012-10-17'
        Statement:
          - Sid: EnableIAMPolicyDelegation
            Effect: Allow
            Principal: { AWS: !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:iam::${AWS::AccountId}:root' }
            Action: 'kms:*'
            Resource: '*'
      Tags:
        - { Key: platform-managed, Value: 'true' }

  RegistryKeyAlias:
    Type: AWS::KMS::Alias
    Properties:
      AliasName: alias/platform-registry
      TargetKeyId: !Ref RegistryKey

  RegistryTable:
    Type: AWS::DynamoDB::Table
    # Retain on both, because this is the one table whose loss is not
    # recoverable from AWS itself. A stack delete that takes the registry with
    # it would leave every account running with no record of what it was meant
    # to be.
    DeletionPolicy: Retain
    UpdateReplacePolicy: Retain
    Properties:
      TableName: !Ref TableName
      BillingMode: PAY_PER_REQUEST
      AttributeDefinitions:
        - { AttributeName: PK,               AttributeType: S }
        - { AttributeName: SK,               AttributeType: S }
        - { AttributeName: record_type,      AttributeType: S }
        - { AttributeName: baseline_version, AttributeType: S }
      KeySchema:
        - { AttributeName: PK, KeyType: HASH }
        - { AttributeName: SK, KeyType: RANGE }

      GlobalSecondaryIndexes:
        # Report 1 — "which accounts are behind the current baseline version".
        #
        # baseline_version is a ZERO-PADDED string, not a number. DynamoDB sorts
        # string sort keys lexicographically, so "10" sorts before "9" unless
        # padded. Enforced in scripts/registry.sh rather than here, because
        # DynamoDB cannot express the constraint — which makes it exactly the
        # kind of thing that works until version 10.
        - IndexName: by-type
          KeySchema:
            - { AttributeName: record_type,      KeyType: HASH }
            - { AttributeName: baseline_version, KeyType: RANGE }
          Projection:
            ProjectionType: ALL

      PointInTimeRecoverySpecification:
        PointInTimeRecoveryEnabled: true

      SSESpecification:
        SSEEnabled: true
        SSEType: KMS
        KMSMasterKeyId: !Ref RegistryKey

      # The stream is the change history of the spine. CloudTrail data events
      # would record that a write happened and by whom; the stream records what
      # the record looked like before and after. For "who moved this account to
      # a different baseline version and what was it before", only the second
      # answers the question.
      #
      # Nothing consumes it yet. That is deliberate — a stream with no consumer
      # costs nothing and retains 24 hours, and turning one on later does not
      # backfill the history you wanted.
      StreamSpecification:
        StreamViewType: NEW_AND_OLD_IMAGES

      Tags:
        - { Key: platform-managed, Value: 'true' }
        - { Key: Purpose,          Value: platform-registry }

Outputs:

  TableName:
    Description: Registry table
    Value: !Ref RegistryTable

  TableArn:
    Description: Registry table ARN
    Value: !GetAtt RegistryTable.Arn

  TableStreamArn:
    Description: Change stream, currently unconsumed
    Value: !GetAtt RegistryTable.StreamArn

  KeyArn:
    Description: Registry encryption key
    Value: !GetAtt RegistryKey.Arn
files.reporting/10-digest-sender.yaml:
AWSTemplateFormatVersion: '2010-09-09'

Description: >-
  AltDigital Managed Platform — instrumentation digest sender. Batched, per
  account, to the application owner's named contact. Deployed to the Platform
  Tooling account.

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Prerequisite: a verified SES identity
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# SES will not send from an unverified domain, and verifying altdigital.ai
# requires DNS records that only someone with access to the zone can add. That
# is an operator action, not something this template can do.
#
# Until it exists, deploy with DigestSender empty: the Lambda runs, gathers,
# renders, and logs what it would have sent without calling SES. That is a
# genuinely useful state — the content can be reviewed before a single message
# reaches a client's technical contact, and getting that wrong in front of a
# customer is harder to undo than a missing email.
#
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Why this is central and not per-account
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# One SES identity, one sending domain, one reputation. A sender in every
# member account would need a verified identity per tenant — and SES sending
# reputation is per-identity, so a tenant whose contact has rotted would be
# quietly damaging a reputation nobody is watching.
#
# It also puts the registry lookup local: Tooling holds the registry, which is
# where the contacts are.

Parameters:

  ArtifactBucket:
    Type: String
    Description: Artifact bucket holding the digest package.

  ArtifactKey:
    Type: String
    Description: >-
      Content-addressed package key. The hash is in the key because
      CloudFormation compares S3Key to decide whether to update a function.

  RegistryTable:
    Type: String
    Default: platform-registry
    Description: Registry table. Supplies the account list and the contacts.

  DigestSender:
    Type: String
    Default: ''
    Description: >-
      Verified SES address messages are sent FROM, e.g.
      platform@altdigital.ai.

      Empty puts the Lambda in a report-only mode: it gathers and renders and
      logs, and calls no SES API. Deliberately the default — the first digest a
      client's technical contact receives should be one somebody has read.

  DigestCc:
    Type: String
    Default: ''
    Description: >-
      AltDigital address CC'd on every digest.

      Design doc 06: "The CC to AltDigital means a bounce or a departed contact
      is visible to us rather than lost." Without it a rotted contact is
      invisible — the send succeeds, the mailbox is gone, and the evidence
      trail says we communicated when we did not.

  WindowHours:
    Type: Number
    Default: 24
    AllowedValues: [24, 168]
    Description: >-
      Digest window. 24 for daily, 168 for weekly. Design doc 06 allows either
      per account; the schedule below must be changed to match.

  ScheduleExpression:
    Type: String
    Default: 'cron(0 13 ? * MON-FRI *)'
    Description: >-
      When the digest runs. Default 13:00 UTC on weekdays — morning in US
      Central, and deliberately NOT a weekend: a digest arriving on Saturday is
      read on Monday alongside Monday's, which is how two get skimmed as one.

  EvidenceBucket:
    Type: String
    Default: ''
    Description: >-
      Object Lock archive receiving the send records.

      Prompt 4.4 wants these in Truveon with timestamp and recipient. Truveon
      does not exist, so they go to the immutable archive — arguably their
      right home regardless, since the record is the evidence that monitoring
      requirements were communicated and an auditor will want it unalterable.
      The Truveon hand-off stays outstanding rather than silently skipped.

Conditions:
  HasSender: !Not [!Equals [!Ref DigestSender, '']]

Resources:

  # Platform Tooling has no logs key of its own — alias/platform-logs is
  # created by the MEMBER baseline, which does not reach platform accounts. So
  # one is created here, under the same alias, so the convention holds
  # everywhere and a future reporting stack in this account has a key to use.
  LogsKey:
    Type: AWS::KMS::Key
    DeletionPolicy: Retain
    UpdateReplacePolicy: Retain
    Properties:
      Description: Encrypts platform log groups in the Tooling account
      EnableKeyRotation: true
      PendingWindowInDays: 30
      KeyPolicy:
        Version: '2012-10-17'
        Statement:
          - Sid: EnableIAMPolicyDelegation
            Effect: Allow
            Principal: { AWS: !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:iam::${AWS::AccountId}:root' }
            Action: 'kms:*'
            Resource: '*'
          # CloudWatch Logs encrypts with the key on the service's own behalf,
          # so the grant is to the regional logs service principal and scoped
          # by the log group ARN it is acting for. Without the EncryptionContext
          # condition this would let the service encrypt for any log group in
          # the account.
          - Sid: AllowCloudWatchLogs
            Effect: Allow
            Principal: { Service: !Sub 'logs.${AWS::Region}.amazonaws.com' }
            Action:
              - 'kms:Encrypt*'
              - 'kms:Decrypt*'
              - 'kms:ReEncrypt*'
              - 'kms:GenerateDataKey*'
              - 'kms:Describe*'
            Resource: '*'
            Condition:
              ArnLike:
                'kms:EncryptionContext:aws:logs:arn': !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:logs:${AWS::Region}:${AWS::AccountId}:log-group:*'
      Tags:
        - { Key: platform-managed, Value: 'true' }

  LogsKeyAlias:
    Type: AWS::KMS::Alias
    Properties:
      AliasName: alias/platform-logs
      TargetKeyId: !Ref LogsKey

  # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # Bounce handling
  # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # Prompt 4.4: "a bounced digest is a finding, because it means the contact
  # has rotted."
  #
  # Without a configuration set SES accepts the message, the recipient's server
  # rejects it, and nothing here ever learns. The send looks successful, the
  # evidence record says a digest was delivered, and the claim that monitoring
  # requirements were communicated is false — which is worse than not sending,
  # because it is a false record rather than an absent one.
  DigestConfigurationSet:
    Type: AWS::SES::ConfigurationSet
    Condition: HasSender
    Properties:
      Name: platform-digest
      ReputationOptions:
        ReputationMetricsEnabled: true
      SendingOptions:
        SendingEnabled: true

  BounceTopic:
    Type: AWS::SNS::Topic
    Condition: HasSender
    Properties:
      TopicName: platform-digest-bounces
      DisplayName: Digest bounces and complaints

  BounceTopicPolicy:
    Type: AWS::SNS::TopicPolicy
    Condition: HasSender
    Properties:
      Topics: [!Ref BounceTopic]
      PolicyDocument:
        Version: '2012-10-17'
        Statement:
          - Sid: AllowSesToPublish
            Effect: Allow
            Principal: { Service: ses.amazonaws.com }
            Action: 'sns:Publish'
            Resource: !Ref BounceTopic
            Condition:
              StringEquals:
                'AWS:SourceAccount': !Ref AWS::AccountId

  DigestEventDestination:
    Type: AWS::SES::ConfigurationSetEventDestination
    Condition: HasSender
    Properties:
      ConfigurationSetName: !Ref DigestConfigurationSet
      EventDestination:
        Name: bounces-and-complaints
        Enabled: true
        # REJECT and RENDERING_FAILURE are included alongside the obvious two.
        # A rejected or unrenderable message never reaches anyone either, and
        # treating only BOUNCE as failure would leave those silent.
        MatchingEventTypes:
          - BOUNCE
          - COMPLAINT
          - REJECT
          - RENDERING_FAILURE
        SnsDestination:
          TopicARN: !Ref BounceTopic

  # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # Sender
  # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  DigestRole:
    Type: AWS::IAM::Role
    Properties:
      RoleName: PlatformDigestSender
      AssumeRolePolicyDocument:
        Version: '2012-10-17'
        Statement:
          - Effect: Allow
            Principal: { Service: lambda.amazonaws.com }
            Action: sts:AssumeRole
      Policies:
        - PolicyName: SendDigests
          PolicyDocument:
            Version: '2012-10-17'
            Statement:
              - Effect: Allow
                Action: ['dynamodb:Query']
                Resource:
                  - !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:dynamodb:${AWS::Region}:${AWS::AccountId}:table/${RegistryTable}'
                  - !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:dynamodb:${AWS::Region}:${AWS::AccountId}:table/${RegistryTable}/index/*'
              # Assume the narrow reader role in member accounts. Named
              # explicitly rather than wildcarded across roles: this function
              # may assume PlatformDigestReader and nothing else, so a
              # compromise of it cannot reach OrganizationAccountAccessRole.
              - Effect: Allow
                Action: 'sts:AssumeRole'
                Resource: !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:iam::*:role/PlatformDigestReader'
              - Effect: Allow
                Action: ['ses:SendEmail']
                Resource: '*'
              - Effect: Allow
                Action: ['s3:PutObject']
                Resource: !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:s3:::${EvidenceBucket}/digest-evidence/*'
              - Effect: Allow
                Action:
                  - 'logs:CreateLogGroup'
                  - 'logs:CreateLogStream'
                  - 'logs:PutLogEvents'
                Resource: !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:logs:${AWS::Region}:${AWS::AccountId}:log-group:/aws/lambda/platform-digest*'
      Tags:
        - { Key: platform-managed, Value: 'true' }

  DigestFunction:
    Type: AWS::Lambda::Function
    Properties:
      FunctionName: platform-digest
      Runtime: python3.13
      Handler: digest.handler
      Role: !GetAtt DigestRole.Arn
      # One assume-role plus two paginated reads per account, serially. Minutes
      # at forty accounts. A timeout part way leaves some clients digested and
      # others not, with no record of which — so the budget is generous.
      Timeout: 900
      MemorySize: 512
      Code:
        S3Bucket: !Ref ArtifactBucket
        S3Key: !Ref ArtifactKey
      Environment:
        Variables:
          REGISTRY_TABLE: !Ref RegistryTable
          DIGEST_SENDER: !Ref DigestSender
          DIGEST_CC: !Ref DigestCc
          READER_ROLE_NAME: PlatformDigestReader
          EVIDENCE_BUCKET: !Ref EvidenceBucket
          WINDOW_HOURS: !Ref WindowHours
          SES_CONFIGURATION_SET: !If [HasSender, !Ref DigestConfigurationSet, '']
      Tags:
        - { Key: platform-managed, Value: 'true' }

  DigestLogGroup:
    Type: AWS::Logs::LogGroup
    DeletionPolicy: Delete
    UpdateReplacePolicy: Delete
    Properties:
      LogGroupName: /aws/lambda/platform-digest
      RetentionInDays: 90
      KmsKeyId: !GetAtt LogsKey.Arn

  DigestScheduleRule:
    Type: AWS::Events::Rule
    Properties:
      Name: platform-digest-schedule
      Description: Batched instrumentation digest, per account.
      ScheduleExpression: !Ref ScheduleExpression
      State: ENABLED
      Targets:
        - Id: digest
          Arn: !GetAtt DigestFunction.Arn

  DigestSchedulePermission:
    Type: AWS::Lambda::Permission
    Properties:
      FunctionName: !GetAtt DigestFunction.Arn
      Action: lambda:InvokeFunction
      Principal: events.amazonaws.com
      SourceArn: !GetAtt DigestScheduleRule.Arn

Outputs:

  FunctionName:
    Description: Digest sender
    Value: !Ref DigestFunction

  Mode:
    Description: Whether digests are actually sent
    Value: !If [HasSender, 'sending', 'report-only — no verified SES sender configured']

  BounceTopicArn:
    Condition: HasSender
    Description: Bounces, complaints, rejects and rendering failures
    Value: !Ref BounceTopic
files.runbooks/catalog.yaml:
# AltDigital Managed Platform — runbook catalog
#
# ===========================================================================
# THIS IS DATA. The framework is generic; this file is what it does.
# ===========================================================================
#
# Prompt 5.1: "a runbook is defined by data — (alarm type x resource type)
# mapped to a set of stage 1 gather actions, stage 2 remediations, stage 3
# remediations — and the framework handles staging, revalidation, safety rails
# and dossier assembly generically."
#
# Adding a runbook is an entry here. Never a code change, never a new SSM
# document: there is ONE automation document and it is driven by this file.
#
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Two audiences, and they are kept apart on purpose
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Prompt 5.2: "document in the runbook file: the common causes, what stage 1
# gathers and why, and what stage 2 and 3 will attempt. That documentation is
# the thing a Tier 2 human reads at 3am, so write it for that reader."
#
# So each runbook carries a `tier2:` block written for someone woken up —
# short, concrete, most likely cause first, no design rationale. The
# engineering reasoning lives in comments, which that reader will not be
# reading. Mixing the two produces a document that serves neither.
#
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The key is (alarm × resource), and the alarm id must be 06a's
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The engine looks up CATALOG[runbooks][resource_type][alarm_id] where alarm_id
# arrives from the alarm itself. A key that is not a real 06a id silently finds
# no runbook — no error, just an incident nobody responded to.
#
# That happened: this file said `rds-storage-low` where 06a says
# `rds-free-storage-low`, and the mismatch was invisible until the ids were
# compared mechanically. scripts/lib/validate_catalog.py now does that at
# packaging.
#
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# What is permitted, and what was refused
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Doc 07 and CLAUDE.md disagreed about stage 3. Resolved action by action on
# 2026-09-18 (D-012b), because the four candidates are not equivalent — two
# destroy no AWS resource at all.
#
# THE TEST IS REVERSIBILITY, NOT COST. An earlier draft refused scale-out
# because it creates cost, which applied a stricter standard than CLAUDE.md's
# own "additive or reversible" and bundled it with RDS storage expansion. Scale
# out is reversible and capped by the circuit breaker; RDS allocated storage
# cannot be shrunk by any means AWS offers, so a runaway log raises the floor
# of that customer's bill permanently. Cost is a consequence; irreversibility
# is the property.
#
#   PERMITTED
#     clear_log_files     stage 2. Deletes files, not a resource. No cost.
#     scale_out           stage 2, only where the target can scale back IN.
#     restart_service     stage 3. A process. Nothing in AWS is destroyed.
#     cycle_ecs_task      stage 3. The task dies, the service does not.
#
#   REFUSED, with what would change the answer
#     expand a volume     irreversible. A property of the AWS API, not a policy
#                         choice, so nothing changes this.
#     release stuck DB
#       connections       needs credentials the platform does not hold, and
#                         identifying a genuinely stuck connection is not
#                         something we can do confidently yet.
#     flush a cache       doc 07 calls it non-destructive; it is not. A flushed
#                         production cache stampedes the backend, and the
#                         stampede can exceed the memory pressure it relieved.
#     RDS failover        not destructive, and slow enough to be an outage.
#                         Refused until there is timing data on real instances.
#     drain and replace   hits two of CLAUDE.md's named verbs, and the recovery
#                         story is "hope the ASG launches a healthy one".

schema_version: 1

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Failure handling — "the fix didn't fix"
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Jamie, 2026-09-18: "if extending something didn't fix it, even if it's
# reversible, we should still escalate to a human ... tried this 3x, still
# having problems, page out."
#
# Three conditions, kept apart because collapsing them loses what distinguishes
# them:
#
#   escalate_on_failure    the remediation ran, the settle period passed, the
#                          alarm still breaches. Escalate the STAGE. Do not
#                          retry the action — clearing logs that did not drop
#                          disk usage will not drop it on a second attempt.
#
#   failed_attempt_limit   the same action failed twice on the same resource.
#                          Stop attempting it. A SHORTER fuse than the circuit
#                          breaker: every failed attempt is time during which
#                          nobody is looking at a real incident.
#
#   circuit breaker        06a's rail — the same remediation fired three times
#                          in an hour, counting SUCCESSES. Doc 07: "repeated
#                          automated repair is masking a real fault."
#
# Note the breaker counts firing, not attempts. A blocked attempt never fired,
# and counting those made the platform self-locking — three kill-switch blocks
# would trip it, so enabling automation found it already refusing to act.
failure_policy:
  escalate_on_failure: true
  failed_attempt_limit: 2
  window_seconds: 3600

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Settle periods
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# How long to wait after an action before revalidating.
#
# Without these the failure logic fires on exactly the remediations that work
# slowly. Scaling out does not take effect when the API returns — capacity has
# to start, pass health checks and begin absorbing load — so revalidating
# immediately reports "did not fix" on something that is working, escalates
# unnecessarily, and eventually trips a breaker on an action that never failed.
#
# These are times for the EFFECT to appear in the metric, not for the API call
# to return. A metric on a 300-second period cannot show a change faster than
# its own period, which is the floor.
settle_seconds:
  clear_log_files: 120
  scale_out: 600
  restart_service: 180
  cycle_ecs_task: 300
  default: 300

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Stage 1 — gather. Always runs, always read-only, on every alarm.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Doc 07 singles one out: "Was there a deployment or configuration change in
# the last 30 minutes? That deployment question resolves a large share of real
# incidents on its own."
#
# So recent_changes is a DEFAULT rather than something each runbook opts into.
# A gather step nobody remembered to add is a dossier missing the answer most
# likely to be the answer.
default_gather:
  - metrics_window
  - recent_changes
  - resource_configuration
  - alarm_history
  - related_health

runbooks:

  # =========================================================================
  "AWS::EC2::Instance":

    # --- prompt 5.2 #3: EC2 disk space exhaustion --------------------------
    ec2-disk-high:
      tier2:
        what_this_means: >
          A filesystem on this instance is close to full. When it fills,
          writes fail — usually the application first, then logging, which is
          how you lose the evidence of what happened.
        common_causes:
          - An application log that is not being rotated, or rotated but not
            compressed. Most common by a distance.
          - A log level left at DEBUG after a deployment.
          - Core dumps or crash artefacts from a process that keeps restarting.
          - A batch job writing temporary files it does not clean up.
          - Container image layers on a Docker host, which look like disk use
            from nowhere.
        stage_1_gathers: >
          Disk usage per mount, so you know WHICH filesystem rather than that
          one of them is full. Plus the standard set — recent changes matters
          here because a log-level change is a deployment, and it is the single
          most likely cause.
        stage_2_will: >
          Delete ROTATED logs only — *.gz, *.1, *.old older than three days —
          and vacuum journald to 200M. It never touches a live log file:
          truncating one breaks the writing process's file handle and destroys
          the evidence you are about to need.
        stage_3_will: >
          Nothing. There is no safe disruptive action for a full disk that
          clearing rotated logs did not fix.
        if_it_escalates_to_you: >
          Clearing rotated logs did not free enough, so something large and
          current is growing. Look at the disk_usage_by_mount output for which
          mount, then find the biggest recent file on it. If the growth is a
          live application log, the fix is the log level or the application,
          not the disk.
      gather:
        - disk_usage_by_mount
      stage_2:
        - action: clear_log_files
          parameters:
            paths: ['/var/log/*.gz', '/var/log/*.1', '/var/log/*.old']
            min_age_days: 3
            journald_vacuum_size: 200M
      stage_3: []

    ec2-memory-high:
      tier2:
        what_this_means: >
          Memory use on this instance is sustained above the threshold. The
          next thing that happens is usually the OOM killer choosing a process,
          and it rarely chooses the one you would have.
        common_causes:
          - A genuine leak in a long-running process. Grows monotonically and
            never recovers.
          - A workload change — bigger requests, more concurrency — after a
            deployment.
          - A JVM or runtime heap sized larger than the instance.
          - Page cache counted as used, which is normal and not a problem.
        stage_1_gathers: >
          The processes using the most memory, so the dossier names what is
          growing rather than reporting that something is. Plus the standard
          set.
        stage_2_will: >
          Nothing. There is no non-disruptive way to reclaim memory from a
          process that wants it.
        stage_3_will: >
          Restart the service named by the instance's platform-managed-service
          tag, but ONLY if the instance has healthy peers behind a load
          balancer. If it is the last healthy target, the restart is refused —
          that would be an outage rather than a remediation.
        if_it_escalates_to_you: >
          Either the restart was refused for lack of redundancy, or it ran and
          memory climbed again. If it climbed again within the settle period
          you are looking at a fast leak; capture a heap dump before restarting
          anything else, because the next restart destroys the evidence.
      gather:
        - top_processes_by_memory
      stage_2: []
      stage_3:
        - action: restart_service
          requires_redundancy: true
          parameters:
            service_name_tag: platform-managed-service

    ec2-cpu-high:
      tier2:
        what_this_means: >
          Sustained high CPU. Worth knowing; not necessarily worth acting on.
          A machine at 95% may be working exactly as intended.
        common_causes:
          - Legitimate load. Check this first and check it honestly.
          - A runaway process or an infinite retry loop after a dependency
            failed.
          - A deployment that changed the work done per request.
          - A batch job overlapping with interactive traffic.
        stage_1_gathers: >
          The standard set only. recent_changes is the useful one — CPU that
          moves usually moves because something shipped.
        stage_2_will: >
          Nothing.
        stage_3_will: >
          Nothing, deliberately. High CPU is as likely to be load as a fault,
          and restarting a busy service to fix busyness is how automation turns
          a slow day into an outage.
        if_it_escalates_to_you: >
          Every alarm here escalates — this runbook only gathers. Start with
          whether the load is real. If it is, this is a capacity conversation,
          not an incident.
      gather: []
      stage_2: []
      stage_3: []

    ec2-status-check-failed:
      tier2:
        what_this_means: >
          AWS cannot reach the instance, or the instance's own status check is
          failing. This is hypervisor-level: the machine is unreachable, not
          merely busy.
        common_causes:
          - Underlying host failure. AWS usually retires the instance.
          - Kernel panic or a failed boot after a patch.
          - Network configuration that removed the instance's own connectivity.
          - The instance was stopped by something outside the platform.
        stage_1_gathers: >
          The standard set. Note that most gather steps need the instance to
          respond, so expect thin output — that thinness is itself consistent
          with the alarm.
        stage_2_will: >
          Nothing.
        stage_3_will: >
          Nothing. The remedies are all restart-shaped, and SSM cannot reach an
          instance that is failing its status check, so the automation could
          not perform them even if permitted.
        if_it_escalates_to_you: >
          Check whether this is a system status check (AWS's problem, usually
          resolved by stop/start onto new hardware) or an instance status check
          (the guest's problem). The AWS console distinguishes them; the alarm
          does not.
      gather: []
      stage_2: []
      stage_3: []

  # =========================================================================
  "AWS::RDS::DBInstance":

    # --- prompt 5.2 #1: RDS high connection count --------------------------
    rds-connections-high:
      tier2:
        what_this_means: >
          Connections to this database are near the instance maximum. When it
          is reached, new connections are refused and the application sees
          errors that look nothing like a database problem.
        common_causes:
          - A connection pool sized larger than the database allows, multiplied
            by more application instances than when it was sized.
          - Connections not returned to the pool — a leak in error handling,
            where the failure path forgets to close.
          - A deployment that increased pool size or task count.
          - Long-running queries holding connections while new work arrives.
          - max_connections lower than expected, because on RDS it is derived
            from instance memory unless set explicitly.
        stage_1_gathers: >
          Connection count over time, so you can tell a step change from a
          gradual climb. A step change points at a deployment; a climb points
          at a leak. Plus the standard set.
        stage_2_will: >
          Nothing. Doc 07 lists "release stuck database connections" as a stage
          2 action, and the platform does not do it: killing connections
          requires credentials to the database that the platform deliberately
          does not hold, and identifying a genuinely stuck connection rather
          than a slow one is not something we can do confidently. Guessing
          wrong disconnects a real user mid-transaction.
        stage_3_will: >
          Nothing.
        if_it_escalates_to_you: >
          Look at the connection_trend shape first. A step change at a
          deployment time is a pool configuration problem and the fix is in the
          application. A steady climb with no plateau is a leak. If you need
          headroom immediately, max_connections can be raised in the parameter
          group — but that is a change, and it needs a change record.
      gather:
        - connection_trend
      stage_2: []
      stage_3: []

    rds-free-storage-low:
      tier2:
        what_this_means: >
          Free storage on this database is below the tier threshold. RDS
          stops accepting writes when it runs out, and the recovery from that
          is slower than you would like.
        common_causes:
          - Normal data growth that nobody projected.
          - Binary or transaction logs retained longer than intended.
          - A large temporary table or an index rebuild in progress.
          - A failed or paused replication slot holding WAL segments on
            PostgreSQL. Grows fast and does not stop.
        stage_1_gathers: >
          The storage trend, because the slope tells you how long you have —
          a cliff and a gentle decline need different responses and the alarm
          cannot distinguish them.
        stage_2_will: >
          Nothing. Doc 07 lists "expand the volume" and the platform refuses
          it: AWS does not permit SHRINKING allocated RDS storage, by any
          means, ever. An automated expansion raises the floor of the
          customer's bill permanently, and a runaway log would do it
          repeatedly. It is the one genuinely irreversible action on doc 07's
          list.
        stage_3_will: >
          Nothing.
        if_it_escalates_to_you: >
          Check the trend slope for how much time you have. If storage
          autoscaling is enabled, AWS may handle it — and you should still find
          out why. If it is a replication slot, resolving the slot frees the
          space without spending anything.
      gather:
        - storage_trend
      stage_2: []
      stage_3: []

  # =========================================================================
  "AWS::ECS::Service":

    ecs-cpu-high:
      tier2:
        what_this_means: >
          Sustained CPU across the tasks of this service. Unlike an EC2
          instance, a service has a defined way to get more capacity, so this
          one is sometimes actionable automatically.
        common_causes:
          - More traffic than the current task count can serve.
          - A deployment that increased the work per request.
          - A task-level CPU limit set lower than the workload needs.
          - A dependency slowing down, so tasks spend longer per request.
        stage_1_gathers: >
          CPU per task, which separates "all tasks are busy" (capacity) from
          "one task is pegged" (a stuck task). Plus the standard set.
        stage_2_will: >
          Add one task — but ONLY if the service has a scaling policy that can
          also remove one. Reversible is not the same as self-reversing: on a
          fixed desired count the automation would add capacity that nothing
          ever takes away, which is reversible in principle and permanent in
          practice until somebody reads the bill.
        stage_3_will: >
          Nothing.
        if_it_escalates_to_you: >
          Either the service has no scale-in policy — in which case adding
          capacity is a decision for a human who can also remove it — or a task
          was added and CPU stayed high. The second usually means the
          bottleneck is downstream, not here.
      gather:
        - ecs_task_cpu_by_task
      stage_2:
        - action: scale_out
          requires_scale_in_policy: true
          parameters:
            increment: 1
      stage_3: []

    ecs-memory-high:
      tier2:
        what_this_means: >
          A task is approaching its memory limit. ECS kills a task that exceeds
          it, so this usually precedes a restart you did not ask for.
        common_causes:
          - A leak in the container. Grows monotonically across the task's life.
          - A memory limit set from a guess rather than a measurement.
          - A workload change after a deployment.
          - A caching layer inside the application with no upper bound.
        stage_1_gathers: >
          Memory per task, so the dossier can say whether one task is leaking
          or all of them are near the limit. Those need different responses.
        stage_2_will: >
          Nothing.
        stage_3_will: >
          Stop ONE task, and only if the service has at least two running. The
          scheduler replaces it, memory returns to baseline, and the service
          keeps serving throughout.
        if_it_escalates_to_you: >
          If cycling was refused, the service has fewer than two running tasks
          and cycling would be an outage. If it ran and memory climbed again,
          the leak is fast — capture what you need from a running task before
          anything cycles it again, because the circuit breaker will stop after
          three and you want the evidence from before that.
      gather:
        - ecs_task_memory_by_task
      stage_2: []
      stage_3:
        - action: cycle_ecs_task
