          requires_redundancy: true
          parameters:
            max_tasks_per_run: 1

    # --- prompt 5.2 #2: ECS task flapping ----------------------------------
    ecs-running-vs-desired:
      tier2:
        what_this_means: >
          Fewer tasks are running than the service wants. ECS is already trying
          to start them and not succeeding.
        common_causes:
          - The container exits immediately — a bad image, a missing
            environment variable, a failed migration on boot.
          - Health checks failing, so ECS kills tasks it just started.
          - >-
            No capacity to place tasks on — the cluster is full, or Fargate
            has no room in the subnets.
            (Note for anyone editing this file: a plain YAML list item cannot
            contain a colon followed by a space. It parses as a mapping and the
            whole catalog fails to load, which fails the packaging step rather
            than anything subtle — but it is an easy thing to reintroduce while
            writing prose.)
          - An image that cannot be pulled, usually a registry permission.
          - A task role missing a permission the container needs at startup.
        stage_1_gathers: >
          Stopped task reasons and recent service events. This IS the answer
          almost every time — ECS records why it stopped a task, and the reason
          string usually names the problem outright.
        stage_2_will: >
          Nothing.
        stage_3_will: >
          NOTHING, and this is deliberate rather than an omission. Cycling a
          task here would race the scheduler that is already trying to start
          tasks, and deepen the deficit the alarm is reporting.
        if_it_escalates_to_you: >
          Read ecs_stopped_task_reasons first and believe it. "Essential
          container exited" with a non-zero code is the application; "unable to
          place task" is capacity; "CannotPullContainerError" is the registry.
          Each has a different owner.
      gather:
        - ecs_stopped_task_reasons
        - ecs_service_events
      stage_2: []
      stage_3: []

    ecs-task-restart-rate:
      tier2:
        what_this_means: >
          Tasks are restarting more often than the threshold allows. The
          service may look healthy from outside while churning underneath.
        common_causes:
          - A crash loop — the container starts, fails, and ECS restarts it.
          - Health check timing too aggressive for the application's startup.
          - Memory limits killing tasks under normal load.
          - A dependency that is intermittently unavailable at startup.
        stage_1_gathers: >
          The same as above: stopped task reasons and service events. The exit
          codes tell you whether the container chose to exit or was killed.
        stage_2_will: >
          Nothing.
        stage_3_will: >
          Nothing. This alarm IS the circuit breaker's scenario written as an
          alarm — tasks are already cycling too often, so cycling one more is
          indistinguishable from the fault it is reporting.
        if_it_escalates_to_you: >
          Exit code 137 means the task was killed, usually for memory. A
          non-zero application exit code means the container chose to stop, and
          the reason is in its logs. If restarts began at a deployment, that is
          your answer.
      gather:
        - ecs_stopped_task_reasons
        - ecs_service_events
      stage_2: []
      stage_3: []

  # =========================================================================
  "AWS::ElasticLoadBalancingV2::LoadBalancer":

    # --- prompt 5.2 #4: ALB 5xx rate elevated ------------------------------
    alb-5xx-rate:
      tier2:
        what_this_means: >
          The load balancer itself is returning 5xx — not the targets behind
          it. Users are seeing errors that the application never saw, because
          their requests did not reach it.
        common_causes:
          - No healthy targets. The commonest cause by far; check this first.
          - Targets that accept a connection and then close it before
            responding.
          - Request or response headers exceeding the ALB's limits.
          - Idle timeout shorter than the application's response time, so the
            ALB gives up on a request the target is still working on.
          - A target group whose health check path stopped existing after a
            deployment.
        stage_1_gathers: >
          The standard set. related_health matters more than usual here: if
          tg-no-healthy-hosts is also firing, that is the whole story and this
          alarm is a symptom of it.
        stage_2_will: >
          Nothing. Everything that fixes an ALB 5xx is on the targets, not on
          the load balancer, and the automation cannot know which target group
          belongs to which application.
        stage_3_will: >
          Nothing. Doc 07 lists "drain and replace an instance behind a load
          balancer" and the platform refuses it: draining deregisters and
          replacing terminates, which are two of the verbs CLAUDE.md names, and
          the recovery story is hoping the replacement comes up healthy.
        if_it_escalates_to_you: >
          Check healthy target count first — if it is zero, this is a
          deployment or a health check problem and the 5xx is a consequence. If
          targets are healthy, compare the ALB 5xx count with the TARGET 5xx
          count: if only the ALB is counting them, the requests are failing
          before they arrive, which points at timeouts or header limits rather
          than at the application.
      gather: []
      stage_2: []
      stage_3: []

  # =========================================================================
  "AWS::Lambda::Function":

    # --- prompt 5.2 #5: Lambda error rate elevated -------------------------
    lambda-error-rate:
      tier2:
        what_this_means: >
          This function is failing on a percentage of its invocations. The
          threshold is a RATE, not a count, so it means the same thing on a
          function invoked twice a day and one invoked ten thousand times a
          minute.
        common_causes:
          - A deployment. Overwhelmingly the most likely, and the one the
            gather stage answers directly.
          - A downstream dependency failing or throttling.
          - Timeouts, which count as errors — often after a dependency slowed
            down rather than failed.
          - Permission changes on the execution role.
          - Malformed input from a new producer.
        stage_1_gathers: >
          The actual exceptions from recent invocations, not just the count.
          Plus the standard set — recent_changes answers this alarm more often
          than any other in the catalog.
        stage_2_will: >
          Nothing. Every remedy for a failing function is a code or
          configuration change, and those belong to a human and a change
          record.
        stage_3_will: >
          Nothing.
        if_it_escalates_to_you: >
          Start with recent_changes. If something deployed in the last thirty
          minutes, that is almost certainly it, and rolling back is faster than
          diagnosing. If nothing deployed, read the exceptions — a dependency
          error and a timeout look similar in the metrics and nothing alike in
          the logs.

          Note the alarm only fires above the minimum invocation count in 06a,
          so this is not one error out of two. There is real volume behind it.
      gather:
        - recent_invocation_errors
      stage_2: []
      stage_3: []
files.scheduling/10-hoop.yaml:
AWSTemplateFormatVersion: '2010-09-09'

Description: >-
  AltDigital Managed Platform — HOOP scheduler (prompt 13.2) and its
  turndown/turnup verification (13.3). Deploys INTO the account it schedules.

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Deployed into the account it acts on, deliberately
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The alternative is a central scheduler assuming a role into each member
# account, and it is worse here for one reason: the blast radius of a bug.
#
# A central scheduler holds stop permissions across every account in the
# estate. A bug in its account-selection logic stops the wrong environment,
# and the wrong environment could be anybody's. This stack has permission in
# exactly one account and none anywhere else, so the same bug stops the
# environment it was already allowed to stop.
#
# That is the second layer of the enforcement hoop.py describes: the code
# refuses production, and the deployment never puts the code where production
# is. Neither layer alone would be enough -- a check is one edit from removal,
# and a permission boundary is one StackSet target from being widened.
#
# A third layer sits above both: AccountTier does not accept `prod` as a
# value, so CloudFormation rejects the stack before any code runs. It is the
# only one of the four refusals that does not require the Lambda to execute.
#
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Two functions, one package
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
#   hoop.handler    turndown and turnup, scheduled or manual, one code path
#   cycle.handler   verifies what just happened, and routes a failure
#
# Separate functions rather than one, because they have different failure
# modes and the verification must be able to run when the scheduler did not.
# A turnup that timed out leaves an environment nobody has checked, and the
# check is the thing that says so.

Parameters:

  ArtifactBucket:
    Type: String

  ArtifactKey:
    Type: String

  AccountId:
    Type: String
    Description: >-
      The account this stack schedules — its own. Passed explicitly rather
      than read from AWS::AccountId so that the value in the schedule payload
      is visible in the template and in the stack's parameters, where somebody
      auditing what may be turned down can read it without inspecting code.

  AccountTier:
    Type: String
    AllowedValues: [dev, test, uat]
    Description: >-
      This account's environment tier, read from the registry by the deploy
      script and fixed here at deploy time.

      `prod` is not an allowed value. CloudFormation refuses the stack before
      any code runs — which is the earliest of the four places production is
      refused, and the only one that does not require the Lambda to execute.

  AccountKind:
    Type: String
    Default: tenant
    AllowedValues: [tenant, shared]
    Description: >-
      Whether this is a customer environment or one of AltDigital's own. A
      `shared` account is refused unless it is the single designated exercise
      account: found while deploying this, because both sandboxes are
      registered `dev` and the scheduler would otherwise have turned down the
      account the canaries run in.

  ManifestParam:
    Type: String
    Default: /platform/hoop/manifest
    Description: >-
      Where turndown records what it stopped. Read by the turnup verification
      to assert the full expected set rather than merely the absence of errors.

  StateParam:
    Type: String
    Default: /platform/hoop/state
    Description: >-
      Whether this environment is scheduled down. Published by the scheduler
      and read by everything else that needs to know, rather than each system
      computing the window itself — see scheduling/src/state.py on why eight
      independent readings of one HOOP disagree.

  AlertBusName:
    Type: String
    Default: platform-alerts

  AlertBusArn:
    Type: String
    Description: Cross-account ARN of the alert bus, for findings.

  HoopConfig:
    Type: String
    Default: '{}'
    Description: >-
      The HOOP as JSON — timezone and windows. questionnaire 3a.7 supplies the
      timezone and it is NEVER defaulted: an empty config means this
      environment is not scheduled, which is a legitimate state, and the
      scheduler refuses rather than assuming UTC.

  ExerciseAccountId:
    Type: String
    Default: ''
    Description: >-
      Set ONLY in the exercise deployment. Names the single platform-owned
      account whose environment may be cycled to prove the path works. Empty
      in every tenant deployment, which is what makes it an absent capability
      rather than a guarded one.

  ScheduleExpression:
    Type: String
    Default: rate(15 minutes)
    Description: >-
      How often the window is evaluated, NOT the HOOP itself. The scheduler
      asks "should this be up now" and acts on the answer, so a 15-minute
      evaluation means an environment comes up within 15 minutes of its window
      opening. Finer costs more invocations; coarser makes somebody wait.

  LogsKeyArn:
    Type: String
    Default: ''

Conditions:

  UseDefaultLogsKey: !Equals [!Ref LogsKeyArn, '']
  IsExercise: !Not [!Equals [!Ref ExerciseAccountId, '']]

Resources:

  SchedulerRole:
    Type: AWS::IAM::Role
    Properties:
      RoleName: PlatformHoopScheduler
      AssumeRolePolicyDocument:
        Version: '2012-10-17'
        Statement:
          - Effect: Allow
            Principal: { Service: lambda.amazonaws.com }
            Action: sts:AssumeRole
      ManagedPolicyArns:
        - !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:iam::aws:policy/service-role/AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole'

  SchedulerPolicy:
    Type: AWS::IAM::Policy
    Properties:
      PolicyName: HoopSchedule
      Roles: [!Ref SchedulerRole]
      PolicyDocument:
        Version: '2012-10-17'
        Statement:
          # Reads are broad because the scheduler has to find what exists.
          - Sid: Discover
            Effect: Allow
            Action:
              - ec2:DescribeInstances
              - ec2:DescribeVolumes
              - rds:DescribeDBInstances
              - rds:DescribeDBClusters
              - rds:ListTagsForResource
              - ecs:ListClusters
              - ecs:ListServices
              - ecs:DescribeServices
              - autoscaling:DescribeAutoScalingGroups
            Resource: '*'

          # Writes are narrow in KIND rather than in resource: stop and start,
          # never terminate, never delete. There is no ec2:TerminateInstances,
          # no rds:DeleteDBInstance and no autoscaling:DeleteAutoScalingGroup
          # here, so CLAUDE.md's rule is enforced by the role and not only by
          # the code. A bug cannot destroy what the role cannot call.
          - Sid: StopAndStart
            Effect: Allow
            Action:
              - ec2:StartInstances
              - ec2:StopInstances
              - ec2:CreateTags
              - rds:StartDBInstance
              - rds:StopDBInstance
              - rds:StartDBCluster
              - rds:StopDBCluster
              - rds:AddTagsToResource
              - ecs:UpdateService
              - ecs:TagResource
              - autoscaling:UpdateAutoScalingGroup
              - autoscaling:CreateOrUpdateTags
            Resource: '*'

          # The manifest, in THIS account's parameter store. Scoped to the
          # one path. The scheduler needs no access to the platform registry
          # at all, which is the point: a cross-account role able to write the
          # registry from every scheduled account in the estate is a large
          # trust relationship to buy one lookup.
          - Sid: ManifestAndState
            Effect: Allow
            Action:
              - ssm:GetParameter
              - ssm:PutParameter
            Resource:
              - !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:ssm:${AWS::Region}:${AWS::AccountId}:parameter${ManifestParam}'
              # The published state, read by alarm suppression, the telemetry
              # gap detector and cost reporting (prompt 13.4). Two parameters
              # named individually rather than a path wildcard: the scheduler
              # writes exactly these two and nothing else under /platform.
              - !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:ssm:${AWS::Region}:${AWS::AccountId}:parameter${StateParam}'

          - Sid: EmitFindings
            Effect: Allow
            Action: events:PutEvents
            Resource: !Ref AlertBusArn

          - Sid: PublishDuration
            Effect: Allow
            Action: cloudwatch:PutMetricData
            Resource: '*'
            Condition:
              StringEquals:
                cloudwatch:namespace: Platform/HOOP

  SchedulerLogGroup:
    Type: AWS::Logs::LogGroup
    DeletionPolicy: Retain
    UpdateReplacePolicy: Retain
    Properties:
      LogGroupName: /aws/lambda/platform-hoop-scheduler
      # A year. What was stopped and when is the answer to "why was the
      # environment down" and to "why is this month's bill different".
      RetentionInDays: 365
      KmsKeyId: !If
        - UseDefaultLogsKey
        - !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:kms:${AWS::Region}:${AWS::AccountId}:alias/platform-logs'
        - !Ref LogsKeyArn

  SchedulerFunction:
    Type: AWS::Lambda::Function
    DependsOn: SchedulerLogGroup
    Properties:
      FunctionName: platform-hoop-scheduler
      Runtime: python3.12
      Handler: hoop.handler
      Role: !GetAtt SchedulerRole.Arn
      # A turndown walks every ASG, service, database and instance in the
      # account. Five minutes is generous for a non-production environment and
      # cheap to leave generous.
      Timeout: 300
      MemorySize: 256
      Code:
        S3Bucket: !Ref ArtifactBucket
        S3Key: !Ref ArtifactKey
      Environment:
        Variables:
          HOOP_ACCOUNT_TIER: !Ref AccountTier
          HOOP_ACCOUNT_KIND: !Ref AccountKind
          HOOP_MANIFEST_PARAM: !Ref ManifestParam
          HOOP_STATE_PARAM: !Ref StateParam
          ALERT_BUS_NAME: !Ref AlertBusName
          HOOP_EXERCISE_ACCOUNT_ID: !Ref ExerciseAccountId

  VerifyLogGroup:
    Type: AWS::Logs::LogGroup
    DeletionPolicy: Retain
    UpdateReplacePolicy: Retain
    Properties:
      LogGroupName: /aws/lambda/platform-hoop-verify
      RetentionInDays: 365
      KmsKeyId: !If
        - UseDefaultLogsKey
        - !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:kms:${AWS::Region}:${AWS::AccountId}:alias/platform-logs'
        - !Ref LogsKeyArn

  VerifyFunction:
    Type: AWS::Lambda::Function
    DependsOn: VerifyLogGroup
    Properties:
      FunctionName: platform-hoop-verify
      Runtime: python3.12
      Handler: cycle.handler
      Role: !GetAtt SchedulerRole.Arn
      Timeout: 300
      MemorySize: 256
      Code:
        S3Bucket: !Ref ArtifactBucket
        S3Key: !Ref ArtifactKey
      Environment:
        Variables:
          HOOP_ACCOUNT_TIER: !Ref AccountTier
          HOOP_ACCOUNT_KIND: !Ref AccountKind
          HOOP_MANIFEST_PARAM: !Ref ManifestParam
          HOOP_STATE_PARAM: !Ref StateParam
          ALERT_BUS_NAME: !Ref AlertBusName
          HOOP_EXERCISE_ACCOUNT_ID: !Ref ExerciseAccountId

  # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # The evaluation schedule
  # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # Fires regardless of the window and asks the scheduler what the window
  # implies. That is why there is one rule rather than a pair of cron rules at
  # the window's edges: a pair would drift out of step with a HOOP edited in
  # the registry, and an environment whose HOOP changed would keep coming up
  # at the old time with nothing reporting why.

  EvaluationSchedule:
    Type: AWS::Events::Rule
    Properties:
      Name: platform-hoop-evaluate
      Description: >-
        Evaluate this environment's HOOP window and turn down or up
        accordingly. Deliberately not two cron rules at the window edges — the
        window is data and this asks it every time.
      ScheduleExpression: !Ref ScheduleExpression
      State: ENABLED
      Targets:
        - Id: scheduler
          Arn: !GetAtt SchedulerFunction.Arn
          Input: !Sub '{"account_id": "${AccountId}", "hoop": ${HoopConfig}}'

  EvaluationPermission:
    Type: AWS::Lambda::Permission
    Properties:
      FunctionName: !GetAtt SchedulerFunction.Arn
      Action: lambda:InvokeFunction
      Principal: events.amazonaws.com
      SourceArn: !GetAtt EvaluationSchedule.Arn

Outputs:

  SchedulerFunctionName:
    Description: Turndown and turnup. Manual invocation uses this same function.
    Value: !Ref SchedulerFunction

  VerifyFunctionName:
    Description: Verifies a cycle and routes a failure.
    Value: !Ref VerifyFunction

  ExerciseMode:
    Description: Whether this deployment may cycle a platform-owned account.
    Value: !If [IsExercise, !Ref ExerciseAccountId, 'no']
files.security/10-log-archive.yaml:
AWSTemplateFormatVersion: '2010-09-09'

Description: >-
  AltDigital Managed Platform — immutable log destination in the Log Archive
  account. S3 with Object Lock, a dedicated KMS key, and a bucket policy
  admitting CloudTrail and Config. Deployed once, directly into the Log Archive
  account; this is platform infrastructure, not part of the member baseline.

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Object Lock cannot be added later
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# ObjectLockEnabled is settable ONLY at bucket creation. A bucket created
# without it can never gain it — the only remedy is a new bucket and a copy of
# every object, which for a log archive means re-writing the evidence trail
# that the archive exists to preserve. That is why this template exists before
# any trail is configured rather than alongside it.
#
# COMPLIANCE mode means exactly what it says: for the retention period, no
# principal can delete or overwrite an object. Not an administrator, not the
# account root, not AWS Support. That is the property that makes the archive
# worth anything to an auditor, and it is also an unbreakable commitment to
# storage cost for the full period. See the RetentionDays parameter.

Parameters:

  RetentionDays:
    Type: Number
    Default: 365
    MinValue: 1
    MaxValue: 36500
    Description: >-
      Default Object Lock retention, in days, applied to every object written.
      In COMPLIANCE mode this is irreversible: the objects cannot be deleted by
      anyone until it expires, and storage is billed for the whole period.
      Design doc 02 derives the retention floor from the union of each tenant's
      frameworks, so this must be at least the longest any tenant requires.

  ObjectLockMode:
    Type: String
    Default: COMPLIANCE
    AllowedValues: [COMPLIANCE, GOVERNANCE]
    Description: >-
      COMPLIANCE — nobody can delete or shorten retention, including the root
      user. This is what design doc 02's "immutable log destination" means and
      what an auditor will look for.
      GOVERNANCE — a principal holding s3:BypassGovernanceRetention can
      override. Weaker, but recoverable from a mistake. The platform SCPs
      already deny BypassGovernanceRetention on platform-managed buckets, which
      narrows the gap but does not close it for the management account.

  TransitionToGlacierDays:
    Type: Number
    Default: 90
    MinValue: 1
    Description: >-
      Age at which objects move to Glacier Instant Retrieval. Object Lock is
      unaffected by storage class, so immutability is preserved. This is the
      main lever on the cost of a long retention period.

  OrganizationId:
    Type: String
    Description: Organization id (o-xxxx), used to scope the bucket policy.
    AllowedPattern: '^o-[a-z0-9]{10,32}$'

  ReplicaRegion:
    Type: String
    Default: ''
    Description: >-
      Region holding the replica buckets. Empty disables replication, which is
      the state before security/20-archive-replicas.yaml has been deployed
      there — a replication rule pointing at a bucket that does not exist fails
      the stack.

  ReplicaKeyArn:
    Type: String
    Default: ''
    Description: KMS key encrypting the replicas. Empty disables replication.

  AlertTopicArn:
    Type: String
    Default: ''
    Description: >-
      SNS topic in the Audit account that alarms publish to. Cross-account on
      purpose: the PagerDuty routing key then exists in one account rather
      than in every account that has an alarm. See alerting/10-alert-topic.yaml.

      Empty leaves the alarms actionless, which is the pre-B-015 state and is
      still better than no alarm — but it is not alerting, and nothing in the
      console distinguishes the two.

  ManagementAccountId:
    Type: String
    Description: >-
      Management account id. The organization trail lives there, and both the
      key policy and the bucket policy scope CloudTrail's access to trails
      owned by that account.
    AllowedPattern: '^[0-9]{12}$'

Conditions:
  HasAlerting: !Not [!Equals [!Ref AlertTopicArn, '']]

  # Replication is off until the destination stack exists in the replica
  # region. Both parameters must be supplied; a half-configured rule is worse
  # than none because it fails the stack on every subsequent deployment.
  WantReplication: !And
    - !Not [!Equals [!Ref ReplicaRegion, '']]
    - !Not [!Equals [!Ref ReplicaKeyArn, '']]

Resources:

  # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # Cross-region replication
  # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # Closes D-011 (design doc 02 requires platform services to be multi-region)
  # and, for the Config archive, B-006.
  #
  # The Config replica has Object Lock enabled even though its SOURCE does not,
  # because AWS Config refuses to deliver to a locked bucket while S3
  # Replication can write into one. If that holds, the authoritative immutable
  # copy of configuration history becomes the replica.
  #
  # Whether it holds is being tested here rather than assumed. If replication
  # into a lock-enabled destination fails, D-011 is still closed and B-006
  # stays open.
  ReplicationRole:
    Type: AWS::IAM::Role
    Condition: WantReplication
    Properties:
      RoleName: PlatformArchiveReplication
      AssumeRolePolicyDocument:
        Version: '2012-10-17'
        Statement:
          - Effect: Allow
            Principal: { Service: s3.amazonaws.com }
            Action: sts:AssumeRole
      # Bucket ARNs are CONSTRUCTED here rather than read with !GetAtt.
      #
      # The buckets name this role in their ReplicationConfiguration, so a
      # !GetAtt back to the buckets closes a cycle and CloudFormation refuses
      # the whole template:
      #   Circular dependency between resources: [LogArchiveBucketPolicy,
      #   ReplicationRole, ConfigArchiveBucketPolicy, FlowLogBucket, ...]
      #
      # The names are deterministic — the same !Sub expression that creates
      # them — so constructing the ARN is exact, not a guess. The cost is that
      # renaming a bucket now means editing two places, which is why the names
      # appear nowhere else in the file.
      Policies:
        - PolicyName: ReplicateArchives
          PolicyDocument:
            Version: '2012-10-17'
            Statement:
              - Effect: Allow
                Action:
                  - 's3:GetReplicationConfiguration'
                  - 's3:ListBucket'
                Resource:
                  - !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:s3:::altdig-log-archive-${AWS::AccountId}'
                  - !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:s3:::altdig-config-archive-${AWS::AccountId}'
                  - !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:s3:::altdig-flow-logs-${AWS::AccountId}'
              - Effect: Allow
                Action:
                  - 's3:GetObjectVersionForReplication'
                  - 's3:GetObjectVersionAcl'
                  - 's3:GetObjectVersionTagging'
                  # The log archive source HAS Object Lock. Replicating an
                  # object carries its retention state across, which means
                  # reading that state first. Without these two, replication
                  # reports FAILED on every object in the locked bucket and
                  # says nothing about why.
                  - 's3:GetObjectRetention'
                  - 's3:GetObjectLegalHold'
                Resource:
                  - !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:s3:::altdig-log-archive-${AWS::AccountId}/*'
                  - !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:s3:::altdig-config-archive-${AWS::AccountId}/*'
                  - !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:s3:::altdig-flow-logs-${AWS::AccountId}/*'
              - Effect: Allow
                Action:
                  - 's3:ReplicateObject'
                  - 's3:ReplicateDelete'
                  - 's3:ReplicateTags'
                Resource:
                  - !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:s3:::altdig-log-archive-replica-${AWS::AccountId}/*'
                  - !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:s3:::altdig-config-archive-replica-${AWS::AccountId}/*'
                  - !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:s3:::altdig-flow-logs-replica-${AWS::AccountId}/*'
              - Effect: Allow
                Action: [ 'kms:Decrypt', 'kms:DescribeKey' ]
                Resource: !GetAtt LogArchiveKey.Arn
              - Effect: Allow
                Action: [ 'kms:Encrypt', 'kms:GenerateDataKey' ]
                Resource: !Ref ReplicaKeyArn
      Tags:
        - { Key: platform-managed, Value: 'true' }

  # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # Backfill
  # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # A replication rule is not retroactive. It applies to objects written AFTER
  # it exists and to nothing already in the bucket. When this rule was created
  # the log archive held 916 CloudTrail objects and the Config archive 46, and
  # every one of them would have stayed single-region forever.
  #
  # That is worth stating plainly because "the bucket is replicated" reads as
  # though it covers the bucket. It covers the future of the bucket. The past
  # needs S3 Batch Replication, which is a one-off job rather than a resource —
  # so the ROLE is declared here, where it is reviewable and versioned, and the
  # job that uses it is scripts/backfill-replication.sh.
  #
  # The role is kept after the backfill rather than deleted: any future gap in
  # the rule, any bucket added to the archive, and any object that fails
  # replication needs the same job run again.
  BatchReplicationRole:
    Type: AWS::IAM::Role
    Condition: WantReplication
    Properties:
      RoleName: PlatformArchiveBatchReplication
      AssumeRolePolicyDocument:
        Version: '2012-10-17'
        Statement:
          - Effect: Allow
            Principal: { Service: batchoperations.s3.amazonaws.com }
            Action: sts:AssumeRole
      Policies:
        - PolicyName: BackfillReplication
          PolicyDocument:
            Version: '2012-10-17'
            Statement:
              # InitiateReplication is what a batch job actually calls. It is
              # NOT s3:ReplicateObject — that is the permission the replication
              # SERVICE uses once a copy is under way. Confusing the two
              # produces a job that fails every task with AccessDenied.
              - Effect: Allow
                Action: 's3:InitiateReplication'
                Resource:
                  - !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:s3:::altdig-log-archive-${AWS::AccountId}/*'
                  - !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:s3:::altdig-config-archive-${AWS::AccountId}/*'
                  - !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:s3:::altdig-flow-logs-${AWS::AccountId}/*'
              # Required to GENERATE the manifest rather than supply one. The
              # generated manifest is filtered to objects whose replication
              # status is NONE or FAILED, so re-running the job is cheap and
              # does not re-copy what already arrived.
              - Effect: Allow
                Action:
                  - 's3:GetReplicationConfiguration'
                  - 's3:ListBucket'
                  - 's3:PutInventoryConfiguration'
                Resource:
                  - !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:s3:::altdig-log-archive-${AWS::AccountId}'
                  - !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:s3:::altdig-config-archive-${AWS::AccountId}'
                  - !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:s3:::altdig-flow-logs-${AWS::AccountId}'
              - Effect: Allow
                Action:
                  - 's3:GetObjectVersion'
                  - 's3:GetObjectVersionAcl'
                Resource:
                  - !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:s3:::altdig-log-archive-${AWS::AccountId}/*'
                  - !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:s3:::altdig-config-archive-${AWS::AccountId}/*'
                  - !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:s3:::altdig-flow-logs-${AWS::AccountId}/*'
      Tags:
        - { Key: platform-managed, Value: 'true' }

  # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # Encryption key
  # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  LogArchiveKey:
    Type: AWS::KMS::Key
    DeletionPolicy: Retain
    UpdateReplacePolicy: Retain
    Properties:
      Description: Encrypts the platform log archive
      EnableKeyRotation: true
      PendingWindowInDays: 30
      KeyPolicy:
        Version: '2012-10-17'
        Statement:
          # Delegates key access control to IAM in this account, which is the
          # AWS-recommended baseline for every customer-managed key.
          #
          # An earlier version enumerated a narrower set (Create*, Describe*,
          # Enable*, List*, Put*, Update*) on the theory that less is safer.
          # It was not: 'Get*' was missing, so kms:GetKeyRotationStatus was
          # denied and rotation status became unverifiable — the precise
          # evidence the Config rule cmk-backing-key-rotation-enabled and any
          # auditor asks for. A key policy that cannot answer questions about
          # itself is a compliance gap, not a hardening measure.
          #
          # More seriously, a customer-managed key whose policy omits something
          # needed later can become permanently unmanageable: key policy is the
          # only way in, and if it does not grant kms:PutKeyPolicy to anyone
          # reachable, nobody can fix it. The root delegation removes that
          # class of failure entirely.
          #
          # Destructive actions are NOT protected here by omission. They are
          # denied by SCP — kms:ScheduleKeyDeletion, DisableKey,
          # DisableKeyRotation, PutKeyPolicy — which is the right layer,
          # because an SCP cannot be edited from inside the account.
          #
          # NOTE: that SCP is attached to the Sandbox and Members OUs, NOT to
          # Security where this account lives. Until it is, this key is
          # protected by its policy alone. See the Security OU gap in
          # policies/scp/README.md.
          - Sid: EnableIAMPolicyDelegation
            Effect: Allow
            Principal: { AWS: !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:iam::${AWS::AccountId}:root' }
            Action: 'kms:*'
            Resource: '*'
          # aws:PrincipalOrgID does NOT work for a service principal.
          #
          # The first version conditioned these grants on aws:PrincipalOrgID,
          # reasoning that only principals inside the Organization should
          # encrypt. But when CloudTrail calls KMS the principal IS
          # cloudtrail.amazonaws.com — an AWS service, not a member of any
          # organization — so the condition could never match and CloudTrail was
          # refused the key. The trail failed to create with "Insufficient
          # permissions to access S3 bucket or KMS key", which names neither the
          # condition nor the reason.
          #
          # Service principals are constrained by aws:SourceArn,
          # aws:SourceAccount or aws:SourceOrgID — properties of the resource
          # the service is ACTING FOR, not of the caller.
          #
          # For CloudTrail the sharper control is the encryption context, which
          # carries the trail ARN. It restricts this key to encrypting trails
          # owned by the management account, so a trail created elsewhere in the
          # Organization cannot use it.
          - Sid: AllowCloudTrailToEncrypt
            Effect: Allow
            Principal: { Service: cloudtrail.amazonaws.com }
            Action:
              - kms:GenerateDataKey*
              - kms:DescribeKey
            Resource: '*'
            Condition:
              StringLike:
                'kms:EncryptionContext:aws:cloudtrail:arn':
                  !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:cloudtrail:*:${ManagementAccountId}:trail/*'

          # Config and VPC flow log delivery act on behalf of each member
          # account, so they are scoped by source organization rather than by an
          # account list: nothing to maintain, and a newly vested account works
          # immediately.
          #
          # An earlier revision removed this condition, on a bisection that
          # concluded aws:SourceOrgID was unpopulated for Config -> KMS. That
          # conclusion was wrong. The bisection was invalid because the Config
          # RECORDER kept being deleted underneath it, and Config checks for a
          # recorder BEFORE it checks the delivery policy — so
          # NoAvailableConfigurationRecorderException was mistaken for the
          # policy check passing.
          #
          # Isolating properly, with a recorder present throughout, showed
          # delivery failing identically whether or not a KMS key was supplied
          # ("provided kms key is 'null'"). KMS was never involved. The real
          # cause was S3 Object Lock, which Config cannot write to at all.
          - Sid: AllowLogDeliveryToEncrypt
            Effect: Allow
            Principal:
              Service:
                - config.amazonaws.com
                - delivery.logs.amazonaws.com
            Action:
              - kms:GenerateDataKey*
              - kms:Encrypt
              - kms:DescribeKey
            Resource: '*'
            Condition:
              StringEquals:
                'aws:SourceOrgID': !Ref OrganizationId

  LogArchiveKeyAlias:
    Type: AWS::KMS::Alias
    Properties:
      AliasName: alias/platform-log-archive
      TargetKeyId: !Ref LogArchiveKey

  # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # The archive bucket
  # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  LogArchiveBucket:
    Type: AWS::S3::Bucket
    DeletionPolicy: Retain
    UpdateReplacePolicy: Retain
    Properties:
      BucketName: !Sub 'altdig-log-archive-${AWS::AccountId}'
      # Object Lock requires versioning, and both must be set at creation.
      ObjectLockEnabled: true
      VersioningConfiguration:
        Status: Enabled
      ObjectLockConfiguration:
        ObjectLockEnabled: Enabled
        Rule:
          DefaultRetention:
            Mode: !Ref ObjectLockMode
            Days: !Ref RetentionDays
      BucketEncryption:
        ServerSideEncryptionConfiguration:
          - ServerSideEncryptionByDefault:
              SSEAlgorithm: aws:kms
              KMSMasterKeyID: !Ref LogArchiveKey
            BucketKeyEnabled: true
      PublicAccessBlockConfiguration:
        BlockPublicAcls: true
        BlockPublicPolicy: true
        IgnorePublicAcls: true
        RestrictPublicBuckets: true
      LifecycleConfiguration:
        Rules:
          - Id: TransitionToGlacier
            Status: Enabled
            Transitions:
              - StorageClass: GLACIER_IR
                TransitionInDays: !Ref TransitionToGlacierDays
            NoncurrentVersionTransitions:
              - StorageClass: GLACIER_IR
                TransitionInDays: !Ref TransitionToGlacierDays
          - Id: AbortIncompleteUploads
            Status: Enabled
            AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload:
              DaysAfterInitiation: 7
      Tags:
        - { Key: platform-managed, Value: 'true' }
        - { Key: Purpose,          Value: log-archive }
        - { Key: DataClassification, Value: regulated }
      ReplicationConfiguration: !If
        - WantReplication
        - Role: !GetAtt ReplicationRole.Arn
          Rules:
            - Id: CrossRegion
              Status: Enabled
              Priority: 1
              Filter: {}
              DeleteMarkerReplication: { Status: Disabled }
              Destination:
                Bucket: !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:s3:::altdig-log-archive-replica-${AWS::AccountId}'
                EncryptionConfiguration:
                  ReplicaKmsKeyID: !Ref ReplicaKeyArn
                # Without this, OperationsFailedReplication is never
                # published, and a rule that has stopped working is
                # indistinguishable from one with nothing to do.
                Metrics:
                  Status: Enabled
              SourceSelectionCriteria:
                SseKmsEncryptedObjects: { Status: Enabled }
        - !Ref AWS::NoValue

  # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # Config archive — a SECOND bucket, without Object Lock
  # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # AWS Config cannot deliver to a bucket with Object Lock enabled. Established
  # by elimination, because the error says nothing of the sort:
  # PutDeliveryChannel returned InsufficientDeliveryPolicyException against the
  # locked bucket with every condition stripped from the policy, and succeeded
  # immediately against an identical scratch bucket whose only difference was
  # Object Lock. Object Lock requires Content-MD5 on PutObject and Config does
  # not send it.
  #
  # This is not a Config quirk. VPC Flow Logs fails against the same bucket with
  # "LogDestination: <bucket> is undeliverable". The rule generalises:
  #
  #   AWS log delivery services cannot write to an Object Lock bucket.
  #   CloudTrail is the exception, because it sends Content-MD5.
  #
  # Design doc 02 asks for an immutable log destination AND for Config to
  # deliver there. Those are mutually exclusive, so the archive splits:
  #
  #   CloudTrail          -> locked bucket   COMPLIANCE, genuinely immutable
  #   Config, flow logs   -> this bucket     versioned, delete-denied,
  #                                          NOT immutable
  #
  # The name says 'config-archive' and it now also holds flow logs. The name is
  # narrower than the role; renaming means a new bucket and a migration, which
  # is not worth it for a label. Treat it as "everything Object Lock refuses".
  #
  # The difference is real and should not be papered over. What narrows it:
  #
  #   * Deleting an object here is denied by bucket policy to every principal
  #     except platform deployment roles — the same control as the locked
  #     bucket. What is missing is the guarantee that survives a compromised
  #     platform role, which is exactly what Object Lock provides and this
  #     cannot.
  #   * Config is not the only copy. The Config aggregator in the Audit account
  #     holds queryable configuration history independently of S3.
  #
  # The route to genuine immutability, if it is wanted: S3 Replication from
  # this bucket into a locked destination. Replication CAN write to an Object
  # Lock bucket where Config cannot. That adds replication cost and a delivery
  # delay, so it is recorded as a decision rather than assumed.
  ConfigArchiveBucket:
    Type: AWS::S3::Bucket
    DeletionPolicy: Retain
    UpdateReplacePolicy: Retain
    Properties:
      BucketName: !Sub 'altdig-config-archive-${AWS::AccountId}'
      VersioningConfiguration:
        Status: Enabled
      BucketEncryption:
        ServerSideEncryptionConfiguration:
          - ServerSideEncryptionByDefault:
              SSEAlgorithm: aws:kms
              KMSMasterKeyID: !Ref LogArchiveKey
            BucketKeyEnabled: true
      PublicAccessBlockConfiguration:
        BlockPublicAcls: true
        BlockPublicPolicy: true
        IgnorePublicAcls: true
        RestrictPublicBuckets: true
      LifecycleConfiguration:
        Rules:
          - Id: TransitionToGlacier
            Status: Enabled
            Transitions:
              - StorageClass: GLACIER_IR
                TransitionInDays: !Ref TransitionToGlacierDays
          - Id: AbortIncompleteUploads
            Status: Enabled
            AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload:
              DaysAfterInitiation: 7
      Tags:
        - { Key: platform-managed, Value: 'true' }
        - { Key: Purpose,          Value: config-archive }
        - { Key: Immutable,        Value: 'false' }
      ReplicationConfiguration: !If
        - WantReplication
        - Role: !GetAtt ReplicationRole.Arn
          Rules:
            - Id: CrossRegion
              Status: Enabled
              Priority: 1
              Filter: {}
              DeleteMarkerReplication: { Status: Disabled }
              Destination:
                Bucket: !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:s3:::altdig-config-archive-replica-${AWS::AccountId}'
                EncryptionConfiguration:
                  ReplicaKmsKeyID: !Ref ReplicaKeyArn
                # Without this, OperationsFailedReplication is never
                # published, and a rule that has stopped working is
                # indistinguishable from one with nothing to do.
                Metrics:
                  Status: Enabled
              SourceSelectionCriteria:
                SseKmsEncryptedObjects: { Status: Enabled }
        - !Ref AWS::NoValue

  ConfigArchiveBucketPolicy:
    Type: AWS::S3::BucketPolicy
    Properties:
      Bucket: !Ref ConfigArchiveBucket
      PolicyDocument:
        Version: '2012-10-17'
        Statement:
          - Sid: DenyInsecureTransport
            Effect: Deny
            Principal: '*'
            Action: 's3:*'
            Resource:
              - !GetAtt ConfigArchiveBucket.Arn
              - !Sub '${ConfigArchiveBucket.Arn}/*'
            Condition:
              Bool: { 'aws:SecureTransport': false }

          # Without Object Lock this is the only thing standing between a
          # mistake and the loss of configuration history.
          - Sid: DenyDeletion
            Effect: Deny
            Principal: '*'
            Action: [ 's3:DeleteObject', 's3:DeleteObjectVersion' ]
            Resource: !Sub '${ConfigArchiveBucket.Arn}/*'
            Condition:
              ArnNotLike:
                'aws:PrincipalArn':
                  - 'arn:aws:sts::*:assumed-role/Platform*/*'
                  - 'arn:aws:sts::*:assumed-role/OrganizationAccountAccessRole/*'
                  - 'arn:aws:sts::*:assumed-role/stacksets-exec-*/*'

          - Sid: ConfigCheckAcl
            Effect: Allow
            Principal: { Service: config.amazonaws.com }
            Action: [ 's3:GetBucketAcl', 's3:ListBucket' ]
            Resource: !GetAtt ConfigArchiveBucket.Arn
            Condition:
              StringEquals:
                'aws:SourceOrgID': !Ref OrganizationId

          - Sid: ConfigWrite
            Effect: Allow
            Principal: { Service: config.amazonaws.com }
            Action: 's3:PutObject'
            Resource: !Sub '${ConfigArchiveBucket.Arn}/AWSLogs/*'
            Condition:
              StringEquals:
                'aws:SourceOrgID': !Ref OrganizationId

  # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # Flow log archive — a THIRD bucket
  # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # VPC Flow Logs would not deliver to either existing bucket:
  # "LogDestination: <bucket> is undeliverable", against the locked bucket AND
  # against the non-locked Config archive.
  #
  # The cause was not isolated. A bare probe bucket with AWS's documented
  # flow-log policy worked immediately, and stayed working as each suspected
  # difference was added back to it one at a time — SSE-KMS with the platform
  # key, DenyInsecureTransport, a delete-deny conditioned on aws:PrincipalArn,
  # and versioning. All four were exonerated. Something in the accumulated
  # Config-archive policy is responsible and it was not worth more bisection to
  # find out which.
  #
  # A dedicated bucket is the better answer regardless. The Config archive had
  # grown statements for Config and then flow logs, and the locked bucket for
  # CloudTrail and then flow logs; each addition risks the previous one, and a
  # policy serving three delivery services is a policy nobody can reason about.
  # One bucket per delivery service, each with the minimal documented policy.
  #
  # Modelled exactly on the configuration proved to work, not on what ought to.
  FlowLogBucket:
    Type: AWS::S3::Bucket
    DeletionPolicy: Retain
    UpdateReplacePolicy: Retain
    Properties:
      BucketName: !Sub 'altdig-flow-logs-${AWS::AccountId}'
      VersioningConfiguration:
        Status: Enabled
      BucketEncryption:
        ServerSideEncryptionConfiguration:
          - ServerSideEncryptionByDefault:
              SSEAlgorithm: aws:kms
              KMSMasterKeyID: !Ref LogArchiveKey
            BucketKeyEnabled: true
      PublicAccessBlockConfiguration:
        BlockPublicAcls: true
        BlockPublicPolicy: true
        IgnorePublicAcls: true
        RestrictPublicBuckets: true
      LifecycleConfiguration:
        Rules:
          # Flow logs are voluminous and their value is operational — tracing an
          # incident — not evidentiary. Shorter retention than the audit trail.
          - Id: TransitionToGlacier
            Status: Enabled
            Transitions:
              - StorageClass: GLACIER_IR
                TransitionInDays: !Ref TransitionToGlacierDays
          - Id: AbortIncompleteUploads
            Status: Enabled
            AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload:
              DaysAfterInitiation: 7
      Tags:
        - { Key: platform-managed, Value: 'true' }
        - { Key: Purpose,          Value: flow-logs }
        - { Key: Immutable,        Value: 'false' }
      ReplicationConfiguration: !If
        - WantReplication
        - Role: !GetAtt ReplicationRole.Arn
          Rules:
            - Id: CrossRegion
              Status: Enabled
              Priority: 1
              Filter: {}
              DeleteMarkerReplication: { Status: Disabled }
              Destination:
                Bucket: !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:s3:::altdig-flow-logs-replica-${AWS::AccountId}'
                EncryptionConfiguration:
                  ReplicaKmsKeyID: !Ref ReplicaKeyArn
                # Without this, OperationsFailedReplication is never
                # published, and a rule that has stopped working is
                # indistinguishable from one with nothing to do.
                Metrics:
                  Status: Enabled
              SourceSelectionCriteria:
                SseKmsEncryptedObjects: { Status: Enabled }
        - !Ref AWS::NoValue

  FlowLogBucketPolicy:
    Type: AWS::S3::BucketPolicy
    Properties:
      Bucket: !Ref FlowLogBucket
      PolicyDocument:
        Version: '2012-10-17'
        Statement:
          - Sid: DenyInsecureTransport
            Effect: Deny
            Principal: '*'
            Action: 's3:*'
            Resource:
              - !GetAtt FlowLogBucket.Arn
              - !Sub '${FlowLogBucket.Arn}/*'
            Condition:
              Bool: { 'aws:SecureTransport': false }

          # AWS's documented flow-log grants, verbatim. The ACL condition is
          # kept because it is what the working probe carried; removing it was
          # not tested and this is not the place to find out.
          - Sid: AWSLogDeliveryAclCheck
            Effect: Allow
            Principal: { Service: delivery.logs.amazonaws.com }
            Action: 's3:GetBucketAcl'
            Resource: !GetAtt FlowLogBucket.Arn

          - Sid: AWSLogDeliveryWrite
            Effect: Allow
            Principal: { Service: delivery.logs.amazonaws.com }
            Action: 's3:PutObject'
            Resource: !Sub '${FlowLogBucket.Arn}/*'
            Condition:
              StringEquals:
                's3:x-amz-acl': 'bucket-owner-full-control'

  LogArchiveBucketPolicy:
    Type: AWS::S3::BucketPolicy
    Properties:
      Bucket: !Ref LogArchiveBucket
      PolicyDocument:
        Version: '2012-10-17'
        Statement:
          # Without this, any of the grants below are reachable over plain HTTP.
          - Sid: DenyInsecureTransport
            Effect: Deny
            Principal: '*'
            Action: 's3:*'
            Resource:
              - !GetAtt LogArchiveBucket.Arn
              - !Sub '${LogArchiveBucket.Arn}/*'
            Condition:
              Bool: { 'aws:SecureTransport': false }

          # Denies only an upload that ASKS for the wrong encryption, not one
          # that asks for nothing.
          #
          # Without the Null guard this denied any PutObject lacking an explicit
          # s3:x-amz-server-side-encryption header — and bucket default
          # encryption never gets a chance, because the Deny is evaluated first.
          # CloudTrail sets the header and worked. AWS Config does not, and
          # failed with InsufficientDeliveryPolicyException: "unable to write to
          # bucket", which names neither the header nor this statement.
          #
          # This does not weaken the control. The bucket's default encryption is
          # aws:kms with the platform key, so a header-less upload is still
          # encrypted with it. What remains denied is the case that matters:
          # a caller explicitly requesting AES256 or no encryption.
          - Sid: DenyWrongEncryptionIfSpecified
            Effect: Deny
            Principal: '*'
            Action: 's3:PutObject'
            Resource: !Sub '${LogArchiveBucket.Arn}/*'
            Condition:
              StringNotEquals:
                's3:x-amz-server-side-encryption': 'aws:kms'
              # Quoted: YAML reads a bare Null as the null value, not the
              # string, and CloudFormation rejects it as a malformed key.
              'Null':
                's3:x-amz-server-side-encryption': 'false'

          # Object Lock stops a VERSION being deleted. It does not stop a
          # delete marker being created over it.
          #
          # Verified on a live delivered object: s3:DeleteObject without a
          # version id returned DeleteMarker:true and succeeded. The underlying
          # version was untouched and refused deletion — "Access Denied because
          # object protected by object lock" — but the object had vanished from
          # a normal listing.
          #
          # That is the dangerous shape. The evidence survives, yet the archive
          # reads as empty to anyone not thinking in versions, and the person
          # discovering it is mid-incident. An attacker who cannot destroy the
          # logs can still make them look destroyed, which buys the same
          # confusion at no cost.
          #
          # Platform deployment principals keep delete rights so a delete
          # marker can be cleared; Object Lock still refuses them the version
          # itself, so this grants no power to destroy anything.
          - Sid: DenyDeleteMarkersAndVersionDeletion
            Effect: Deny
            Principal: '*'
            Action:
              - 's3:DeleteObject'
              - 's3:DeleteObjectVersion'
            Resource: !Sub '${LogArchiveBucket.Arn}/*'
            Condition:
              ArnNotLike:
                'aws:PrincipalArn':
                  - 'arn:aws:sts::*:assumed-role/Platform*/*'
                  - 'arn:aws:sts::*:assumed-role/OrganizationAccountAccessRole/*'
                  - 'arn:aws:sts::*:assumed-role/stacksets-exec-*/*'

          - Sid: CloudTrailCheckAcl
            Effect: Allow
            Principal: { Service: cloudtrail.amazonaws.com }
            Action: 's3:GetBucketAcl'
            Resource: !GetAtt LogArchiveBucket.Arn
            Condition:
              StringLike:
                'aws:SourceArn': !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:cloudtrail:*:${ManagementAccountId}:trail/*'

          - Sid: CloudTrailWrite
            Effect: Allow
            Principal: { Service: cloudtrail.amazonaws.com }
            Action: 's3:PutObject'
            Resource: !Sub '${LogArchiveBucket.Arn}/AWSLogs/*'
            Condition:
              StringEquals:
                's3:x-amz-acl': 'bucket-owner-full-control'
              StringLike:
                'aws:SourceArn': !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:cloudtrail:*:${ManagementAccountId}:trail/*'


  # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # Detection for the replication itself
  # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # A replication rule fails silently. The source bucket keeps accepting
  # writes, the replica keeps holding whatever arrived before the failure, and
  # every API that describes the configuration keeps returning it unchanged.
  # The only signal is a per-object ReplicationStatus nobody reads.
  #
  # These alarms have NO AlarmActions, because the platform has no alerting
  # path yet — see B-015. That is a real limitation and is recorded as one
  # rather than papered over: an unrouted alarm is visible in the console and
  # nowhere else, which is better than nothing and much worse than an alert.
  LogArchiveReplicationFailureAlarm:
    Type: AWS::CloudWatch::Alarm
    Condition: WantReplication
    Properties:
      AlarmName: platform-replication-failed-log-archive
      AlarmDescription: >-
        Replication of the log-archive bucket to its cross-region replica is
        failing. The source copy is intact, so nothing is lost yet — what is
        lost is the second region, and with it the guarantee D-011 was closed
        on. For the Config archive it is also the immutable copy (B-006), so
        the window during which configuration history is deletable is open
        again for as long as this alarm is firing.
        Diagnose with head-object ReplicationStatus on a recent object, then
        re-run scripts/backfill-replication.sh once the cause is fixed.
      Namespace: AWS/S3
      MetricName: OperationsFailedReplication
      Dimensions:
        - Name: SourceBucket
          Value: !Sub 'altdig-log-archive-${AWS::AccountId}'
        - Name: DestinationBucket
          Value: !Sub 'altdig-log-archive-replica-${AWS::AccountId}'
        - Name: RuleId
          Value: CrossRegion
      Statistic: Sum
      Period: 300
      EvaluationPeriods: 1
      Threshold: 1
      ComparisonOperator: GreaterThanOrEqualToThreshold
      # No failures is the normal state, and for the flow log bucket no
      # ACTIVITY is also normal. Neither must read as a problem.
      TreatMissingData: notBreaching
      AlarmActions: !If [HasAlerting, [!Ref AlertTopicArn], !Ref 'AWS::NoValue']
      OKActions: !If [HasAlerting, [!Ref AlertTopicArn], !Ref 'AWS::NoValue']

  ConfigArchiveReplicationFailureAlarm:
    Type: AWS::CloudWatch::Alarm
    Condition: WantReplication
    Properties:
      AlarmName: platform-replication-failed-config-archive
      AlarmDescription: >-
        Replication of the config-archive bucket to its cross-region replica is
        failing. The source copy is intact, so nothing is lost yet — what is
        lost is the second region, and with it the guarantee D-011 was closed
        on. For the Config archive it is also the immutable copy (B-006), so
        the window during which configuration history is deletable is open
        again for as long as this alarm is firing.
        Diagnose with head-object ReplicationStatus on a recent object, then
        re-run scripts/backfill-replication.sh once the cause is fixed.
      Namespace: AWS/S3
      MetricName: OperationsFailedReplication
      Dimensions:
        - Name: SourceBucket
          Value: !Sub 'altdig-config-archive-${AWS::AccountId}'
        - Name: DestinationBucket
          Value: !Sub 'altdig-config-archive-replica-${AWS::AccountId}'
        - Name: RuleId
          Value: CrossRegion
      Statistic: Sum
      Period: 300
      EvaluationPeriods: 1
      Threshold: 1
      ComparisonOperator: GreaterThanOrEqualToThreshold
      # No failures is the normal state, and for the flow log bucket no
      # ACTIVITY is also normal. Neither must read as a problem.
      TreatMissingData: notBreaching
      AlarmActions: !If [HasAlerting, [!Ref AlertTopicArn], !Ref 'AWS::NoValue']
      OKActions: !If [HasAlerting, [!Ref AlertTopicArn], !Ref 'AWS::NoValue']

  FlowLogReplicationFailureAlarm:
    Type: AWS::CloudWatch::Alarm
    Condition: WantReplication
    Properties:
      AlarmName: platform-replication-failed-flow-logs
      AlarmDescription: >-
        Replication of the flow-logs bucket to its cross-region replica is
        failing. The source copy is intact, so nothing is lost yet — what is
        lost is the second region, and with it the guarantee D-011 was closed
        on. For the Config archive it is also the immutable copy (B-006), so
        the window during which configuration history is deletable is open
        again for as long as this alarm is firing.
        Diagnose with head-object ReplicationStatus on a recent object, then
        re-run scripts/backfill-replication.sh once the cause is fixed.
      Namespace: AWS/S3
      MetricName: OperationsFailedReplication
      Dimensions:
        - Name: SourceBucket
          Value: !Sub 'altdig-flow-logs-${AWS::AccountId}'
        - Name: DestinationBucket
          Value: !Sub 'altdig-flow-logs-replica-${AWS::AccountId}'
        - Name: RuleId
          Value: CrossRegion
      Statistic: Sum
      Period: 300
      EvaluationPeriods: 1
      Threshold: 1
      ComparisonOperator: GreaterThanOrEqualToThreshold
      # No failures is the normal state, and for the flow log bucket no
      # ACTIVITY is also normal. Neither must read as a problem.
      TreatMissingData: notBreaching
      AlarmActions: !If [HasAlerting, [!Ref AlertTopicArn], !Ref 'AWS::NoValue']
      OKActions: !If [HasAlerting, [!Ref AlertTopicArn], !Ref 'AWS::NoValue']

Outputs:

  BucketName:
    Description: Log archive bucket name (CloudTrail, Object Lock COMPLIANCE)
    Value: !Ref LogArchiveBucket

  ConfigBucketName:
    Description: Config archive bucket name (versioned, NOT Object Lock)
    Value: !Ref ConfigArchiveBucket

  FlowLogBucketName:
    Description: Flow log bucket name (versioned, NOT Object Lock)
    Value: !Ref FlowLogBucket

  BucketArn:
    Description: Log archive bucket ARN
    Value: !GetAtt LogArchiveBucket.Arn

  BatchReplicationRoleArn:
    Condition: WantReplication
    Description: Role used by scripts/backfill-replication.sh
    Value: !GetAtt BatchReplicationRole.Arn

  KeyArn:
    Description: Log archive KMS key ARN
    Value: !GetAtt LogArchiveKey.Arn
files.security/20-archive-replicas.yaml:
AWSTemplateFormatVersion: '2010-09-09'

Description: >-
  AltDigital Managed Platform — cross-region replica buckets for the evidence
  archives. Deployed to the REPLICA region in the Log Archive account. The
  source buckets and their replication rules live in security/10-log-archive.yaml
  in the home region.

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Two problems, one mechanism
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# D-011 — design doc 02 requires platform services to be multi-region
# "regardless of tenant tier", because "a regional event must not blind us
# across every tenant simultaneously". Everything was in us-east-2.
#
# B-006 — the Config archive is not immutable, because AWS Config refuses to
# deliver to a bucket with Object Lock enabled.
#
# Replication closes both. S3 Replication CAN write into an Object Lock bucket
# where Config cannot, so the Config replica here is lock-enabled even though
# its source is not. The authoritative copy for retention purposes becomes the
# replica, not the source.
#
# THAT CLAIM IS TESTED, NOT ASSUMED. If replication into a lock-enabled
# destination does not work, this template still delivers D-011 and B-006 stays
# open — which is why the two are recorded separately rather than as one item.
#
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Why a separate template
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# A CloudFormation stack is regional. A cross-region pair is necessarily two
# stacks, and the destination must exist before the source's replication rule
# can reference it. Deploy this one first.

Parameters:

  ReplicaRetentionDays:
    Type: Number
    Default: 2190
    Description: >-
      Object Lock retention on the replicas, matching the source archive.
      Six years, per the HIPAA documentation retention expectation.

Resources:

  ReplicaKey:
    Type: AWS::KMS::Key
    DeletionPolicy: Retain
    UpdateReplacePolicy: Retain
    Properties:
      Description: Encrypts the cross-region evidence replicas
      EnableKeyRotation: true
      PendingWindowInDays: 30
      KeyPolicy:
        Version: '2012-10-17'
        Statement:
          - Sid: EnableIAMPolicyDelegation
            Effect: Allow
            Principal: { AWS: !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:iam::${AWS::AccountId}:root' }
            Action: 'kms:*'
            Resource: '*'
      Tags:
        - { Key: platform-managed, Value: 'true' }

  ReplicaKeyAlias:
    Type: AWS::KMS::Alias
    Properties:
      AliasName: alias/platform-archive-replica
      TargetKeyId: !Ref ReplicaKey

  # Replica of the CloudTrail archive. Source is already Object Lock
  # COMPLIANCE; the replica matches it.
  LogArchiveReplica:
    Type: AWS::S3::Bucket
    DeletionPolicy: Retain
    UpdateReplacePolicy: Retain
    Properties:
      BucketName: !Sub 'altdig-log-archive-replica-${AWS::AccountId}'
      ObjectLockEnabled: true
      VersioningConfiguration:
        Status: Enabled
      ObjectLockConfiguration:
        ObjectLockEnabled: Enabled
        Rule:
          DefaultRetention:
            Mode: COMPLIANCE
            Days: !Ref ReplicaRetentionDays
      BucketEncryption:
        ServerSideEncryptionConfiguration:
          - ServerSideEncryptionByDefault:
              SSEAlgorithm: aws:kms
              KMSMasterKeyID: !Ref ReplicaKey
            BucketKeyEnabled: true
      PublicAccessBlockConfiguration:
        BlockPublicAcls: true
        BlockPublicPolicy: true
        IgnorePublicAcls: true
        RestrictPublicBuckets: true
      Tags:
        - { Key: platform-managed, Value: 'true' }
        - { Key: Purpose,          Value: log-archive-replica }

  # Replica of the Config archive, WITH Object Lock — which its source cannot
  # have. This is the B-006 fix, and the reason to care about replication
  # beyond the regional argument.
  ConfigArchiveReplica:
    Type: AWS::S3::Bucket
    DeletionPolicy: Retain
    UpdateReplacePolicy: Retain
    Properties:
      BucketName: !Sub 'altdig-config-archive-replica-${AWS::AccountId}'
      ObjectLockEnabled: true
      VersioningConfiguration:
        Status: Enabled
      ObjectLockConfiguration:
        ObjectLockEnabled: Enabled
        Rule:
          DefaultRetention:
            Mode: COMPLIANCE
            Days: !Ref ReplicaRetentionDays
      BucketEncryption:
        ServerSideEncryptionConfiguration:
          - ServerSideEncryptionByDefault:
              SSEAlgorithm: aws:kms
              KMSMasterKeyID: !Ref ReplicaKey
            BucketKeyEnabled: true
      PublicAccessBlockConfiguration:
        BlockPublicAcls: true
        BlockPublicPolicy: true
        IgnorePublicAcls: true
        RestrictPublicBuckets: true
      Tags:
        - { Key: platform-managed, Value: 'true' }
        - { Key: Purpose,          Value: config-archive-replica }
        - { Key: Immutable,        Value: 'true' }

  # Flow logs replicate for the regional argument only. No Object Lock: flow
  # logs are operational rather than evidentiary, voluminous, and locking six
  # years of them would cost more than the diagnosis is worth.
  FlowLogReplica:
    Type: AWS::S3::Bucket
    DeletionPolicy: Retain
    UpdateReplacePolicy: Retain
    Properties:
      BucketName: !Sub 'altdig-flow-logs-replica-${AWS::AccountId}'
      VersioningConfiguration:
        Status: Enabled
      BucketEncryption:
        ServerSideEncryptionConfiguration:
          - ServerSideEncryptionByDefault:
              SSEAlgorithm: aws:kms
              KMSMasterKeyID: !Ref ReplicaKey
            BucketKeyEnabled: true
      PublicAccessBlockConfiguration:
        BlockPublicAcls: true
        BlockPublicPolicy: true
        IgnorePublicAcls: true
        RestrictPublicBuckets: true
      Tags:
        - { Key: platform-managed, Value: 'true' }
        - { Key: Purpose,          Value: flow-log-replica }

Outputs:

  LogArchiveReplicaArn:
    Description: CloudTrail archive replica
    Value: !GetAtt LogArchiveReplica.Arn

  ConfigArchiveReplicaArn:
    Description: Config archive replica, Object Lock enabled
    Value: !GetAtt ConfigArchiveReplica.Arn

  FlowLogReplicaArn:
    Description: Flow log replica
    Value: !GetAtt FlowLogReplica.Arn

  ReplicaKeyArn:
    Description: Replica encryption key
    Value: !GetAtt ReplicaKey.Arn
files.telemetry/00-telemetry-reader.yaml:
AWSTemplateFormatVersion: '2010-09-09'

Description: >-
  AltDigital Managed Platform — the read-only role the telemetry gap scan
  assumes in each account (prompt 10.3). Observes; cannot change anything.

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Why this is not PlatformQuorumReader
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The telemetry stack's first draft said the two could share a role, on the
# reasoning that both need cross-account read and neither should be able to
# change anything -- so a second role would be a second thing to audit for the
# same guarantee.
#
# That was an assumption made before checking what each actually needs, and it
# was wrong in both directions:
#
#   PlatformQuorumReader holds cloudtrail:LookupEvents and nothing else.
#   The telemetry scan needs ec2:Describe*, ssm:Describe*, cloudwatch metric
#   reads and logs:Describe* -- and no CloudTrail at all except for the
#   Session Manager attribution.
#
# Sharing would have meant widening a deliberately minimal role to a general
# observation grant, which loses the property that made it worth pointing at:
# that the component checking whether quorum actions were approved can see
# almost nothing else.
#
# Two roles, each minimal, each named for what it does. The cost is one more
# stack instance per account; the alternative was one role whose name stopped
# describing it.
#
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Read-only, and deliberately not "read-only plus restart the agent"
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The obvious next feature is having the scan reinstall an agent it finds
# stopped. It must not.
#
# design 11 frames the finding as something a human acts on, and the reason is
# in the attribution section: the interesting question is WHO stopped it, not
# getting it running again. An automated reinstall destroys the state somebody
# would investigate and turns a signal into a silent self-healing loop -- the
# agent goes down, comes back, goes down, and nobody ever sees a finding that
# persisted long enough to matter.
#
# The SSM association already reinstalls on a daily schedule. That is the
# repair path, and a gap surviving it is precisely the escalation signal.

Parameters:

  TelemetryScanRoleArn:
    Type: String
    AllowedPattern: '^arn:aws:iam::\d{12}:role/.+$'
    Description: >-
      The Audit-account role that runs the scan. Exactly one principal, named
      in full.

Resources:

  TelemetryReaderRole:
    Type: AWS::IAM::Role
    Properties:
      RoleName: PlatformTelemetryReader
      Description: >-
        Read-only observation for the telemetry gap scan. Holds no permission
        to start, stop, restart or reconfigure anything.
      MaxSessionDuration: 3600
      AssumeRolePolicyDocument:
        Version: '2012-10-17'
        Statement:
          - Sid: OnlyTheTelemetryScan
            Effect: Allow
            Principal:
              AWS: !Ref TelemetryScanRoleArn
            Action: sts:AssumeRole
      Tags:
        - Key: platform:component
          Value: telemetry
        - Key: platform:managed-by
          Value: altdigital

  TelemetryReaderPolicy:
    Type: AWS::IAM::Policy
    Properties:
      PolicyName: ObserveInstanceHealth
      Roles:
        - !Ref TelemetryReaderRole
      PolicyDocument:
        Version: '2012-10-17'
        Statement:

          # design 11's signal-dependency table, one permission per signal.
          #
          # Describe* only. Not Get*, not Start*, not Send* -- the scan reads
          # four facts and forms an opinion, and every one of these APIs is a
          # question rather than an instruction.
          - Sid: InstanceStateAndStatusChecks
            Effect: Allow
            Action:
              - 'ec2:DescribeInstances'
              - 'ec2:DescribeInstanceStatus'
            Resource: '*'

          - Sid: SsmPingAndAssociationHistory
            Effect: Allow
            Action:
              - 'ssm:DescribeInstanceInformation'
              - 'ssm:DescribeInstanceAssociationsStatus'
              - 'ssm:DescribeMaintenanceWindows'
            Resource: '*'

          # The sentinel metric and the hypervisor traffic metric. Both are
          # CloudWatch reads and neither can be scoped to a resource: metric
          # data is not an addressable resource, so '*' is the only
          # expressible form and the action list is the narrowing.
          - Sid: SentinelAndTrafficMetrics
            Effect: Allow
            Action:
              - 'cloudwatch:GetMetricStatistics'
              - 'cloudwatch:ListMetrics'
            Resource: '*'

          # Log stream staleness. Describe only -- the question is whether
          # anything arrived, which does not need the contents, and granting
          # the contents would put this role inside the data plane design 11
          # keeps developers out of.
          - Sid: LogStreamStalenessOnly
            Effect: Allow
            Action:
              - 'logs:DescribeLogGroups'
              - 'logs:DescribeLogStreams'
            Resource: '*'

          # Session Manager attribution. LookupEvents only, which is the one
          # CloudTrail call that answers "who started a session" without
          # granting the trail itself.
          - Sid: SessionAttribution
            Effect: Allow
            Action:
              - 'cloudtrail:LookupEvents'
            Resource: '*'

Outputs:

  TelemetryReaderRoleArn:
    Description: Assumed by the telemetry gap scan in the Audit account.
    Value: !GetAtt TelemetryReaderRole.Arn
files.telemetry/10-telemetry-gap.yaml:
AWSTemplateFormatVersion: '2010-09-09'

Description: >-
  AltDigital Managed Platform — telemetry gap detection (prompt 10.3).
  Detects an agent stopped on a live instance, per design 11's discriminator
  table. Deploys to the Audit account.

Parameters:

  ArtifactBucket:
    Type: String

  ArtifactKey:
    Type: String

  AlertBusName:
    Type: String
    Default: platform-alerts

  MemberReadRoleName:
    Type: String
    Default: PlatformTelemetryReader
    Description: >-
      The read-only role assumed in each account, from
      telemetry/00-telemetry-reader.yaml.

      NOT PlatformQuorumReader, though an earlier draft said it could be. That
      role holds cloudtrail:LookupEvents and nothing else; this scan needs
      ec2, ssm, cloudwatch and logs describes. Sharing would have meant
      widening a deliberately minimal role into a general observation grant,
      losing the property worth having -- that the component checking whether
      quorum actions were approved can see almost nothing else.

  GraceMinutes:
    Type: Number
    Default: 30
    Description: >-
      How long telemetry may be absent before it counts as a gap.

      design 11: "Grace period longer than a normal agent restart." An agent
      reinstalled by the SSM association returns within minutes; a patch reboot
      takes longer. Thirty is past both and far short of the daily association
      run, which is what provides the escalation signal rather than this.

  ScanSchedule:
    Type: String
    Default: 'rate(15 minutes)'
    Description: >-
      Frequent, because the window between an agent being stopped and whatever
      it was stopped for is short. Cheap: the scan is a handful of API calls
      per instance and most instances answer healthy immediately.

  LogsKeyArn:
    Type: String
    Default: ''

Conditions:

  UseDefaultLogsKey: !Equals [!Ref LogsKeyArn, '']

Resources:

  ScanRole:
    Type: AWS::IAM::Role
    Properties:
      RoleName: PlatformTelemetryGapScan
      AssumeRolePolicyDocument:
        Version: '2012-10-17'
        Statement:
          - Effect: Allow
            Principal: { Service: lambda.amazonaws.com }
            Action: sts:AssumeRole
      ManagedPolicyArns:
        - !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:iam::aws:policy/service-role/AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole'

  ScanPolicy:
    Type: AWS::IAM::Policy
    Properties:
      PolicyName: ObserveInstanceTelemetry
      Roles: [!Ref ScanRole]
      PolicyDocument:
        Version: '2012-10-17'
        Statement:
          # Read-only into member accounts. This component observes and
          # reports; it has no business restarting an agent, and design 11
          # frames the finding as something a human acts on because the
          # interesting question is WHO stopped it, not getting it running
          # again.
          - Sid: ReadMemberAccounts
            Effect: Allow
            Action: sts:AssumeRole
            Resource: !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:iam::*:role/${MemberReadRoleName}'
          - Sid: ReadTierMap
            Effect: Allow
            Action: ssm:GetParameter
            Resource: !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:ssm:${AWS::Region}:${AWS::AccountId}:parameter/platform/*'
          - Sid: ReportFindings
            Effect: Allow
            Action: events:PutEvents
            Resource: !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:events:${AWS::Region}:${AWS::AccountId}:event-bus/${AlertBusName}'

  ScanLogGroup:
    Type: AWS::Logs::LogGroup
    DeletionPolicy: Retain
    UpdateReplacePolicy: Retain
    Properties:
      LogGroupName: /aws/lambda/platform-telemetry-gap
      RetentionInDays: 2557
      KmsKeyId: !If
        - UseDefaultLogsKey
        - !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:kms:${AWS::Region}:${AWS::AccountId}:alias/platform-logs'
        - !Ref LogsKeyArn

  ScanFunction:
    Type: AWS::Lambda::Function
    DependsOn: ScanLogGroup
    Properties:
      FunctionName: platform-telemetry-gap
      Runtime: python3.12
      Handler: gap.handler
      Role: !GetAtt ScanRole.Arn
      # Every account, every platform-managed instance, five signals each.
      Timeout: 600
      MemorySize: 512
      Code:
        S3Bucket: !Ref ArtifactBucket
        S3Key: !Ref ArtifactKey
      Environment:
        Variables:
          ALERT_BUS_NAME: !Ref AlertBusName
