# package into member accounts. Shipping the whole spec here to read five lines
# of it would be worse. The instrumentation Lambda is authoritative and computes
# the routing class; this only needs to know what each class DOES.
#
# If these ever disagree, the tag wins, because the tag is what the alarm was
# created with.
DESTINATIONS = {
    "pagerduty":           {"pages": True,  "ticket": True,  "digest": True},
    "jira_and_commercial": {"pages": False, "ticket": True,  "digest": True,
                            "commercial_event": True},
    "digest_and_jira":     {"pages": False, "ticket": True,  "digest": True},
    "digest":              {"pages": False, "ticket": False, "digest": True},
    "review_queue":        {"pages": False, "ticket": False, "digest": False},
}

# Tier defaults from 06a, used only when an event carries no routing decision of
# its own — a Security Hub or GuardDuty finding, which no alarm tag covers.
TIER_DEFAULT_ROUTING = {
    "dev": "digest", "test": "digest_and_jira",
    "uat": "jira_and_commercial", "prod": "pagerduty",
}

# Finding severities that page in a production account. Below this they are
# tickets, because design/06 is explicit that nothing pages which a human
# cannot act on right now, and a MEDIUM GuardDuty finding at 3am is not that.
FINDING_PAGES_AT = {"CRITICAL", "HIGH"}


def _now():
    return datetime.datetime.now(datetime.timezone.utc)


def account_tier(account_id):
    """Environment tier for an account. Returns (tier, note).

    Cached for the life of the execution environment: the map changes when an
    account is vested, which is rarely, and a Parameter Store read per event
    would put a throttleable dependency on the path that pages people.

    An account that is not in the map returns "prod", which PAGES. That is the
    deliberate direction to fail: treating an unknown account as dev would
    silence a real production incident, while treating it as prod produces a
    page that says the tier was unknown. The note travels into the routing
    record so the gap is visible rather than inferred.
    """
    if not account_id:
        return "prod", "no account id on the event; treated as prod"
    if "map" not in _TIER_CACHE:
        try:
            raw = ssm.get_parameter(Name=ACCOUNT_TIER_PARAM)["Parameter"]["Value"]
            _TIER_CACHE["map"] = json.loads(raw)
        except Exception as exc:
            _TIER_CACHE["map"] = {}
            _TIER_CACHE["error"] = f"{type(exc).__name__}"
    mapping = _TIER_CACHE["map"]
    if account_id in mapping:
        return mapping[account_id], None
    why = _TIER_CACHE.get("error")
    return "prod", (
        f"account {account_id} is not in {ACCOUNT_TIER_PARAM}"
        + (f" ({why} reading it)" if why else "")
        + ". Treated as prod, which pages — an unknown account is more likely "
          "to be an unregistered production account than a forgotten sandbox. "
          "Run scripts/sync-account-tiers.sh.")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Normalising the sources
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Four event shapes arrive and every one puts the account, the resource and the
# severity somewhere different. Everything downstream works on the normalised
# form, so adding a fifth source is a function here and nothing else.


def from_alarm(event):
    d = event.get("detail") or {}
    name = d.get("alarmName") or ""
    state = (d.get("state") or {}).get("value")
    return {
        "kind": "alarm",
        "source": "cloudwatch",
        "account_id": event.get("account"),
        "region": event.get("region"),
        "title": name,
        "state": state,
        # The alarm's own description, which carries the routing trailer. The
        # RESOURCE comes out of that trailer rather than out of the alarm name:
        # the name is platform-auto-RESOURCEID-ALARMID and both halves may
        # contain dashes, so parsing it is guesswork. B-031.
        "description": (d.get("configuration") or {}).get("description"),
        "resource": name,
        # No alarm_arn. It was here for the tag lookup that turned out to be
        # impossible, and it crashed on the way out: event.get("resources",
        # [None])[0] raises IndexError when `resources` is PRESENT and empty,
        # because a default only applies to a missing key. EventBridge supplies
        # an empty list, so the router died on an event it was built to handle
        # and the whole invocation dead-lettered.
        "reason": (d.get("state") or {}).get("reason"),
        "occurred_at": event.get("time"),
        # Resolved from the alarm's tags below. An alarm the platform did not
        # create has none, which is itself a finding — see route().
        "routing": None,
    }


def from_security_hub(event):
    d = event.get("detail") or {}
    findings = d.get("findings") or [{}]
    f = findings[0]
    res = (f.get("Resources") or [{}])[0]
    return {
        "kind": "finding",
        "source": "securityhub",
        "account_id": f.get("AwsAccountId") or event.get("account"),
        "region": event.get("region"),
        "title": f.get("Title") or "Security Hub finding",
        "severity": ((f.get("Severity") or {}).get("Label") or "").upper(),
        "resource": res.get("Id") or "unknown",
        "reason": f.get("Description"),
        "occurred_at": f.get("UpdatedAt") or event.get("time"),
        "generator": f.get("GeneratorId"),
        "routing": None,
    }


def from_guardduty(event):
    d = event.get("detail") or {}
    # GuardDuty severity is numeric 1-8.9. The published bands are
    # low 1-3.9, medium 4-6.9, high 7-8.9; 9+ is documented as reserved and has
    # never been observed, so it is folded into CRITICAL rather than dropped.
    sev = d.get("severity") or 0
    label = ("CRITICAL" if sev >= 9 else "HIGH" if sev >= 7
             else "MEDIUM" if sev >= 4 else "LOW")
    res = d.get("resource") or {}
    return {
        "kind": "finding",
        "source": "guardduty",
        "account_id": d.get("accountId") or event.get("account"),
        "region": event.get("region"),
        "title": d.get("title") or "GuardDuty finding",
        "severity": label,
        "resource": (res.get("instanceDetails") or {}).get("instanceId")
                    or (res.get("accessKeyDetails") or {}).get("userName")
                    or res.get("resourceType") or "unknown",
        "reason": d.get("description"),
        "occurred_at": d.get("updatedAt") or event.get("time"),
        "routing": None,
    }


def from_config(event):
    d = event.get("detail") or {}
    ni = (d.get("newEvaluationResult") or {})
    return {
        "kind": "finding",
        "source": "config",
        "account_id": event.get("account"),
        "region": event.get("region"),
        "title": f"Config rule {d.get('configRuleName')} NON_COMPLIANT",
        # Config has no severity. Treated as MEDIUM so it tickets rather than
        # pages: a drifted control is real and dated work, and waking somebody
        # for it is how the rotation learns to ignore the pager.
        "severity": "MEDIUM",
        "resource": (d.get("resourceId") or "unknown"),
        "reason": ni.get("annotation") or d.get("configRuleName"),
        "occurred_at": event.get("time"),
        "routing": None,
    }


def from_dossier(event):
    """The response engine's incident readout, after it has tried and failed."""
    d = event.get("detail") or {}
    alarm = d.get("alarm") or {}
    return {
        "kind": "dossier",
        # The emitting source, not a hardcoded name. There are two dossier
        # emitters now — platform.response and platform.recovery — and the
        # routing log is what answers "why was I not paged about this". A log
        # line attributing a restore test to the response engine sends whoever
        # is reading it to the wrong component.
        "source": event.get("source") or "response-engine",
        "account_id": alarm.get("account_id") or event.get("account"),
        "region": event.get("region"),
        "title": alarm.get("name") or "response engine",
        "resource": alarm.get("resource_id") or "unknown",
        "environment_tier": alarm.get("environment_tier"),
        "reason": (d.get("assessment") or {}).get("probable_cause"),
        "occurred_at": d.get("recorded_at") or event.get("time"),
        "state": d.get("current_state"),
        "dossier": d,
        # The emitter's own routing class, if it stated one. Honoured only as a
        # DOWNGRADE -- see decide(). The response engine states none and is
        # unaffected; recovery/src/worker.py states one for a restore test that
        # was merely slow.
        "routing": d.get("routing"),
    }


def from_platform_event(event, spec):
    """A raw AWS event that matches one of 06a's `metric: event` alarms.

    The event arrives exactly as AWS emitted it — the forwarding rule cannot add
    anything, because an EventBridge rule cannot transform its input when the
    target is an event bus. So the 06a alarm is identified by matching the same
    pattern the rule was built from, and everything else is read out of the
    event itself.
    """
    d = event.get("detail") or {}

    # Two shapes, because the sources disagree. An RDS or Auto Scaling event
    # puts ARN STRINGS in the top-level `resources`; a CloudTrail event leaves
    # that empty and puts a list of DICTS under detail.resources
    # ({"ARN": ..., "type": ...}). Assuming strings crashed the router on the
    # very event class this was written to handle.
    candidates = list(event.get("resources") or []) + list(d.get("resources") or [])
    resource = None
    for c in candidates:
        arn = c.get("ARN") if isinstance(c, dict) else c
        if isinstance(arn, str) and arn:
            resource = arn.rsplit("/", 1)[-1].rsplit(":", 1)[-1]
            break
    if not resource:
        # CloudTrail puts the target under requestParameters, and what it is
        # called depends on the service. These two cover the only cloudtrail
        # source 06a defines today (S3); an unmatched one falls back to the
        # event name, which at least says what happened.
        rp = d.get("requestParameters") or {}
        resource = (rp.get("bucketName") or d.get("SourceIdentifier")
                    or d.get("AutoScalingGroupName") or d.get("eventName")
                    or "unknown")
    return {
        "kind": "platform-event",
        "source": (event.get("source") or "aws").replace("aws.", ""),
        "account_id": event.get("account"),
        "region": event.get("region"),
        "title": f"{spec['alarm_id']} — {d.get('eventName') or d.get('Message') or event.get('detail-type')}",
        "resource": resource,
        "alarm_id": spec["alarm_id"],
        "resource_type": spec["resource_type"],
        "severity_by_tier": spec.get("severity_by_tier") or {},
        "reason": spec.get("note"),
        "occurred_at": event.get("time"),
        "actor": ((d.get("userIdentity") or {}).get("arn")
                  or (d.get("userIdentity") or {}).get("type")),
        "raw_detail": d,
        "routing": None,
    }


def match_event_spec(event):
    """Which 06a event alarm, if any, this raw AWS event belongs to."""
    for spec in EVENT_SPECS:
        if eventspec.matches(spec["pattern"], event):
            return spec
    return None


NORMALISERS = {
    "CloudWatch Alarm State Change": from_alarm,
    "Security Hub Findings - Imported": from_security_hub,
    "GuardDuty Finding": from_guardduty,
    "Config Rules Compliance Change": from_config,
    "Platform Incident Dossier": from_dossier,
}


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Deciding
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


# Written into every AlarmDescription by the instrumentation Lambda. Must match
# ROUTING_MARKER there.
ROUTING_MARKER = "[platform-routing]"


def alarm_routing(description):
    """Read the routing class the instrumentation Lambda already decided.

    Out of the alarm's DESCRIPTION, which arrives inside the event as
    detail.configuration.description — not out of its tags.

    The tags carry the same facts and were the obvious source, and they are
    unreachable. CloudWatch alarms have no resource-based policy, so there is no
    IAM grant that lets the Audit account read another account's alarm tags; the
    call fails and every alarm falls through to the review queue. Found on the
    first live event, where the log read
    "could not read alarm tags: ClientError".

    Reading the description is better than fixing that would have been. The
    alternative was assuming a role per member account per alarm, which puts a
    cross-account round trip on the path that pages people, at the moment an
    incident is starting and the account may itself be unhealthy.

    Returns (routing, tier, note).
    """
    if not description or ROUTING_MARKER not in description:
        return None, None, ("no routing marker in the alarm description — this "
                            "alarm was not created by the instrumentation "
                            "Lambda, or predates the marker")
    trailer = description.split(ROUTING_MARKER, 1)[1]
    fields = {}
    for token in trailer.split():
        if "=" in token:
            k, v = token.split("=", 1)
            fields[k] = v
    return fields.get("routing"), fields.get("tier"), None


def decide(norm):
    """Turn a normalised event into a routing class.

    Every path ends in a named class, and an unrecognised one is treated as
    pagerduty rather than dropped — the same else rule the response engine
    follows. An event nobody anticipated is the one most likely to matter.
    """
    if norm["kind"] == "alarm":
        routing, tier, note = alarm_routing(norm.get("description"))
        norm["environment_tier"] = tier
        if norm.get("description") and ROUTING_MARKER in norm["description"]:
            trailer = norm["description"].split(ROUTING_MARKER, 1)[1]
            for token in trailer.split():
                if token.startswith("resource-id="):
                    # The real resource, so the page names the database rather
                    # than the alarm about the database.
                    norm["resource"] = token.split("=", 1)[1]
                # B-127. Which team owns the resource, and whether the resource
                # said so or the instrumentation Lambda defaulted it. Both are
                # carried: they route the same way today, and a reader that
                # could not tell them apart would make the default permanent by
                # making it invisible.
                elif token.startswith("layer-source="):
                    norm["layer_source"] = token.split("=", 1)[1]
                elif token.startswith("layer="):
                    norm["layer"] = token.split("=", 1)[1]
        if routing:
            return routing, f"alarm tag platform-routing={routing}"
        # No tag. Either an alarm the platform did not create, or one created
        # before tagging existed. Not silently dropped and not silently paged:
        # it goes to the review queue WITH the reason, because the finding is
        # that an untagged alarm exists rather than whatever the alarm says.
        return "review_queue", (
            f"no platform-routing tag ({note or 'alarm not created by the platform'}). "
            "Routed to review rather than guessed at. An untagged alarm is a gap "
            "in instrumentation, not an incident.")

    if norm["kind"] == "platform-event":
        tier, note = account_tier(norm.get("account_id"))
        norm["environment_tier"] = tier
        sev = norm.get("severity_by_tier") or {}
        if tier not in sev:
            # 06a omits a tier to mean "not watched here". The rule should not
            # have been created in that account at all, so this is a mismatch
            # between what is deployed and what the spec says — reviewable, not
            # pageable.
            return "review_queue", (
                f"06a does not watch {norm.get('alarm_id')} at tier {tier}, yet an "
                "event rule forwarded one. The rule is stale relative to the "
                "specification." + (f" {note}" if note else ""))
        return sev[tier], (f"06a {norm.get('alarm_id')} at tier {tier}"
                           + (f". {note}" if note else ""))

    if norm["kind"] == "dossier":
        # The response engine only emits a dossier when it has decided a human
        # is needed, so the routing class is not in question — what varies is
        # urgency, and that is the tier's business below.
        # LOOK THE TIER UP before falling back to prod.
        #
        # This defaulted straight to "prod" when a dossier carried no tier of
        # its own, and the consequence arrived the first time an emitter other
        # than the response engine sent one: a change-reconciliation finding
        # about a DEV sandbox deployment raised a real PagerDuty incident,
        # because the dossier had an account_id and no environment_tier.
        #
        # The response engine always sets the tier, so the gap was invisible
        # for two phases. Every later emitter has to remember to, and
        # "remember to" is what the shared account-tier map exists to remove --
        # the finding path below has looked the tier up all along.
        #
        # account_tier() still answers "prod" for an account genuinely absent
        # from the map, which pages, and that remains the right way to fail.
        tier = norm.get("environment_tier")
        if not tier:
            tier, note = account_tier(norm.get("account_id"))
            if note:
                norm["tier_note"] = note
        default = "pagerduty" if tier in ("uat", "prod") else "digest_and_jira"

        # An emitter may DOWNGRADE its own dossier, and may never escalate one.
        #
        # The asymmetry is the point. Downgrading is a statement about the
        # emitter's own event that only the emitter can make — a restore test
        # that merely ran slow knows it is not an outage, and nothing here
        # could work that out from the tier. Escalating is a statement about
        # who gets woken up, and that decision belongs in one place: design/06a
        # and the tier, read here.
        #
        # B-041 is the reason it is written as a rule rather than left to each
        # emitter's judgement. Two components reduced 06a's five routing
        # classes to "pages" and "does not page", picked the wrong half, and
        # sent non-paging alarms to a PagerDuty-subscribed topic — five false
        # pages, and a full day to trace, because a wrong routing decision
        # looks exactly like a working one.
        declared = norm.get("routing")
        if declared:
            spec = DESTINATIONS.get(declared)
            if spec is None:
                return default, (
                    f"emitter declared routing class '{declared}', which is not "
                    f"one of 06a's. Ignored and routed by tier {tier} instead — "
                    "an unrecognised class is a bug in the emitter, not a "
                    "reason to route somewhere undefined")
            if spec["pages"] and not DESTINATIONS[default]["pages"]:
                return default, (
                    f"emitter declared '{declared}', which pages, but tier "
                    f"{tier} does not. REFUSED: an emitter may lower its own "
                    "urgency and may not raise it — escalation is the tier's "
                    "decision (06a). See B-041")
            return declared, (
                f"emitter declared '{declared}'; tier {tier} would have given "
                f"'{default}'. Honoured as a downgrade")

        # Named by SOURCE. There are three dossier emitters now, and this
        # string is the answer to "why was I not paged about this" — attributing
        # a security containment to the response engine sends whoever is reading
        # it to the wrong component.
        return default, f"{norm.get('source') or 'dossier'} escalation, tier {tier}"

    # Findings. No routing decision travels with them, so the tier default
    # applies — and the tier is now LOOKED UP rather than assumed. It used to
    # default to prod for everything, which meant findings in a dev sandbox were
    # evaluated as production.
    tier, note = account_tier(norm.get("account_id"))
    norm["environment_tier"] = tier
    default = TIER_DEFAULT_ROUTING.get(tier, "digest")
    sev = (norm.get("severity") or "").upper()
    suffix = f". {note}" if note else ""
    # Floored by the finding's own severity: a LOW GuardDuty finding in
    # production is not a page just because production pages by default.
    if default == "pagerduty" and sev not in FINDING_PAGES_AT:
        return "digest_and_jira", (
            f"{tier} defaults to pagerduty, but a {sev or 'UNRATED'} finding is "
            "not actionable right now — ticketed instead" + suffix)
    return default, f"tier default for {tier}, severity {sev or 'UNRATED'}{suffix}"


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Delivering
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def dedup_key(norm):
    """One incident per (account, resource, alarm), not one per event.

    This is what merges the raw alarm with the dossier that arrives minutes
    later. Both derive the same key from the same three facts, so PagerDuty
    treats the second as an update to the first — the page goes out
    immediately and the evidence catches up, instead of two pages about one
    outage.
    """
    raw = "|".join([
        norm.get("account_id") or "", norm.get("resource") or "",
        norm.get("title") or "",
    ])
    return hashlib.sha256(raw.encode()).hexdigest()[:32]


def tenant_facts(account_id):
    """The tenant record for an account, or None. Cached for the container."""
    if not account_id:
        return None
    if "map" not in _FACTS_CACHE:
        try:
            raw = ssm.get_parameter(Name=TENANT_FACTS_PARAM)["Parameter"]["Value"]
            _FACTS_CACHE["map"] = json.loads(raw)
        except Exception as exc:                      # noqa: BLE001
            _FACTS_CACHE["map"] = {}
            _FACTS_CACHE["error"] = type(exc).__name__
    return (_FACTS_CACHE["map"] or {}).get(account_id)


def platform_key(tier):
    """AltDigital's own routing key for this tier.

    The destination for AltDigital's own accounts, and the fallback for every
    tenant lookup that cannot complete.
    """
    name = PD_SECRET_NAME_LOW if tier in ("dev", "test") and PD_SECRET_NAME_LOW \
        else PD_SECRET_NAME
    if not name:
        return None
    raw = secrets.get_secret_value(SecretId=name)["SecretString"]
    return json.loads(raw).get("events_v2_routing_key")


def routing_key(tier, layer=None, account_id=None):
    """(key, destination, note) for one alarm.

    Three dimensions, each from a different place so none can be quietly
    re-derived here:

      tenant   the account id, through the tenant facts map in SSM
      tier     the alarm's own platform-tier, parsed from the description
      layer    the alarm's platform-layer, ditto -- B-127

    The LAYER decides who, and it does so independently of the tier. AltDigital
    owns the infrastructure in a tenant's account at every tier, so a dev-tier
    VPC fault is still ours; the application at that same tier belongs to
    whoever owns the application, which for Arc8 is Wayne's team and for a later
    client is the client's own developers.

    Every failure falls back to AltDigital's key WITH A NOTE rather than
    raising. A routing lookup that fails during an incident must not turn a page
    into no page, and the wrong page is recoverable in a way silence is not. The
    note is printed so the fallback is visible rather than inferred.
    """
    # Infrastructure at any tier is AltDigital's to answer for, but it still
    # belongs on the TENANT's infra service rather than the platform's own, so
    # the tenant's own console shows their estate.
    #
    # ONLY an exact "application" routes to the application team. Written this
    # way round deliberately, and the first version was written the other way:
    # `INFRA_OBJECT if (not layer or layer == "infrastructure") else None` sends
    # every value it does not recognise -- a typo, a future third layer, a
    # truncated trailer -- to the APPLICATION team, which is the one direction
    # that wakes a client at 3am for something that may well be ours.
    #
    # The instrumentation Lambda already maps an unrecognised value to
    # infrastructure before it reaches the trailer, so this should be
    # unreachable. It is written to be safe anyway: this function also receives
    # alarms that predate the field, and a routing default should not depend on
    # another component having been correct.
    object_name = None if layer == "application" else INFRA_OBJECT

    facts = tenant_facts(account_id)
    if not facts:
        return platform_key(tier), "platform", (
            "no tenant facts for account " + str(account_id) + " in "
            + TENANT_FACTS_PARAM
            + ((" (" + _FACTS_CACHE["error"] + " reading it)")
               if _FACTS_CACHE.get("error") else "")
            + "; paged AltDigital's own service. Correct for AltDigital's own "
              "accounts, a gap for anything else.")

    client = facts.get("client")
    if not client:
        return platform_key(tier), "platform", (
            "account " + str(account_id) + " has tenant facts with no client; "
            "paged AltDigital's own service.")

    if object_name is None:
        # Application layer. The object is the account's app, which is the same
        # granularity the PagerDuty services were built at.
        object_name = facts.get("app")
        if not object_name:
            return platform_key(tier), "platform", (
                "account " + str(account_id) + " is a tenant account with no "
                "`app` recorded, so its application service cannot be named. "
                "Paged AltDigital rather than guessing which of a tenant's "
                "services should wake somebody.")

    secret_name = "/".join(
        [TENANT_KEY_PREFIX, client, tier or "prod", object_name])
    if secret_name in _KEY_CACHE:
        return _KEY_CACHE[secret_name], "tenant:" + secret_name, None
    try:
        raw = secrets.get_secret_value(SecretId=secret_name)["SecretString"]
        key = json.loads(raw).get("events_v2_routing_key")
    except Exception as exc:                          # noqa: BLE001
        return platform_key(tier), "platform", (
            "could not read " + secret_name + " (" + type(exc).__name__
            + "), so this tenant's service could not be paged. Fell back to "
              "AltDigital's own: a page to the wrong rotation is recoverable, "
              "silence is not. Run scripts/sync-pagerduty-tenants.sh.")
    if not key:
        return platform_key(tier), "platform", (
            secret_name + " holds no events_v2_routing_key.")
    _KEY_CACHE[secret_name] = key
    return key, "tenant:" + secret_name, None


def page(norm, routing, why):
    tier = norm.get("environment_tier") or "prod"
    key, destination, key_note = routing_key(
        tier, norm.get("layer"), norm.get("account_id"))
    if key_note:
        # Printed, never swallowed. A fallback nobody can see becomes permanent,
        # and this one routes a tenant's alarm to AltDigital -- which looks
        # exactly like working until the tenant asks why they never hear from us.
        print(json.dumps({"record_type": "routing-key-fallback",
                          "account_id": norm.get("account_id"),
                          "tier": tier, "layer": norm.get("layer"),
                          "layer_source": norm.get("layer_source"),
                          "destination": destination, "why": key_note}))
    if not key:
        raise RuntimeError(
            "No Events API v2 routing key. Refusing to silently not page: the "
            "caller records this and the DLQ retains the event.")

    body = {
        "routing_key": key,
        "event_action": "resolve" if norm.get("state") == "OK" else "trigger",
        "dedup_key": dedup_key(norm),
        "payload": {
            # B-027 will make this readable at a glance. Until then the account
            # and resource are in the summary, because the alarm name alone
            # answers roughly one of the four questions design/07 asks.
            "summary": (f"[{tier}] {norm.get('title')} — "
                        f"{norm.get('resource')} in {norm.get('account_id')}")[:1024],
            "source": f"{norm.get('source')}/{norm.get('account_id')}",
            "severity": "critical" if tier == "prod" else "warning",
            "component": norm.get("resource"),
            "group": norm.get("account_id"),
            "class": norm.get("kind"),
            "timestamp": norm.get("occurred_at"),
            # The whole dossier, which is the point of prompt 5.3. When the
            # response engine has not run there is none, and the payload says
            # so rather than arriving looking complete.
            "custom_details": norm.get("dossier") or {
                "note": "No dossier. Either no runbook covers this alarm, or the "
                        "response engine has not finished gathering — if it has, "
                        "a second event will update this incident in place.",
                "reason": norm.get("reason"),
                "routing_decision": why,
            },
        },
    }

    # ensure_ascii and an explicit charset, both.
    #
    # The first live page rendered an em dash as mojibake in PagerDuty. Dossier
    # text is full of them, so every real page would have carried garbled
    # characters through to whoever was reading it at 3am. ensure_ascii=True
    # escapes non-ASCII to \uXXXX so nothing depends on the receiver guessing an
    # encoding, and the charset header says so regardless.
    req = urllib.request.Request(
        PD_ENQUEUE, data=json.dumps(body, ensure_ascii=True).encode("utf-8"),
        headers={"Content-Type": "application/json; charset=utf-8"},
        method="POST")
    with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=10) as resp:
        return {"status": resp.status, "dedup_key": body["dedup_key"],
                "event_action": body["event_action"]}


def enqueue(url, norm, routing, why, destination):
    if not url:
        return {"sent": False, "reason": f"{destination} queue not configured"}
    sqs.send_message(QueueUrl=url, MessageBody=json.dumps({
        "destination": destination,
        "routing": routing,
        "why": why,
        "recorded_at": _now().isoformat(),
        "event": norm,
    }, default=str))
    return {"sent": True}


def handler(event, context):
    detail_type = event.get("detail-type") or ""
    normalise = NORMALISERS.get(detail_type)

    if normalise is None:
        # Before giving up: is this a raw AWS event belonging to one of 06a's
        # event alarms? Those arrive with the service's own detail-type — "AWS
        # API Call via CloudTrail", "RDS DB Instance Event" — and carry no
        # routing decision, because the rule that forwarded them could not
        # attach one.
        spec = match_event_spec(event)
        if spec is not None:
            norm = from_platform_event(event, spec)
            return deliver(norm, detail_type)

    if normalise is None:
        # The else. An event shape nobody anticipated is not dropped — it goes
        # to review with the raw event attached, because a router that silently
        # discards what it does not recognise is indistinguishable from one that
        # is working.
        enqueue(REVIEW_QUEUE_URL,
                {"kind": "unknown", "source": event.get("source"),
                 "title": detail_type or "(no detail-type)",
                 "account_id": event.get("account"), "raw": event},
                "review_queue",
                f"no normaliser for detail-type '{detail_type}'", "review")
        out = {"routed": "review_queue", "reason": "unrecognised event shape",
               "detail_type": detail_type}
        print(json.dumps(out))
        return out

    norm = normalise(event)

    # An alarm returning to OK is only interesting as a PagerDuty resolve. It is
    # not a ticket and not a review item; filing one per recovery would bury the
    # queues in work nobody asked for.
    if norm["kind"] == "alarm" and norm.get("state") not in ("ALARM", "OK"):
        out = {"routed": "ignored", "reason": f"alarm state {norm.get('state')}"}
        print(json.dumps(out))
        return out

    return deliver(norm, detail_type)


def deliver(norm, detail_type):
    """Decide, deliver, and record. One implementation for every event kind.

    Separate from handler() so the raw-AWS-event path and the normalised paths
    cannot diverge: the thing that decides where something goes, and the thing
    that records why, are the same code regardless of what arrived.
    """
    routing, why = decide(norm)
    spec = DESTINATIONS.get(routing)
    if spec is None:
        # Unrecognised routing class. Paged, deliberately: this means 06a named
        # a class this router does not implement, and the alarm it belongs to is
        # currently going nowhere. Under-routing is the failure that hides.
        spec = DESTINATIONS["pagerduty"]
        why = (f"routing class '{routing}' is not implemented by the router, so "
               "the event was escalated rather than dropped. Fix the router or "
               "06a — until then this alarm has no correct destination.")
        routing = "pagerduty"

    recovery = norm["kind"] == "alarm" and norm.get("state") == "OK"

    delivered = {}
    if spec["pages"]:
        delivered["pagerduty"] = page(norm, routing, why)
    elif recovery:
        # A recovery on a non-paging alarm has nowhere useful to go.
        out = {"routed": "ignored", "reason": "recovery on a non-paging alarm"}
        print(json.dumps(out))
        return out

    if recovery:
        # Resolve the incident and stop. A recovery is not work: filing a
        # ticket for it would mean every alarm that clears on its own produces
        # something for a human to close, and a queue of those is how the real
        # ones get closed unread.
        record = {"record_type": "routing-decision",
                  "recorded_at": _now().isoformat(),
                  "detail_type": detail_type, "source": norm.get("source"),
                  "account_id": norm.get("account_id"),
                  "title": norm.get("title"), "routing": routing,
                  "why": "recovery — incident resolved, no ticket raised",
                  "delivered": delivered}
        print(json.dumps(record, default=str))
        return record

    if spec.get("ticket"):
        delivered["jira"] = enqueue(JIRA_QUEUE_URL, norm, routing, why, "jira")
    if spec.get("commercial_event"):
        delivered["commercial"] = enqueue(
            COMMERCIAL_QUEUE_URL, norm, routing, why, "commercial")
    if not spec["pages"] and not spec.get("ticket"):
        delivered["review"] = enqueue(
            REVIEW_QUEUE_URL, norm, routing, why, "review")

    # Every decision is recorded, including the ones that deliberately did
    # nothing. "Why was I not paged about this" is the question this log exists
    # to answer, and it is asked after the fact.
    record = {
        "record_type": "routing-decision",
        "recorded_at": _now().isoformat(),
        "detail_type": detail_type,
        "source": norm.get("source"),
        "account_id": norm.get("account_id"),
        "environment_tier": norm.get("environment_tier"),
        "title": norm.get("title"),
        "resource": norm.get("resource"),
        "routing": routing,
        "why": why,
        "delivered": delivered,
        # digest is a FLAG on the destination, not a delivery: 4.4 builds the
        # digest by reading records like this one, rather than by being pushed
        # to. Recorded so that reading is possible.
        "digest": spec.get("digest", False),
    }
    print(json.dumps(record, default=str))
    return record

"""CloudWatch Synthetics canary: does the service actually work?

Prompt 4.3, design/06 "Synthetic monitoring". Generic infrastructure alarms
tell you a thing is running. They do not tell you it works. This runs the one
transaction the tenant named in questionnaire 7.1 and asserts on it.

What it deliberately does NOT do
--------------------------------
Evaluate a customer-supplied expression. Questionnaire 7.3 is free text, and a
canary that executed it would be a remote code execution path into a tenant
account reachable through an intake form. The assertion here is two fixed
checks — a status code and a substring — and anything richer takes the Fargate
path with the tenant's own Playwright suite.

The Selenium runtime
--------------------
syn-python-selenium is used for the runtime's reporting, not for a browser.
This is an HTTP check, so it drives urllib directly rather than starting
Chrome: a browser adds ~4s of startup to every run, several hundred MB of
memory, and a second failure mode (the browser itself) that reports as a
service failure. A tenant whose "working" genuinely requires a rendered page
has a user journey, not a heartbeat, and that is the Fargate path.
"""
import json
import os
import ssl
import time
import urllib.error
import urllib.request

import boto3

try:
    # Present in the Synthetics runtime. Gives the run a named step, which is
    # what produces the SuccessPercent and Duration metrics and the screenshot
    # and HAR capture the design calls out as useful for triage.
    from aws_synthetics.common import synthetics_configuration
    from aws_synthetics.common import synthetics_logger as logger
    from aws_synthetics.selenium import synthetics_webdriver as syn_webdriver
    IN_RUNTIME = True

    # execute_step screenshots the browser at step start, success and failure.
    # There is no browser here — this is an HTTP check — so every run failed
    # with 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'save_screenshot', which names the
    # screenshot and not the missing driver, and looks like a runtime bug rather
    # than a configuration one. Found on the first live run.
    #
    # The cost is that design/06's "screenshots and HAR files captured on
    # failure" does not apply to a heartbeat. There is no rendered page to
    # capture; a tenant whose "working" needs one has a user journey, and that
    # is the Fargate path.
    synthetics_configuration.set_config({
        "screenshot_on_step_start": False,
        "screenshot_on_step_success": False,
        "screenshot_on_step_failure": False,
    })
except ImportError:  # local testing
    import logging as logger
    syn_webdriver = None
    IN_RUNTIME = False

ssm = boto3.client("ssm")
secrets = boto3.client("secretsmanager")
cloudwatch = boto3.client("cloudwatch")

CANARY_NAME = os.environ.get("CANARY_NAME", "")

ENDPOINT = os.environ.get("ENDPOINT", "")
EXPECTED_STATUS = int(os.environ.get("EXPECTED_STATUS", "200"))
BODY_MUST_CONTAIN = os.environ.get("BODY_MUST_CONTAIN", "")
RESPONSE_MS_PARAM = os.environ.get("RESPONSE_MS_PARAM", "")
AUTH_SECRET_ARN = os.environ.get("AUTH_SECRET_ARN", "")

# A hard ceiling on the request itself, separate from the pass condition. See
# the RunConfig comment in 10-canary.yaml: exceeding the pass condition must
# produce a recorded failure with a duration, not a killed run with no data.
REQUEST_TIMEOUT_S = 30


def acceptable_response_ms():
    """Questionnaire 7.4, read from the one place that holds it.

    Read at RUN TIME rather than baked into an environment variable at deploy
    time. The same value is the SLA alarm threshold and the ALB alarm
    threshold; if it is changed, the canary's idea of "acceptable" must change
    in the same moment, not at the next stack update. A stale pass condition
    would report the service as meeting an SLA it no longer has.
    """
    if not RESPONSE_MS_PARAM:
        raise RuntimeError(
            "RESPONSE_MS_PARAM is unset. The canary has no pass condition and "
            "will not guess one: a canary that passes everything is worse than "
            "no canary, because it reports health it never checked.")
    return int(ssm.get_parameter(Name=RESPONSE_MS_PARAM)["Parameter"]["Value"])


def auth_header():
    """Credentials from Secrets Manager, never from the canary configuration.

    Synthetics environment variables are stored and displayed in plaintext, so
    a credential placed in one is readable by anyone who can describe the
    canary. The canary holds the ARN and fetches the value on each run, which
    also means a rotated secret takes effect without redeploying anything.

    Two shapes are accepted, because both turn up in practice:
        {"header": "Authorization", "value": "Bearer ..."}
        {"username": "...", "password": "..."}       -> HTTP basic
    """
    if not AUTH_SECRET_ARN:
        return {}
    raw = secrets.get_secret_value(SecretId=AUTH_SECRET_ARN)["SecretString"]
    data = json.loads(raw)
    if "header" in data and "value" in data:
        return {data["header"]: data["value"]}
    if "username" in data and "password" in data:
        import base64
        token = base64.b64encode(
            f"{data['username']}:{data['password']}".encode()).decode()
        return {"Authorization": f"Basic {token}"}
    raise RuntimeError(
        "The auth secret matched neither supported shape. Expected either "
        "header/value or username/password. The secret VALUE is not logged "
        "here and must not be added to this message.")


def publish_response_time(elapsed_ms):
    """Emit ResponseTimeMs. Best-effort: a metric failure must not fail the run.

    The check has already happened by the time this is called. Raising here
    would turn "the service is fine but CloudWatch was briefly unavailable" into
    a canary failure, and the canary failing is the signal that pages someone.
    """
    if not CANARY_NAME:
        return
    try:
        cloudwatch.put_metric_data(
            Namespace="CloudWatchSynthetics",
            MetricData=[{
                "MetricName": "ResponseTimeMs",
                "Dimensions": [{"Name": "CanaryName", "Value": CANARY_NAME}],
                "Value": elapsed_ms,
                "Unit": "Milliseconds",
            }])
    except Exception as exc:
        logger.info(json.dumps({
            "could_not_publish_response_time": f"{type(exc).__name__}: {exc}"}))


def check():
    limit_ms = acceptable_response_ms()
    headers = {"User-Agent": "AltDigital-Platform-Canary/1.0"}
    headers.update(auth_header())

    req = urllib.request.Request(ENDPOINT, headers=headers, method="GET")
    ctx = ssl.create_default_context()

    started = time.monotonic()
    try:
        with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=REQUEST_TIMEOUT_S,
                                    context=ctx) as resp:
            status = resp.status
            body = resp.read(65536).decode("utf-8", errors="replace")
    except urllib.error.HTTPError as exc:
        # An HTTP error is a RESULT, not a transport failure — a 503 is exactly
        # the thing this canary exists to catch, so it is measured rather than
        # raised.
        status = exc.code
        body = exc.read(65536).decode("utf-8", errors="replace")
    elapsed_ms = int((time.monotonic() - started) * 1000)

    failures = []
    if status != EXPECTED_STATUS:
        failures.append(f"status {status}, expected {EXPECTED_STATUS}")
    if BODY_MUST_CONTAIN and BODY_MUST_CONTAIN not in body:
        # The body itself is NOT logged. It is tenant application output and may
        # carry anything the application renders for an authenticated user.
        failures.append(
            f"body did not contain the expected marker "
            f"({len(BODY_MUST_CONTAIN)} chars); response was {len(body)} bytes")
    if elapsed_ms > limit_ms:
        # The pass condition from questionnaire 7.4. A service that answers
        # correctly but too slowly has failed — that is the whole point of
        # asking for an acceptable response time rather than inferring one.
        failures.append(f"took {elapsed_ms}ms, acceptable is {limit_ms}ms")

    # The SLA measurement, published as its own metric.
    #
    # NOT the built-in Duration metric, which measures the whole canary RUN:
    # container start, boto3 initialisation, the step, and teardown. Measured on
    # the first live run against a service that answered in 185ms, Duration
    # reported 10,100ms. An SLA alarm on Duration therefore thresholds our own
    # cold start against the tenant's agreed response time and fires constantly
    # — and worse, would have been reported to the tenant as their number.
    #
    # This is the elapsed time of the request itself and nothing else.
    publish_response_time(elapsed_ms)

    logger.info(json.dumps({
        "endpoint": ENDPOINT, "status": status, "elapsed_ms": elapsed_ms,
        "acceptable_ms": limit_ms, "passed": not failures,
    }))

    if failures:
        raise RuntimeError(
            f"Canary failed against {ENDPOINT}: " + "; ".join(failures))
    return elapsed_ms


async def handler(event=None, context=None):
    """Async because execute_step is a coroutine from syn-python-selenium 3.0 on.

    A synchronous handler calling it does not fail in any way that names the
    cause: the coroutine is never awaited, the runtime tries to serialise it
    into the run report, and the canary reports

        Object of type coroutine is not JSON serializable

    which reads like a bug in the canary's own data handling. Found on the first
    live run against syn-python-selenium-12.0.
    """
    if not ENDPOINT:
        raise RuntimeError("ENDPOINT is unset; nothing to check.")
    if IN_RUNTIME:
        # Wrapping in a named step is what emits SuccessPercent and Duration.
        # Without it the canary runs and reports nothing, which looks identical
        # to a canary that is passing.
        return await syn_webdriver.execute_step("heartbeat", check)
    return check()

"""Turn a finished Fargate test run into CloudWatch Synthetics metrics.

Prompt 4.3: the Fargate runner must publish "on the same metric names, so the
downstream alarm path is identical either way". This is the piece that makes
that true.

Why this exists at all
----------------------
CloudWatch Synthetics has no Playwright runtime, so a tenant with an existing
Playwright suite cannot be monitored natively. The suite runs on Fargate
instead — unmodified, with nothing injected into their image — and this
function reads the outcome from the task's exit code.

The contract is the exit code and nothing else. A reporting shim mounted into
their container would make the platform a participant in their test run: a shim
that breaks takes their suite down, and a shim that needs their Node version
makes their image upgrade our problem. Exit code zero is the one contract every
test runner already honours.

Namespace
---------
Publishing into `CloudWatchSynthetics` is possible because it is not an `AWS/`
reserved namespace — CloudWatch only refuses PutMetricData for namespaces
beginning `AWS/`. That single fact is what lets one alarm serve both runners
instead of two alarms that must be kept in step by hand.
"""
import datetime
import json
import os

import boto3

cloudwatch = boto3.client("cloudwatch")

CANARY_NAME = os.environ.get("CANARY_NAME", "")
NAMESPACE = "CloudWatchSynthetics"


def _parse(ts):
    """ECS timestamps are ISO 8601 with a Z suffix Python 3.11+ accepts."""
    if not ts:
        return None
    return datetime.datetime.fromisoformat(ts.replace("Z", "+00:00"))


def handler(event, context):
    detail = (event or {}).get("detail") or {}

    containers = detail.get("containers") or []
    # `suite` is the essential container in the task definition. Reading it by
    # name rather than taking containers[0] because a task with a sidecar would
    # otherwise report the sidecar's exit code, and the failure mode of that is
    # a canary that passes while the suite fails.
    suite = next((c for c in containers if c.get("name") == "suite"), None)

    if suite is None:
        # No verdict is available. Publishing a 0 here would report the service
        # as broken when what actually happened is that the platform could not
        # find the result, and publishing a 100 would report health nobody
        # measured. Neither is honest, so this raises: the function's Errors
        # alarm fires, and CanaryFailedAlarm breaches on missing data anyway,
        # which is the correct outcome for "the check did not produce a result".
        raise RuntimeError(json.dumps({
            "reason": "no container named 'suite' in the task state change",
            "task": detail.get("taskArn"),
            "containers": [c.get("name") for c in containers],
            "note": "not publishing a metric; a guessed verdict is worse than "
                    "a missing one, and CanaryFailedAlarm treats missing data "
                    "as breaching.",
        }))

    exit_code = suite.get("exitCode")
    stop_code = detail.get("stopCode")

    if exit_code is None:
        # The container never reported an exit code — killed by the agent,
        # out of memory, image pull failure, or capacity. That is a failed
        # check: the suite did not run, so the service is unverified, and an
        # unverified service is reported as failing rather than silently
        # skipped.
        success = 0.0
        reason = f"no exit code (stopCode={stop_code}, " \
                 f"reason={suite.get('reason') or detail.get('stoppedReason')})"
    else:
        success = 100.0 if exit_code == 0 else 0.0
        reason = f"exit code {exit_code}"

    started, stopped = _parse(detail.get("startedAt")), _parse(detail.get("stoppedAt"))
    # startedAt, not createdAt: the gap between them is Fargate provisioning
    # the task, which is platform latency and not the tenant's response time.
    # Including it would make the SLA alarm fire on our own scheduling.
    duration_ms = int((stopped - started).total_seconds() * 1000) \
        if started and stopped else None

    metrics = [{
        "MetricName": "SuccessPercent",
        "Dimensions": [{"Name": "CanaryName", "Value": CANARY_NAME}],
        "Value": success,
        "Unit": "Percent",
    }]
    if duration_ms is not None:
        metrics.append({
            "MetricName": "Duration",
            "Dimensions": [{"Name": "CanaryName", "Value": CANARY_NAME}],
            "Value": duration_ms,
            "Unit": "Milliseconds",
        })
    if stopped:
        # Timestamped to when the run finished rather than to now. A results
        # event delivered late would otherwise land in the wrong period and
        # could clear an alarm with a stale verdict.
        for m in metrics:
            m["Timestamp"] = stopped

    cloudwatch.put_metric_data(Namespace=NAMESPACE, MetricData=metrics)

    out = {"canary": CANARY_NAME, "success_percent": success,
           "duration_ms": duration_ms, "reason": reason,
           "task": (detail.get("taskArn") or "").rsplit("/", 1)[-1]}
    print(json.dumps(out))
    return out

"""Files change records. Prompt 8.2's write half, kept deliberately apart.

Why this is a separate module from jira.py
------------------------------------------
`jira.py` is read-only by construction and `scripts/publish-change.sh` refuses
to package it if a write-shaped function appears. That guard exists because a
credential able to edit issues could manufacture the approval it then verifies,
which would make the quorum control (8.3) circular.

None of that changes because the platform now files records. What changes is
that there are two jobs, and they get two modules, two Lambda functions and two
IAM roles:

    jira.py      reads.  Used by reconciliation and by quorum verification.
    filer.py     writes. Used by nothing that verifies anything.

WHAT THIS DOES NOT BUY, stated plainly: real separation needs two Atlassian
accounts, and there is one. The account behind the shared credential can write
regardless of which module reads the secret, and it is currently a human who is
also an approver. So this is code-level separation over a credential that does
not yet have it. B-070 carries the fix -- a genuine service account, which will
not be an approver -- and that is the thing that makes the quorum control sound
rather than merely tidy.

One hard line, enforced in the publish guard: this module never APPROVES and
never TRANSITIONS. Filing a change and approving it are different acts, and the
platform may only do the first. If it could do both, the record it files would
prove nothing.

Two ways to create a record, and the difference matters
-------------------------------------------------------
A change record created through `/rest/api/3/issue` is a valid Change issue and
is NOT a JSM request. It carries no Request Type -- JSM calls that field
`vp-origin` -- and every servicedeskapi endpoint returns 404 for it, including
the approval endpoint. It will not appear in a portal queue and cannot carry an
approval.

That was discovered by asking AMI-1 for its approvals and getting:

    404  Either you do not have access to this request type, or it does not
         exist.   i18nKey: sd.customerview.error.vpOriginMissing

So where the project is a service desk with a matching request type, records are
raised as REQUESTS, which is what makes them approvable and therefore what makes
quorum verification (8.3) possible at all. Where it is not -- a tenant on plain
Jira Software, which not every tenant project will avoid being -- the issue API
is used and the record is still a record, just not an approvable one.

The two paths take different payloads for the same field, which is the trap
this module exists to absorb: the issue API takes rich text as ADF, the request
API takes it as a plain string. Values are therefore held in their raw form and
rendered per path, rather than being built once and sent to whichever endpoint
happened to answer.

Field ids are resolved by NAME, never hardcoded
-----------------------------------------------
`customfield_10059` is "Implementation plan" on this site and something else
entirely on another. The ids are discovered per run from read-only metadata, so
this survives a different Jira, a reconfigured project, and the tenant projects
that do not exist yet.
"""
import datetime
import json
import os
import urllib.error
import urllib.parse
import urllib.request

import boto3

import jira

secrets = boto3.client("secretsmanager")

JIRA_SECRET_NAME = os.environ.get("JIRA_SECRET_NAME",
                                  "platform/jira/service-account")
OPS_PROJECT = os.environ.get("JIRA_OPS_PROJECT", "")
CHANGE_ISSUETYPE = os.environ.get("JIRA_CHANGE_ISSUETYPE", "[System] Change")
# The request type whose issues are change records. Matched by NAME because the
# numeric id differs per site; "Request a change" is JSM's own default name for
# the change management request type.
CHANGE_REQUEST_TYPE = os.environ.get("JIRA_CHANGE_REQUEST_TYPE",
                                     "Request a change")
TIMEOUT = int(os.environ.get("JIRA_TIMEOUT_SECONDS", "30"))

# Groups whose members authorise a change.
#
# The Authorize stage of the change workflow requires one approval from each
# group named in the record's "Approver groups" field. A record filed without
# any group is therefore UNAPPROVABLE -- and an unapproved record does not
# cover a deployment, so the platform's own build work would be reported as
# unapproved change by the control the build work is creating.
#
# Worth being exact about what this does and does not achieve: one group
# containing one person satisfies Jira's rule and does NOT satisfy design 03,
# which requires two approvals from distinct people with the requester
# excluded. Nothing here enforces that. The quorum verifier counts distinct
# approver identities itself, which is design 08's instruction to validate
# rather than trust the ticket.
APPROVER_GROUPS = [g.strip() for g in
                   os.environ.get("JIRA_APPROVER_GROUPS", "").split(",")
                   if g.strip()]

# Defaults for build-phase records, decided with Jamie 2026-09-19.
#
# Standard, and the label is not decoration. "Standard" in ITIL means
# pre-approved, low-risk and repeatable, and novel platform build work is none
# of those -- it is being called Standard so that records count as approved
# while the platform is being built, and `build-phase` is what stops that
# category being silently overclaimed later. Switch to Normal once the platform
# is in service.
DEFAULT_CHANGE_TYPE = os.environ.get("CHANGE_TYPE_DEFAULT", "Standard")
DEFAULT_REASON = os.environ.get("CHANGE_REASON_DEFAULT", "New functionality")
BUILD_LABEL = "build-phase"


def _now():
    return datetime.datetime.now(datetime.timezone.utc)


def _jira_dt(dt):
    """Jira wants an offset without a colon: 2026-09-19T12:00:00.000+0000."""
    return dt.astimezone(datetime.timezone.utc).strftime(
        "%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S.000+0000")


def _adf(text):
    """Plain text as an Atlassian Document Format document.

    The issue API takes rich text as ADF, not as a string. Newlines become
    separate paragraphs, because a plan collapsed onto one line is not a plan
    anybody can follow at 3am.
    """
    paragraphs = str(text or "").split("\n")
    return {
        "type": "doc", "version": 1,
        "content": [
            {"type": "paragraph",
             "content": ([{"type": "text", "text": p}] if p.strip() else [])}
            for p in paragraphs
        ] or [{"type": "paragraph", "content": []}],
    }


# Jira custom field types that take ADF on the ISSUE api. Substring match:
# Atlassian namespaces these as
# com.atlassian.jira.plugin.system.customfieldtypes:textarea and JSM adds its
# own, so the discriminating part is the tail.
_RICH_TEXT_CUSTOM_TYPES = ("textarea", "richtext")

# System fields that are rich text and carry no `custom` type at all.
_RICH_TEXT_SYSTEM_FIELDS = ("description", "environment")


def _is_rich_text(field):
    """Does this field take ADF on the issue API?

    `schema.type` says "string" for both plain and rich text, which is the trap
    that cost the first filing attempt: three fields rejected as "not valid
    Atlassian Document Format" with nothing in the metadata obviously saying
    why. The custom type is the discriminator. B-075.
    """
    custom = (field.get("custom") or "").lower()
    if any(t in custom for t in _RICH_TEXT_CUSTOM_TYPES):
        return True
    return field.get("id") in _RICH_TEXT_SYSTEM_FIELDS


def _request(path, payload, method="POST"):
    url = f"{jira._site()}{path}"
    req = urllib.request.Request(
        url, data=json.dumps(payload).encode("utf-8"),
        headers={"Authorization": jira._auth_header(),
                 "Accept": "application/json",
                 "Content-Type": "application/json"},
        method=method)
    try:
        with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=TIMEOUT) as resp:
            body = resp.read().decode("utf-8")
            return json.loads(body) if body else {}
    except urllib.error.HTTPError as exc:
        detail = ""
        try:
            detail = exc.read().decode("utf-8")[:800]
        except Exception:                          # noqa: BLE001
            pass
        # Jira reports a rejected field by its CUSTOM FIELD ID, not its label,
        # so the raw body is kept whole. "customfield_10059 is not valid
        # Atlassian Document Format" means nothing without it, and the three
        # plausible causes -- wrong format, wrong value, field not on the
        # screen -- are not distinguishable from a summarised message.
        raise jira.JiraUnavailable(
            f"Jira rejected {method} {path} with HTTP {exc.code}: {detail}"
        ) from exc
    except (urllib.error.URLError, TimeoutError, OSError) as exc:
        raise jira.JiraUnavailable(f"could not reach Jira: {exc}") from exc


def _post(path, payload):
    return _request(path, payload, "POST")


def _field_ids(project, issue_type_name):
    """Map field NAME -> metadata for creating this issue type."""
    id_to_name = jira.project_issue_type_map(project)
    type_id = {v: k for k, v in id_to_name.items()}.get(issue_type_name)
    if not type_id:
        raise jira.JiraUnavailable(
            f"project {project} has no issue type '{issue_type_name}'. "
            f"It has: {', '.join(sorted(id_to_name.values()))}")
    by_name = {}
    for f in jira.field_requirements(project, type_id):
        if f.get("name"):
            by_name[f["name"]] = f
    return by_name


def _request_form(project):
    """The service desk and request type that raise a change, or None.

    None is a normal answer, not an error: a tenant on plain Jira Software has
    no service desk, and a record filed there is still a record. What it is not
    is approvable, and the caller says so in its output rather than letting a
    quorum check discover it later as a 404.
    """
    try:
        desks = jira.service_desks()
    except jira.JiraUnavailable:
        # No JSM on this site at all. Not fatal; the issue API still works.
        return None
    for desk in desks:
        if desk.get("project_key") != project:
            continue
        for rt in jira.request_types(desk["id"]):
            if (rt.get("name") or "").lower() == CHANGE_REQUEST_TYPE.lower():
                form = jira.request_type_fields(desk["id"], rt["id"])
                return {"service_desk_id": desk["id"],
                        "request_type_id": rt["id"],
                        "request_type_name": rt.get("name"),
                        "fields": form["fields"]}
    return None


def file_change(event, context=None):
    """Open a change record BEFORE the work, per Jamie's decision.

    Returns the issue key. Everything the platform then does is expected to
    reference it, which is what lets reconciliation match a deployment to the
    record that authorised it rather than to whatever else was open at the time.
    """
    project = event.get("project") or OPS_PROJECT
    if not project:
        raise ValueError("no project: set JIRA_OPS_PROJECT or pass project")
    summary = event.get("summary")
    if not summary:
        raise ValueError("a change record without a summary is not a record")

    start = _now()
    end = start + datetime.timedelta(
        hours=float(event.get("window_hours") or 4))

    # Values in their RAW form, keyed by field name. Rendering is deferred
    # because the two creation paths disagree about the shape of rich text:
    # the issue API wants ADF, the request API wants a plain string. Building
    # the payload once and sending it to whichever endpoint answered is exactly
    # how this module would send ADF to an endpoint that rejects it.
    desired = {
        "Change type": {"value": event.get("change_type")
                        or DEFAULT_CHANGE_TYPE},
        "Change reason": {"value": event.get("reason") or DEFAULT_REASON},
        "Change risk": {"value": event.get("risk") or "Low"},
        "Impact": {"value": event.get("impact") or "Minor / Localized"},
        "Planned start": _jira_dt(start),
        "Planned end": _jira_dt(end),
        "Implementation plan": event.get("plan"),
        "Backout plan": event.get("backout"),
        "Test plan": event.get("test_plan"),
        "Business Test Plan": event.get("business_test_plan"),
        "Description": event.get("description") or event.get("reason_text"),
    }
    # A multigrouppicker takes [{"name": ...}]. Omitted entirely when no group
    # is configured, rather than sent empty: an empty value would overwrite a
    # default the project might set for itself.
    groups = event.get("approver_groups") or APPROVER_GROUPS
    if groups:
        desired["Approver groups"] = [{"name": g} for g in groups]
    # `extra` reaches a field this code has never heard of, by name:
    # {"Business Test Plan": "..."}. Tenant projects will not all look like
    # AMI, and a field added to a screen should not need a code change.
    desired.update(event.get("extra") or {})

    # Accounts travel as labels. Reconciliation reads `account-<id>` to decide
    # which deployments a change record covers, so a record that loses them
    # matches nothing and every deployment in that account is reported as
    # unapproved. That is why a label failure below is fatal rather than
    # cosmetic.
    labels = [BUILD_LABEL] + [f"account-{a}"
                              for a in (event.get("accounts") or [])]

    form = _request_form(project)
    if form:
        result = _raise_request(project, form, summary, desired, labels)
    else:
        result = _create_issue(project, summary, desired, labels)

    out = {"record_type": "change-record-filed",
           "project": project, "summary": summary,
           "planned_start": _jira_dt(start), "planned_end": _jira_dt(end),
           "labels": labels,
           "approvable": bool(form),
           **result}
    print(json.dumps(out, default=str))
    return out


def _create_issue(project, summary, desired, labels):
    """Plain issue API. Everything in one call, but not a JSM request."""
    available = _field_ids(project, CHANGE_ISSUETYPE)
    fields = {"project": {"key": project},
              "issuetype": {"name": CHANGE_ISSUETYPE},
              "summary": summary[:250]}
    wrapped = []
    for name, value in desired.items():
        f = available.get(name)
        if f is None or value is None:
            continue
        if _is_rich_text(f) and isinstance(value, str):
            value = _adf(value)
            wrapped.append(name)
        fields[f["id"]] = value
    if "Labels" in available and labels:
        fields["labels"] = labels

    created = _post("/rest/api/3/issue", {"fields": fields})
    return {"key": created.get("key"),
            "created_via": "issue-api",
            "rich_text_fields": sorted(wrapped),
            "fields_set": sorted(k for k in fields
                                 if k not in ("project", "issuetype",
                                              "summary")),
            "fields_unavailable": sorted(n for n, v in desired.items()
                                         if v is not None
                                         and n not in available),
            # Said plainly rather than left to be discovered by a 404 during a
            # quorum check: this record cannot carry a JSM approval.
            "approval_note": (
                f"{project} has no '{CHANGE_REQUEST_TYPE}' request type, so "
                "this record was created through the issue API. It is not a "
                "JSM request and cannot carry an approval.")}


def _raise_request(project, form, summary, desired, labels):
    """JSM request API. Approvable, but the form takes a narrower field set.

    Two differences from the issue API, both learned from the live form rather
    than assumed:

    - Rich text goes as a PLAIN STRING. The request API renders it; sending ADF
      here is the mirror image of B-075.
    - The form is NARROWER than the issue. Labels and Approver groups are both
      absent from it, and both are load-bearing. So anything the form cannot
      take but the issue can is applied immediately afterwards in one edit.

    That edit happens before any approval can exist -- the record is created in
    the stage preceding Authorize -- so it cannot disturb design 08 condition
    4, "the issue has not been reopened or edited since approval".
    """
    by_name = {f.get("name"): f for f in form["fields"] if f.get("name")}

    values = {"summary": summary[:250]}
    deferred = {}
    for name, value in desired.items():
        if value is None:
            continue
        f = by_name.get(name)
        if f is None:
            # Not rejected -- postponed. The issue may still accept it.
            deferred[name] = value
            continue
        values[f["id"]] = value

    created = _post("/rest/servicedeskapi/request", {
        "serviceDeskId": str(form["service_desk_id"]),
        "requestTypeId": str(form["request_type_id"]),
        "requestFieldValues": values,
    })
    key = created.get("issueKey") or created.get("issueId")

    applied, unavailable = _apply_deferred(project, key, deferred, labels)
    return {"key": key,
            "created_via": "jsm-request",
            "request_type": form.get("request_type_name"),
            "fields_set": sorted(k for k in values if k != "summary"),
            "fields_deferred_to_edit": sorted(applied),
            "fields_unavailable": sorted(unavailable)}


def _apply_deferred(project, key, deferred, labels):
    """Set what the request form could not, in one edit on the issue.

    Returns (applied field names, names nothing can carry).

    FATAL on failure, deliberately, and the two fields that drive that are the
    reason this function is not best-effort:

      labels          reconciliation reads `account-<id>` to decide which
                      deployments a record covers. A record that lost them
                      matches nothing, so every deployment in that account is
                      reported as unapproved -- a false accusation produced by
                      a half-successful filing.

      Approver groups the Authorize stage needs one approval per named group.
                      A record with none cannot be approved at all, and an
                      unapproved record does not cover a deployment either.

    Both failure modes are silent and both surface later as findings about
    somebody else. A loud failure naming the key and what to add by hand is
    strictly better than a record that looks complete and quietly breaks the
    control that reads it.
    """
    if not key or (not deferred and not labels):
        return [], []

    available = _field_ids(project, CHANGE_ISSUETYPE)
    fields = {}
    applied = []
    unavailable = []
    for name, value in deferred.items():
        f = available.get(name)
        if f is None:
            # On neither the form nor the issue. Genuinely not configured.
            unavailable.append(name)
            continue
        # The issue API's shapes, not the request API's -- this is the same
        # value rendered for a different endpoint. B-075 in the other
        # direction.
        if _is_rich_text(f) and isinstance(value, str):
            value = _adf(value)
        fields[f["id"]] = value
        applied.append(name)

    payload = {}
    if fields:
        payload["fields"] = fields
    if labels:
        # `update` rather than `fields`, so this adds to whatever the project
        # may already have set rather than replacing it.
        payload["update"] = {"labels": [{"add": l} for l in labels]}
        applied.append("Labels")
    if not payload:
        return applied, unavailable

    try:
        _request(f"/rest/api/3/issue/{urllib.parse.quote(key)}",
                 payload, method="PUT")
    except jira.JiraUnavailable as exc:
        wanted = ", ".join(sorted(applied))
        raise jira.JiraUnavailable(
            f"{key} was raised, but these could not be set on it: {wanted}\n"
            f"      {exc}\n"
            f"      Fix {key} by hand before relying on it. Without labels "
            "reconciliation cannot match this record to the deployments it "
            "authorises, and without an approver group it cannot be approved "
            "at all -- either way the deployments it covers will be reported "
            "as unapproved.") from exc
    return applied, unavailable


def complete_change(event, context=None):
    """Record what actually happened, after the work.

    A comment rather than a field edit. The plan is what was intended and
    should stay legible as such; the outcome is a separate statement with its
    own timestamp. Overwriting the plan with the result would destroy the one
    comparison an auditor wants to make -- and would also be an edit after
    approval, which design 08 condition 4 treats as invalidating.
    """
    key = event.get("key")
    if not key:
        raise ValueError("complete_change needs the issue key")
    result = event.get("result") or "Completed."
    body = f"*Completed* {_now().isoformat()}\n\n{result}"
    _post(f"/rest/api/3/issue/{urllib.parse.quote(key)}/comment",
          {"body": _adf(body)})
    out = {"record_type": "change-record-completed", "key": key}
    print(json.dumps(out, default=str))
    return out


HANDLERS = {"file": file_change, "complete": complete_change}


def handler(event, context):
    action = event.get("action") or "file"
    fn = HANDLERS.get(action)
    if fn is None:
        raise ValueError(
            f"unknown action '{action}'. Known: {', '.join(sorted(HANDLERS))}")
    return fn(event, context)
