#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Validate design/06a-alarm-specification.yaml and emit it as JSON.

    validate_alarm_spec.py <spec.yaml> <out.json>

Run by scripts/publish-instrumentation.sh before packaging. A malformed
specification would otherwise surface as every instrumentation invocation
erroring at cold start, in every member account, with a stack trace instead of
a reason.

The structural checks matter more than the field checks. An in-scope resource
type with no resolvable alarm set means resources of that type come up with no
alarms AND no exception record — the handler would look them up, find nothing,
and raise "no-alarm-set", which is at least visible. Worse is a type in neither
list: that produces an exception per resource forever. Both are caught here,
before anything is deployed.
"""
import json
import sys

try:
    import yaml
except ImportError:
    sys.exit("PyYAML is required: python -m pip install --user pyyaml")

VALID_TMD = {"missing", "ignore", "breaching", "notBreaching"}
REQUIRED_TOP = ("tiers", "routing_destinations", "defaults",
                "resource_types_in_scope", "resource_types_no_alarms", "alarm_sets")


def main():
    src, dst = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2]
    with open(src, encoding="utf-8") as fh:
        cfg = yaml.safe_load(fh)

    for key in REQUIRED_TOP:
        if key not in cfg:
            sys.exit(f"06a is missing required key: {key}")

    problems = []
    tier_names = set(cfg["tiers"])
    valid_routing = set(cfg["routing_destinations"])
    sets = cfg["alarm_sets"]

    def resolve(rt, seen=None):
        """Flatten inherits. Returns None when the type has no entry at all."""
        seen = seen or set()
        if rt in seen:
            problems.append(f"inherits cycle at {rt}")
            return []
        seen.add(rt)
        c = sets.get(rt)
        if c is None:
            return None
        out = []
        if c.get("inherits"):
            parent = resolve(c["inherits"], seen)
            if parent is None:
                problems.append(f"{rt} inherits {c['inherits']}, which has no alarm set")
            else:
                out.extend(parent)
        out.extend(c.get("alarms") or [])
        out.extend(c.get("additional_alarms") or [])
        return out

    total = 0
    for rt in cfg["resource_types_in_scope"]:
        alarms = resolve(rt)
        if alarms is None:
            problems.append(f"{rt} is in resource_types_in_scope but alarm_sets has no entry")
            continue
        if not alarms:
            problems.append(f"{rt} is in scope but resolves to zero alarms")
        total += len(alarms)
        for a in alarms:
            aid = a.get("id", "?")

            # Two shapes, and conflating them was the first thing this
            # validator got wrong.
            #
            #   metric: <name>   a CloudWatch metric alarm. Needs a comparison
            #                    and a threshold per tier.
            #   metric: event    an EventBridge rule. 06a says so in as many
            #                    words: "EventBridge rule, not a metric alarm."
            #                    It has event_categories or event_names and a
            #                    source, and a threshold would be meaningless.
            #
            # Requiring `comparison` of an event entry rejected six perfectly
            # valid alarms in the authoritative spec.
            if a.get("metric") == "event":
                if not a.get("source"):
                    problems.append(f"{rt}/{aid}: event alarm without a 'source'")
                # Three different keys carry the event selector, one per
                # source: event_categories (RDS), event_names (CloudTrail),
                # event_types (Auto Scaling). Accepting only the first two
                # rejected asg-failed-scaling, which is valid.
                if not any(a.get(k) for k in
                           ("event_categories", "event_names", "event_types")):
                    problems.append(
                        f"{rt}/{aid}: event alarm with no selector — needs one of "
                        "event_categories, event_names or event_types")
                if not a.get("severity_by_tier"):
                    problems.append(
                        f"{rt}/{aid}: event alarm without severity_by_tier, so it routes nowhere")
                continue

            for field in ("metric", "comparison", "threshold_by_tier"):
                if field not in a:
                    problems.append(f"{rt}/{aid}: missing '{field}'")
            tmd = a.get("treat_missing_data")
            if tmd and tmd not in VALID_TMD:
                problems.append(f"{rt}/{aid}: treat_missing_data '{tmd}' is not valid")
            for t in (a.get("threshold_by_tier") or {}):
                if t not in tier_names:
                    problems.append(f"{rt}/{aid}: threshold_by_tier names unknown tier '{t}'")
            for t, r in (a.get("severity_by_tier") or {}).items():
                if r not in valid_routing:
                    problems.append(
                        f"{rt}/{aid}: severity_by_tier[{t}] = '{r}' is not a routing destination")

    overlap = set(cfg["resource_types_in_scope"]) & set(cfg["resource_types_no_alarms"])
    if overlap:
        problems.append(f"types in BOTH in_scope and no_alarms: {sorted(overlap)}")

    for tier, tcfg in cfg["tiers"].items():
        dr = tcfg.get("default_routing")
        if dr not in valid_routing:
            problems.append(f"tiers.{tier}.default_routing = '{dr}' is not a routing destination")

    if problems:
        sys.exit("06a is invalid:\n  " + "\n  ".join(problems))

    with open(dst, "w", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
        json.dump(cfg, fh, indent=2)

    # Per-tier counts, printed because they are the quickest sanity check that
    # the tier gradation is doing anything: dev and prod should differ a lot.
    print(f"  {len(cfg['resource_types_in_scope'])} type(s) in scope, "
          f"{len(cfg['resource_types_no_alarms'])} known-no-alarms, "
          f"{total} resolved alarm spec(s)")
    for tier in cfg["tiers"]:
        creatable = nulls = 0
        for rt in cfg["resource_types_in_scope"]:
            for a in (resolve(rt) or []):
                if a.get("metric") == "event":
                    continue
                bt = a.get("threshold_by_tier") or {}
                if tier in bt:
                    if bt[tier] is None:
                        nulls += 1
                    else:
                        creatable += 1
        note = f"  ({nulls} [TUNE] unset -> exceptions)" if nulls else ""
        print(f"    {tier:5s} {creatable:3d} creatable{note}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Validate runbooks/catalog.yaml against actions.py, and emit it as JSON.

    validate_catalog.py <catalog.yaml> <actions.py> <out.json>

Two failure modes this exists to prevent, both of which would otherwise appear
for the first time when an alarm fires on a customer's production resource:

  a catalog naming an action with no implementation
      the engine raises mid-incident, having already decided to act

  an implementation of a REFUSED action
      the platform quietly regains a capability somebody decided against, and
      nothing about the deployment looks unusual

The second is the reason the refused list is duplicated here rather than only
in the catalog's comments. A comment records a decision; this enforces it.
"""
import json
import re
import sys

try:
    import yaml
except ImportError:
    sys.exit("PyYAML is required: python -m pip install --user pyyaml")

# Refused on 2026-09-18, D-012b. Implementing one of these is caught at
# packaging rather than discovered later.
REFUSED = {
    "expand_volume", "expand_storage", "flush_cache", "rds_failover",
    "drain_and_replace", "release_db_connections", "terminate_instance",
    "deregister_target", "promote_read_replica",
}

REQUIRED_TOP = ("schema_version", "default_gather", "failure_policy",
                "settle_seconds", "runbooks")


def alarm_ids_from_spec(spec_path):
    """Every alarm id 06a defines, following inherits.

    The catalog is keyed on these. A key that is not one of them silently finds
    no runbook — no error, no log line, just an incident nobody responded to.
    That happened once: `rds-storage-low` against 06a's `rds-free-storage-low`.
    """
    with open(spec_path, encoding="utf-8") as fh:
        spec = yaml.safe_load(fh)
    sets = spec.get("alarm_sets") or {}

    def resolve(rt, seen=None):
        seen = seen or set()
        if rt in seen:
            return []
        seen.add(rt)
        c = sets.get(rt)
        if c is None:
            return None
        out = []
        if c.get("inherits"):
            out.extend(resolve(c["inherits"], seen) or [])
        out.extend(c.get("alarms") or [])
        out.extend(c.get("additional_alarms") or [])
        return out

    return {rt: {a["id"] for a in (resolve(rt) or [])} for rt in sets}


def main():
    cat_path, actions_path, out_path = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2], sys.argv[3]
    spec_path = sys.argv[4] if len(sys.argv) > 4 else None
    with open(cat_path, encoding="utf-8") as fh:
        cat = yaml.safe_load(fh)
    src = open(actions_path, encoding="utf-8").read()

    problems = [f"missing top-level key: {k}" for k in REQUIRED_TOP if k not in cat]
    if problems:
        sys.exit("catalog is invalid:\n  " + "\n  ".join(problems))

    implemented = set(re.findall(r'^\s+"([a-z_]+)": _', src, re.M))

    named_actions = set()
    named_gather = set(cat.get("default_gather") or [])
    stage3_unchecked = []
    scale_out_unchecked = []

    for rtype, rbs in (cat.get("runbooks") or {}).items():
        for aid, rb in (rbs or {}).items():
            named_gather |= set(rb.get("gather") or [])
            for spec in (rb.get("stage_3") or []):
                named_actions.add(spec["action"])
                if spec.get("requires_redundancy") is not True:
                    stage3_unchecked.append(f"{rtype}/{aid}/{spec['action']}")
            for spec in (rb.get("stage_2") or []):
                named_actions.add(spec["action"])
                if spec["action"] == "scale_out" and \
                        spec.get("requires_scale_in_policy") is not True:
                    scale_out_unchecked.append(f"{rtype}/{aid}")

    for a in sorted(named_actions - implemented):
        problems.append(f"catalog names action '{a}' with no implementation")
    for a in sorted(named_actions & REFUSED):
        problems.append(f"catalog names REFUSED action '{a}' (D-012b)")
    for a in sorted(implemented & REFUSED):
        problems.append(f"actions.py implements REFUSED action '{a}' (D-012b)")
    for g in sorted(named_gather - implemented):
        problems.append(f"catalog names gather step '{g}' with no entry")
    for s in stage3_unchecked:
        problems.append(f"stage 3 action without requires_redundancy: {s}")
    for s in scale_out_unchecked:
        problems.append(f"scale_out without requires_scale_in_policy: {s}")

    # Cross-check against 06a. Optional only so the validator still runs
    # without the design package present; when the path is supplied, a
    # mismatched id is fatal.
    if spec_path:
        by_type = alarm_ids_from_spec(spec_path)
        import difflib
        for rtype, rbs in (cat.get("runbooks") or {}).items():
            valid = by_type.get(rtype)
            if valid is None:
                problems.append(f"{rtype} is not a resource type in 06a")
                continue
            for aid in (rbs or {}):
                if aid not in valid:
                    near = difflib.get_close_matches(aid, sorted(valid), n=1, cutoff=0.6)
                    hint = f" (did you mean '{near[0]}'?)" if near else ""
                    problems.append(
                        f"{rtype}/'{aid}' is not a 06a alarm id{hint} — this runbook "
                        "would never be found")

    settle = cat.get("settle_seconds") or {}
    if "default" not in settle:
        for a in sorted(named_actions - set(settle)):
            problems.append(f"no settle period for '{a}' and no default")

    if problems:
        sys.exit("catalog is invalid:\n  " + "\n  ".join(problems))

    with open(out_path, "w", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
        json.dump(cat, fh, indent=2)

    runbooks = sum(len(v) for v in cat["runbooks"].values())
    print(f"  {runbooks} runbook(s), {len(named_actions)} permitted action(s), "
          f"{len(named_gather)} gather step(s)")
    print(f"  {len(REFUSED)} refused action(s) blocked at packaging")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

# people, because `terraform destroy` would then delete them.

data "pagerduty_user" "responder" {
  for_each = toset(var.responder_emails)
  email    = each.value
}

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Schedule
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# A schedule with one person in it looks like pointless indirection, and it is
# not. Design doc 13 says the escalation policy references the on-call
# schedule; pointing the policy straight at a user instead means that adding
# the second responder later is a restructure rather than an edit, and it
# happens at the moment someone is trying to hand over a pager.
#
# The layer is a 24/7 rotation because there is currently no rotation. When
# there is, this becomes a real handoff and nothing downstream changes.
#
# DEPRECATED RESOURCE, KEPT DELIBERATELY. The provider wants
# pagerduty_schedulev2, and this will have to move before v1 is removed.
#
# Not moved now because v2 replaces the simple "rotate every N seconds" model
# with calendar events carrying RRULE recurrence, effective_since and explicit
# start and end times. A mis-specified RRULE does not fail — it produces a
# schedule with a GAP, and the gap is discovered when an incident at 3am on a
# Tuesday pages nobody.
#
# That is only safe to write alongside a verification step that queries actual
# on-call coverage across a full week after applying, and that step cannot be
# written or run until PagerDuty credentials exist. Migrating blind, to clear a
# warning, would trade a deprecation notice for a silent coverage hole.
# Tracked as B-018.

resource "pagerduty_schedule" "platform" {
  name      = "AltDigital Platform On-Call"
  time_zone = "America/Chicago"

  layer {
    name                         = "Primary"
    start                        = "2026-09-17T00:00:00-05:00"
    rotation_virtual_start       = "2026-09-17T00:00:00-05:00"
    rotation_turn_length_seconds = 604800 # one week

    # Ordered by the variable, not by the set, so escalation order is the
    # order written rather than alphabetical by email.
    users = [for e in var.responder_emails : data.pagerduty_user.responder[e].id]
  }

  teams = []
}

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Escalation policy
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

resource "pagerduty_escalation_policy" "platform" {
  name      = "AltDigital Platform Escalation"
  num_loops = 2

  rule {
    escalation_delay_in_minutes = var.escalation_timeout_minutes

    target {
      type = "schedule_reference"
      id   = pagerduty_schedule.platform.id
    }
  }

  # Second rule pages every responder directly, bypassing the schedule. This
  # is the "the schedule is wrong, or the person on it is unreachable" case,
  # which is precisely when an evidence platform must not fail quietly. With a
  # single responder it is the same phone twice, fifteen minutes apart — which
  # is still the correct behaviour, and becomes materially useful the moment a
  # second name exists.
  dynamic "rule" {
    for_each = length(var.responder_emails) > 0 ? [1] : []
    content {
      escalation_delay_in_minutes = var.escalation_timeout_minutes

      dynamic "target" {
        for_each = var.responder_emails
        content {
          type = "user_reference"
          id   = data.pagerduty_user.responder[target.value].id
        }
      }
    }
  }
}

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Platform service
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

resource "pagerduty_service" "platform" {
  name                    = var.platform_service_name
  description             = "Alarms raised by the AltDigital Managed Platform itself, not by a tenant application."
  escalation_policy       = pagerduty_escalation_policy.platform.id
  alert_creation          = "create_alerts_and_incidents"
  auto_resolve_timeout    = var.auto_resolve_timeout_minutes == 0 ? "null" : tostring(var.auto_resolve_timeout_minutes * 60)
  acknowledgement_timeout = tostring(var.acknowledgement_timeout_minutes * 60)

  incident_urgency_rule {
    type    = "constant"
    urgency = "high"
  }
}

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Alert grouping
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# A separate resource rather than an alert_grouping_parameters block on the
# service. The inline block is deprecated and this is the provider's
# replacement — note that the direction inverts: the SETTING names the
# services, the service does not name the setting.
#
# "intelligent" rather than "time". Time-based grouping folds an unrelated
# second failure into the first incident, and the second failure is then
# acknowledged by someone who only read the first — which on this service could
# mean acknowledging away the alarm saying the evidence archive has stopped
# replicating.
#
# The config block is REQUIRED even though the documentation reads as though it
# is optional. Omitting it does not produce a validation error — provider
# v3.36.0 panics with a nil pointer dereference and terraform reports "Plugin
# did not respond". Worth knowing before spending time looking for the mistake
# in this file.
#
# `time_window`, not `timeout`. The provider rejects `timeout` here with
# "'timeout' is only applicable when type is time", so the two names are not
# interchangeable: `timeout` is how long a time-grouped incident stays open,
# `time_window` is the window intelligent grouping considers. 900 seconds
# matches the CloudWatch alarm period plus SNS lag, so a flapping alarm
# produces one incident rather than a page per cycle.

resource "pagerduty_alert_grouping_setting" "platform" {
  count = var.alert_grouping_type == "none" ? 0 : 1

  name     = "AltDigital Platform Grouping"
  type     = var.alert_grouping_type
  services = [pagerduty_service.platform.id]

  # Each grouping type takes a DIFFERENT set of config fields, and supplying
  # one that does not belong to the active type is rejected rather than
  # ignored. Hence the nulls: every field is present in the block and only the
  # relevant ones carry a value.
  #
  #   intelligent    time_window            (403 on non-AIOps accounts)
  #   content_based  aggregate, fields, time_window
  #   time           timeout
  config {
    # Group on the alert summary, which for the CloudWatch vendor integration
    # IS the alarm name. So repeats of one alarm collapse into one incident,
    # and two different alarms stay two incidents — which is the behaviour
    # that matters on a service carrying "the evidence archive has stopped
    # replicating".
    aggregate = var.alert_grouping_type == "content_based" ? "all" : null
    fields    = var.alert_grouping_type == "content_based" ? ["summary"] : null

    time_window = var.alert_grouping_type == "time" ? null : 900
    timeout     = var.alert_grouping_type == "time" ? 900 : null
  }
}

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# CloudWatch integration
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The vendor lookup matters. A generic Events API v2 integration would accept
# an SNS POST and render it as an unparsed JSON blob; the CloudWatch vendor
# integration understands the SNS envelope and produces an incident whose title
# is the alarm name and whose body is the alarm description.
#
# That is why the alarm descriptions in security/10-log-archive.yaml and
# alerting/10-alert-topic.yaml are written as instructions to a woken engineer
# rather than as labels. They are the page.

data "pagerduty_vendor" "cloudwatch" {
  name = "Amazon CloudWatch"
}

resource "pagerduty_service_integration" "cloudwatch" {
  name    = "AWS CloudWatch"
  service = pagerduty_service.platform.id
  vendor  = data.pagerduty_vendor.cloudwatch.id
}

# Events API v2, alongside the CloudWatch integration rather than replacing it.
#
# The CloudWatch integration exists to parse an SNS-wrapped CloudWatch alarm,
# and that is all it can do. Prompt 5.3 requires the page to carry "the full
# dossier, not just the alarm name", which means an arbitrary JSON body in
# custom_details — and a dedup_key, so that the raw alarm and the dossier that
# follows it minutes later become ONE incident rather than two pages about the
# same outage.
#
# Both integrations point at the same service and the same escalation policy.
# Keeping the CloudWatch one is deliberate: it is the path that still works if
# the router is broken, which is exactly when a page matters most.
resource "pagerduty_service_integration" "events_v2" {
  name    = "Platform Router (Events API v2)"
  service = pagerduty_service.platform.id
  type    = "events_api_v2_inbound_integration"
}

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Low-urgency service — dev and test
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 06a routes dev to `digest` and test to `digest_and_jira`, neither of which
# pages and neither of which has a destination built yet (phases 4.4 and 8).
# Until they exist those alarms were being created with no actions at all:
# real, evaluating, and heard by nobody.
#
# Sending them here instead is strictly better than silence and strictly better
# than sending them to the high-urgency service. A low-urgency PagerDuty
# incident does not ring a phone — it lands in the UI and follows the
# responder's low-urgency notification rules — so dev noise becomes something
# you can look at when you choose to, rather than something that wakes you or
# something that vanishes.
#
# INTERIM. When the digest (4.4) and Jira routing (8) exist, dev and test
# should move there and this service becomes the fallback for anything with no
# destination rather than the destination itself.

resource "pagerduty_service" "platform_low" {
  name                    = var.low_urgency_service_name
  description             = "Dev and test alarms from the AltDigital Managed Platform. Low urgency by design: these do not page."
  escalation_policy       = pagerduty_escalation_policy.platform.id
  alert_creation          = "create_alerts_and_incidents"
  acknowledgement_timeout = "null"

  # Auto-resolve IS enabled here, unlike the production service.
  #
  # On the production service auto-resolve is off because an untouched incident
  # is still a true incident. Dev is the opposite case: a build machine at 95%
  # CPU that nobody looked at for four hours is not an outstanding problem, and
  # leaving hundreds of stale dev incidents open is how the low-urgency queue
  # becomes unreadable and therefore ignored.
  auto_resolve_timeout = "14400" # 4 hours

  incident_urgency_rule {
    type    = "constant"
    urgency = "low"
  }
}

resource "pagerduty_service_integration" "cloudwatch_low" {
  name    = "AWS CloudWatch (low urgency)"
  service = pagerduty_service.platform_low.id
  vendor  = data.pagerduty_vendor.cloudwatch.id
}

resource "pagerduty_service_integration" "events_v2_low" {
  name    = "Platform Router (Events API v2)"
  service = pagerduty_service.platform_low.id
  type    = "events_api_v2_inbound_integration"
}

# Priority is set by an Event Orchestration catch-all, not by the service.
# There is no "default priority" field on a PagerDuty service — priority is an
# incident property applied by a rule, which is why this needs a whole extra
# resource to express one label.
data "pagerduty_priority" "low" {
  count = var.low_urgency_priority == "" ? 0 : 1
  name  = var.low_urgency_priority
}

resource "pagerduty_event_orchestration_service" "platform_low" {
  count = var.low_urgency_priority == "" ? 0 : 1

  service                                = pagerduty_service.platform_low.id
  enable_event_orchestration_for_service = true

  # An orchestration must declare at least one rule set even when every event
  # is meant to fall through to the catch-all. "start" is the entry point by
  # convention; leaving it ruleless means nothing is matched specially and
  # everything reaches catch_all, which is exactly the intent here — one
  # priority on everything, no conditions.
  set {
    id = "start"
  }

  catch_all {
    actions {
      priority = data.pagerduty_priority.low[0].id
    }
  }
}

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The client-conversation class — design 12's fourth destination
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# design/12-commercial-access.md:
#
#     A fourth destination in the routing design of 06, alongside PagerDuty,
#     Jira and the review queue. Defined by WHO NEEDS TO HAVE A CONVERSATION,
#     not by severity.
#
#     Implemented as a PagerDuty business service with notification rules
#     rather than paging rules.
#
# Two resources, because PagerDuty splits what that sentence joins. A BUSINESS
# service is the subscribable object — it represents a customer-facing
# capability and people subscribe to its status. It does not ingest events. A
# TECHNICAL service ingests events and has an escalation policy.
#
# So the technical service below receives what platform.commercial emits, and
# the business service is what Tina and Wayne subscribe to. Building only the
# business service would have produced something that looks right in the
# console and receives nothing.

resource "pagerduty_escalation_policy" "commercial" {
  name      = "AltDigital Commercial"
  num_loops = 0 # Do not loop. This is not a page; repeating it is not useful.

  rule {
    escalation_delay_in_minutes = 60

    target {
      type = "schedule_reference"
      id   = pagerduty_schedule.platform.id
    }
  }
}

resource "pagerduty_service" "commercial" {
  name              = var.commercial_service_name
  description       = "Client-conversation events. design 12's fourth routing destination: defined by who needs to have a conversation, not by severity. These NOTIFY; they do not page."
  escalation_policy = pagerduty_escalation_policy.commercial.id
  alert_creation    = "create_alerts_and_incidents"

  # Low, constant, and not a threshold.
  #
  # An SLA outage is commercially urgent and operationally already handled by
  # the production service — the commercial team needs to know before a
  # customer calls, which is a different job from being woken up. Two people
  # paged for one event is how one of them stops reading the other's channel.
  incident_urgency_rule {
    type    = "constant"
    urgency = "low"
  }

  # Auto-resolve OFF, unlike the low-urgency operational service.
  #
  # A conversation that nobody had is not resolved by four hours passing. The
  # dev queue auto-resolves because a build machine at 95% CPU stops mattering;
  # an unacknowledged "a customer's budget broke" still matters tomorrow.
  auto_resolve_timeout = "null"
}

resource "pagerduty_service_integration" "commercial_events_v2" {
  name    = "Platform Commercial Router (Events API v2)"
  service = pagerduty_service.commercial.id
  type    = "events_api_v2_inbound_integration"
}

# The subscribable half. design 12's "business service" literally.
resource "pagerduty_business_service" "commercial" {
  name             = "Client Conversations"
  description      = "Events where somebody at AltDigital needs to talk to a customer. Subscribe to be informed; notification of a customer is governed elsewhere — see design 12, 'Informed is not notifier'."
  point_of_contact = var.commercial_point_of_contact
}

resource "pagerduty_service_dependency" "commercial" {
  dependency {
    dependent_service {
      id   = pagerduty_business_service.commercial.id
      type = "business_service"
    }
    supporting_service {
      id   = pagerduty_service.commercial.id
      type = "service"
    }
  }
}
files.pagerduty/tenants.tf:
# Per-tenant PagerDuty, driven by DATA rather than by generated code.
#
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Why the saga renders a tfvars file and not a .tf file
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Provisioning step 3 writes `tenants.auto.tfvars.json` from the registry. It
# does not write Terraform.
#
# Generated .tf is reviewable only by reading Terraform, diffs noisily when the
# generator's formatting changes, and makes it possible for a generator bug to
# create a resource nobody intended. Generated DATA can only populate the
# shapes this file already declares: a generator bug produces a wrong value,
# never a wrong resource. Adding a tenant becomes a one-line diff in a JSON
# map, which is something Art or Wayne can read in a pull request without
# knowing Terraform.
#
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Why tenants.json and not tenants.auto.tfvars.json
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The tfvars name was the obvious choice and is the wrong one. Both .gitignore
# and the pre-commit hook block `*.tfvars.json`, because tfvars files here hold
# responder email addresses -- personal data under CLAUDE.md.
#
# This file holds client slugs, partner slugs and app slugs. None of that is
# personal data, all of it is already in the registry, and it MUST be
# reviewable: the thing a reviewer needs to see is which clients exist and
# which of them page, and hiding the estate's paging surface in a gitignored
# file would put it beyond review entirely.
#
# The fix is a rename rather than an exception. Adding `!tenants.auto.tfvars.json`
# to the ignore rules would weaken a data-protection control to make one safe
# file convenient, and the next tfvars file to want an exception would have a
# precedent. A plain .json read through jsondecode gets the same result and
# leaves the control intact.

locals {
  tenants_file = "${path.module}/tenants.json"

  # Absent is treated as empty, and that is a deliberate choice rather than
  # laziness: a fresh clone that has never run the renderer should plan
  # cleanly rather than fail on a missing file. The renderer reports how many
  # registry records it examined, so "no clients" is distinguishable from
  # "never looked" at the point where that distinction can still be acted on.
  tenants = fileexists(local.tenants_file) ? jsondecode(file(local.tenants_file)).tenants : {}
}

module "tenant" {
  source   = "./modules/tenant"
  for_each = local.tenants

  tenant_id = each.key
  partner   = each.value.partner
  tiers     = each.value.tiers

  # Every tier falls back to the platform escalation policy today.
  #
  # design 13 says the escalation policy references "the on-call schedule",
  # singular, and there is one. A per-tier policy over the same schedule would
  # be separation in name only -- the same phone rings either way -- so none is
  # created until there is a second rotation to point at.
  #
  # Non-production escalation is an open question owned by Jamie and Wayne
  # (B-117). Dev is the developer's own production, so the answer is probably a
  # different policy rather than no policy; `tier_escalation_policy_ids` is
  # where it lands, as data.
  default_escalation_policy_id = pagerduty_escalation_policy.platform.id

  acknowledgement_timeout_minutes = var.acknowledgement_timeout_minutes
  auto_resolve_timeout_minutes    = var.auto_resolve_timeout_minutes
}
files.pagerduty/variables.tf:
variable "responder_emails" {
  type = list(string)

  description = <<-EOT
    PagerDuty user emails, in escalation order, forming the on-call schedule.

    These are looked up rather than created: the users must already exist in
    the PagerDuty account. Creating them here would mean this configuration
    owns people, and destroying it would delete them.

    Direct email addresses are personal data under the repository rules, so
    this is supplied through a gitignored terraform.tfvars rather than a
    default. See CLAUDE.md, "No personal data in the repository".
  EOT

  validation {
    condition     = length(var.responder_emails) > 0
    error_message = "At least one responder is required; an escalation policy with no target pages nobody."
  }
}

variable "escalation_timeout_minutes" {
  type        = number
  default     = 15
  description = <<-EOT
    Minutes before an unacknowledged incident escalates to the next rule.

    Fifteen is a deliberate compromise: long enough not to page a second
    person because the first was driving, short enough that an overnight
    incident does not sit for an hour. Revisit when there is a rotation
    rather than an individual.
  EOT
}

variable "auto_resolve_timeout_minutes" {
  type        = number
  default     = 0
  description = <<-EOT
    Minutes before PagerDuty auto-resolves an untouched incident. Zero
    disables it.

    Disabled on purpose. Auto-resolve is for services that emit an alert per
    occurrence and never send a resolve. CloudWatch sends a real OK
    transition, so an incident that is still open is still true — and a
    replication failure or a sensitive-data finding that quietly closed
    itself overnight is the worst possible outcome for an evidence platform.
  EOT
}

variable "acknowledgement_timeout_minutes" {
  type        = number
  default     = 30
  description = "Minutes before an acknowledged-but-unresolved incident re-triggers."
}

variable "platform_service_name" {
  type        = string
  default     = "AltDigital Platform"
  description = <<-EOT
    The service carrying the PLATFORM's own alarms — log archive replication,
    data protection findings, guardrail drift.

    Distinct from the per-application services design doc 13 creates during
    tenant onboarding. A tenant's application going down is that tenant's
    incident; the evidence archive failing to replicate is AltDigital's, and
    routing them to one service means the noisiest tenant buries the alarm
    that says the platform can no longer prove anything.
  EOT
}

variable "alert_grouping_type" {
  type    = string
  default = "intelligent"

  description = <<-EOT
    How PagerDuty groups alerts on the platform service, or "none" to disable.

    THIS IS PLAN-TIER DEPENDENT, and that is the only reason it is a variable.
    Intelligent Alert Grouping is a Business / AIOps feature. On a lower plan
    the apply fails at this resource with a permissions or feature error rather
    than a configuration error, which reads like a mistake in the Terraform and
    is not one.

      intelligent   — Business / AIOps. Groups on observed alert behaviour.
      content_based — Professional and up. Groups on matching fields.
      time          — Professional and up. Groups anything within a window.
      none          — creates no grouping resource at all.

    "time" is the one to avoid on this service if it can be helped: it folds an
    unrelated second failure into the first incident, and the second is then
    acknowledged by someone who only read the first. On a service that carries
    "the evidence archive has stopped replicating", that matters.
  EOT

  validation {
    condition     = contains(["intelligent", "content_based", "time", "none"], var.alert_grouping_type)
    error_message = "alert_grouping_type must be intelligent, content_based, time, or none."
  }
}

variable "low_urgency_service_name" {
  type    = string
  default = "AltDigital Platform — Low Urgency"

  description = <<-EOT
    Service carrying dev and test alarms.

    A SECOND service, not a second routing rule on the first, because urgency
    in PagerDuty is a property of the service (incident_urgency_rule), not of
    the individual alert. One service cannot raise some incidents at high
    urgency and others at low unless it derives urgency from an alert severity
    field — which the CloudWatch vendor integration does not populate.

    Two services, two integration keys, two SNS topics. It also means dev noise
    can be muted, snoozed or re-escalated independently of production without
    touching production's configuration.
  EOT
}

variable "low_urgency_priority" {
  type    = string
  default = "P5"

  description = <<-EOT
    Incident priority applied to everything on the low-urgency service, or ""
    to set none.

    PRIORITY AND URGENCY ARE DIFFERENT THINGS, and conflating them is the usual
    confusion:

      urgency   high | low. Decides whether PagerDuty NOTIFIES you, and how.
                Low urgency respects your low-urgency notification rules, which
                by default means it appears in the UI and does not ring a phone.
      priority  P1..P5. A label used for triage, filtering and reporting. It
                changes nothing about notification on its own.

    So "low urgency, P5" means: does not wake you, and is labelled as the
    lowest triage tier.

    PLAN-TIER DEPENDENT. Priorities and Event Orchestration are Business /
    AIOps features, and this account already returned 403 on Intelligent Alert
    Grouping. If apply fails on pagerduty_event_orchestration_service or on the
    pagerduty_priority lookup, set this to "" — the low-urgency service still
    works, it just carries no priority label.
  EOT
}

variable "commercial_service_name" {
  description = "Technical service that ingests client-conversation events. These notify; they do not page."
  type        = string
  default     = "AltDigital Client Conversations"
}

variable "commercial_point_of_contact" {
  description = "Role reference for the business service, not a person's name. A name here goes stale and is personal data besides."
  type        = string
  default     = "Commercial lead"
}
files.pagerduty/versions.tf:
terraform {
  required_version = ">= 1.5"

  required_providers {
    pagerduty = {
      source  = "PagerDuty/pagerduty"
      version = "~> 3.0"
    }
  }

  # State holds integration keys in cleartext. That is not a Terraform defect —
  # a routing key IS the credential, and any tool that can create one can read
  # it back. The consequences are what matter:
  #
  #   - terraform.tfstate must never be committed. Enforced in .gitignore and
  #     by the pre-commit hook, not by anyone remembering.
  #   - local state means one operator at a time and no locking.
  #
  # A remote backend belongs in the Log Archive account alongside the other
  # evidence, with the same encryption and versioning. Not configured here
  # because the bucket does not exist yet and pointing at a missing backend
  # fails init rather than degrading. Tracked as B-016.
}

provider "pagerduty" {
  # Read from the PAGERDUTY_TOKEN environment variable. Deliberately NOT a
  # Terraform variable: a variable ends up in .tfvars, in shell history, or in
  # a CI log the first time someone debugs a plan.
  #
  # See open item B10 — this should be a service account token, not a personal
  # one. A personal token ties platform automation to one person's employment
  # and inherits their permissions rather than the automation's.
}
files.pagerduty/modules/tenant/main.tf:
# One client's PagerDuty footprint: a business service per tier, a technical
# service per object, and the dependencies between them.
#
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Business and technical services are different kinds of thing
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
#   technical service   INGESTS events and can page. Has an integration and an
#                       escalation policy. One per monitored OBJECT.
#   business service    is SUBSCRIBED to and notifies. Ingests nothing, has no
#                       integration. One per TIER, representing "this client's
#                       dev environment" as a capability.
#
# Getting this backwards is not a naming mistake. A business service cannot
# receive events at all, so routing alarms at one produces events that vanish
# silently, with no error anywhere.
#
# The dependency is what makes the pair useful: an incident on any technical
# service rolls up to the tier's business service, so "is ACME's UAT healthy"
# is answerable without knowing which objects are underneath it.
#
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Every tier, not production only -- D-018
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# design 13 says "Service per application (production only)". This creates
# services for every tier, which is a deliberate departure recorded in
# docs/deviations.md.
#
# The design's reasoning is sound and incompletely applied: a dev account that
# pages the production rotation trains that rotation to ignore pages, and the
# habit does not stay confined to dev. But the conclusion drawn from it -- that
# non-production gets no service at all -- confuses "must not page the on-call
# rotation" with "nobody is told".
#
# A dev environment is the developer's own production. When it breaks, their
# work stops, and the person who needs to know is the developer or whoever
# supports their infrastructure. Creating no service means that alert has
# nowhere to go and the failure is discovered by someone noticing.
#
# So every tier gets services, and the SEPARATION is expressed as urgency and
# escalation policy rather than as absence. This mirrors what the platform
# already does for itself with its own low-urgency service.

terraform {
  required_providers {
    pagerduty = {
      source  = "PagerDuty/pagerduty"
      version = "~> 3.0"
    }
  }
}

locals {
  # The reserved object every tier carries. B-127.
  #
  # Inside one tenant account two teams own resources: AltDigital owns the VPC,
  # KMS keys, log groups and backup vault the baseline puts there, and a
  # separate team owns the application. They page different people even when
  # both teams work for the same company. This is the service AltDigital's half
  # routes to, and `platform-layer: infrastructure` on the resource is what
  # selects it.
  #
  # Added HERE rather than in scripts/render-pagerduty-tenants.sh on purpose.
  # The renderer derives objects from the `app` field on each account, so an
  # account with no app, or a renderer that changed, could produce a tier with
  # no infrastructure service -- and the failure would be silent: infrastructure
  # alarms would fall back to the platform's own service and page the right
  # people for the wrong reason, until the first tenant where that was not the
  # same thing.
  infra_object = "infra"

  # Flattened tier x object, because Terraform has no nested for_each. The key
  # is "<tier>/<object>" and an empty object is a real key meaning the
  # account's single unnamed application.
  services = merge([
    for tier, cfg in var.tiers : {
      for obj in distinct(concat(cfg.objects, [local.infra_object])) :
      "${tier}/${obj}" => { tier = tier, object = obj }
    }
  ]...)

  # Written into every description rather than living only in Terraform state.
  # Somebody looking at this service in the PagerDuty console at 3am should be
  # able to see that it is managed here, and whose client it is, without going
  # to find out. The drift detector also keys on this string -- the account
  # holds services this configuration does not own, and a sweep that treated
  # everything it found as drift would report other people's work.
  provenance = "Managed by AltDigital platform Terraform (pagerduty/modules/tenant). Client ${var.tenant_id}, partner ${var.partner}. Console edits are drift and are reported."
}

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# One business service per tier
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

resource "pagerduty_business_service" "tier" {
  for_each = var.tiers

  name             = "tenant-${var.tenant_id}-${each.key}"
  description      = "${var.tenant_id} ${each.key} environment, as a capability. Technical services for its objects roll up here. ${local.provenance}"
  point_of_contact = var.commercial_point_of_contact
}

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# One technical service per object
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

resource "pagerduty_service" "object" {
  for_each = local.services

  name = "tenant-${var.tenant_id}-${each.value.tier}-${each.value.object == "" ? "app" : each.value.object}"
  description = join(" ", [
    each.value.object == local.infra_object
    ? "AltDigital-owned infrastructure alarms for"
    : "${each.value.object == "" ? "Application" : each.value.object} alarms for",
    "${var.tenant_id} ${each.value.tier}.",
    local.provenance,
  ])

  # Infrastructure escalates to AltDigital REGARDLESS of tier, because the
  # thing that determines who answers is which team owns the resource, not
  # which environment it is in. A tenant's dev-tier VPC failing is still
  # AltDigital's to fix.
  #
  # Everything else takes the per-tier override, falling back to the platform
  # policy. B-117 will replace that fallback for non-production once Jamie and
  # Wayne settle what should happen there.
  escalation_policy = (
    each.value.object == local.infra_object
    ? coalesce(var.infrastructure_escalation_policy_id, var.default_escalation_policy_id)
    : lookup(var.tier_escalation_policy_ids, each.value.tier, var.default_escalation_policy_id)
  )

  alert_creation          = "create_alerts_and_incidents"
  auto_resolve_timeout    = var.auto_resolve_timeout_minutes == 0 ? "null" : tostring(var.auto_resolve_timeout_minutes * 60)
  acknowledgement_timeout = tostring(var.acknowledgement_timeout_minutes * 60)

  incident_urgency_rule {
    type = "constant"
    # Low still NOTIFIES. See variables.tf: the tier separation is urgency,
    # not silence.
    # Infrastructure keeps the tier's urgency like everything else. The layer
    # decides WHO is woken, not how loudly -- a dev-tier infrastructure fault is
    # still a dev-tier fault, and making it high because AltDigital owns it
    # would page us at 3am for an environment design 14 gives no SLA.
    urgency = lookup(var.tier_urgency, each.value.tier, "low")
  }
}

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# CloudWatch integration -- the routing key the alarm layer uses
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The vendor integration, not a generic Events API v2 one, for the same reason
# the platform service uses it: the vendor integration understands the SNS
# envelope and produces an incident titled with the alarm name. A generic
# integration renders the whole SNS payload as an unparsed blob, which is what
# a woken engineer would then be reading.

data "pagerduty_vendor" "cloudwatch" {
  name = "Amazon CloudWatch"
}

resource "pagerduty_service_integration" "cloudwatch" {
  for_each = local.services

  name    = "AWS CloudWatch"
  service = pagerduty_service.object[each.key].id
  vendor  = data.pagerduty_vendor.cloudwatch.id
}

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Objects roll up to their tier
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The relationship is what makes the business service answer a question. More
# nuanced relationships are expected -- an object depending on another object,
# a tier depending on a shared service -- and they attach here without
# disturbing what exists, because a dependency is its own resource.

resource "pagerduty_service_dependency" "object_to_tier" {
  for_each = local.services

  dependency {
    dependent_service {
      id   = pagerduty_business_service.tier[each.value.tier].id
      type = "business_service"
    }
    supporting_service {
      id   = pagerduty_service.object[each.key].id
      type = "service"
    }
  }
}

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The client-conversation business service -- commercial, not operational
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Separate from the per-tier services and deliberately not one of them.
# design 12's client-conversation class is defined by who needs to have a
# conversation, not by which environment broke; a commercial contact
# subscribing to it should not also inherit every dev alert.

resource "pagerduty_business_service" "conversations" {
  name             = "tenant-${var.tenant_id}-conversations"
  description      = "Client-conversation event class for ${var.tenant_id} (design 12). Subscribed to, never paged from. ${local.provenance}"
  point_of_contact = var.commercial_point_of_contact
}
files.pagerduty/modules/tenant/variables.tf:
variable "tenant_id" {
  type        = string
  description = <<-EOT
    The registry id (client slug). This is the idempotency key for the whole
    module: every resource name derives from it, so re-rendering the tenant map
    produces the same names and Terraform sees no change.

    Not the client's display name. A display name gets corrected for spelling
    six months in, and every PagerDuty resource would be renamed by an apply
    nobody connected to the edit.
  EOT
}

variable "partner" {
  type        = string
  description = "Partner slug. Appears in descriptions so an incident makes it obvious whose client this is, which matters at 3am."
}

variable "tiers" {
  type = map(object({
    objects = list(string)
  }))
  default = {}

  description = <<-EOT
    Environment tiers this client has, keyed by tier name (dev/test/uat/prod),
    each listing the OBJECTS monitored within it.

    Every tier gets a business service; every object gets a technical service
    linked to it. See main.tf on why those are different things.

    `objects` currently holds app slugs, with the empty string meaning the
    account's single unnamed application. That is the coarsest useful
    granularity and the finest the registry can currently supply -- it carries
    `app` on ACCOUNT records and nothing below it. Finer objects (a database, a
    queue, a specific service) slot into this list without changing any shape
    here, which is why it is a list rather than a single value.
  EOT
}

variable "default_escalation_policy_id" {
  type        = string
  description = <<-EOT
    The escalation policy used by any tier without its own.

    Passed in rather than created here. A tenant with its own policy but the
    SAME schedule behind it looks like separation and provides none -- the same
    phone rings either way. When a tier genuinely needs its own rotation, that
    is a schedule, and it belongs at the root config where the coverage
    verification (B-018) can see it.
  EOT
}

variable "tier_escalation_policy_ids" {
  type        = map(string)
  default     = {}
  description = <<-EOT
    Per-tier escalation policy overrides, keyed by tier name.

    Empty today. Non-production escalation is an open question owned by Jamie
    and Wayne (B-117): dev is the developer's own production, so "does not
    page the on-call rotation" is not the same as "nobody is told", and the
    right answer is probably a different policy rather than no policy.

    The override exists now so that answering it later is a data change here
    rather than a restructuring.
  EOT
}

variable "tier_urgency" {
  type = map(string)
  default = {
    prod = "high"
    uat  = "low"
    test = "low"
    dev  = "low"
  }

  description = <<-EOT
    Incident urgency per tier.

    Production is high; the rest are low PENDING B-117, and low is deliberately
    not the same as silent. A low-urgency PagerDuty incident still notifies
    according to each responder's rules -- it just does not force a page. That
    is the distinction that makes a dev-tier alert reach the developer whose
    working environment it is without waking the production rotation.

    This mirrors the platform's own split, where `AltDigital Platform` and
    `AltDigital Platform - Low Urgency` already separate paging from
    notification rather than separating alerting from nothing.
  EOT

  validation {
    condition     = alltrue([for u in values(var.tier_urgency) : contains(["high", "low"], u)])
    error_message = "urgency must be high or low."
  }
}

variable "acknowledgement_timeout_minutes" {
  type        = number
  default     = 30
  description = "Minutes before an acknowledged-but-unresolved incident re-triggers."
}

variable "auto_resolve_timeout_minutes" {
  type        = number
  default     = 0
  description = "0 disables auto-resolve. An incident that resolves itself because nobody looked is an incident nobody looked at."
}

variable "commercial_point_of_contact" {
  type        = string
  default     = "AltDigital Platform"
  description = "Role reference for the client-conversation business service. A person's name here goes stale and is personal data besides."
}

variable "infrastructure_escalation_policy_id" {
  type        = string
  default     = null
  description = <<-EOT
    Escalation policy for the reserved `infra` service in every tier -- the one
    holding alarms on resources tagged `platform-layer: infrastructure`, which
    AltDigital owns. B-127.

    Null falls back to default_escalation_policy_id, which today IS AltDigital's
    policy, so the fallback is correct rather than merely tolerable. It becomes
    load-bearing the moment a tenant sets a per-tier policy of their own: at
    that point the application services move to the tenant's people and the
    infrastructure service must NOT follow them, which is exactly what this
    variable exists to prevent.
  EOT
}

config.description: Tier table, vesting rules and alerting configuration

files.config/tiers.yaml:
# Environment tiers, as two axes rather than four columns.
#
# Source: design/14-environment-tiers.md, "Revised environment matrix".
# Consumed by: scripts/lib/tiers.py, scripts/publish-tiers.sh
#
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Why this file exists at all
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# prompt 13.1: "Do not implement UAT by copying the test parameterisation and
# adjusting. Build the tier table in design 14 as explicit configuration so the
# two axes stay visibly separate."
#
# The instruction is unusually specific, and the reason is in design 14:
#
#   | Axis            | dev / test     | uat                   | prod       |
#   | Data handling   | Non-production | Production-equivalent | Production |
#   | Resilience      | Non-production | Non-production        | Production |
#
# dev, test and prod keep those two axes ALIGNED, which is why three tiers can
# be implemented as a single ordered scale and why doing so works right up
# until UAT exists. UAT is the tier where they diverge: its data is real and
# its infrastructure is not.
#
# Copying test and adjusting produces a UAT that is out of compliance scope
# with a reduced retention floor, because those are the settings you do not
# think to change. The failure is quiet, it is discovered during an audit, and
# by then the environment has been holding regulated data for months.
#
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# So nothing about a tier is written per tier
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Each tier declares only its POSITION on the two axes. Every attribute that
# follows an axis is resolved from that position. UAT's compliance scope is
# not set here — it falls out of `data_handling: production_equivalent`, which
# is the same value production uses.
#
# That makes the failure mode structurally unavailable. There is no field to
# forget, because there is no per-tier field.
#
# A handful of attributes genuinely follow neither axis. They are in
# `tier_specific` below, which is deliberately small and deliberately awkward:
# anything added there is a claim that it depends on the tier's NAME rather
# than on what the tier is, and that claim should have to be defended.

version: 1

axes:

  # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # Data handling — what the environment HOLDS
  # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # Drives compliance, retention, evidence and the severity at which a finding
  # about the data is treated. design 14: "The distinction that matters is not
  # its purpose but what data it holds."
  data_handling:
    attributes:
      - compliance_scope
      - retention_floor
      - regulated_data_expected
      - regulated_data_is_finding
      - finding_severity
      - restore_testing
      - canary_required
      - backup_policy

    values:
      non_production:
        compliance_scope: out
        retention_floor: reduced
        regulated_data_expected: false
        # The scope-change finding that fires when regulated data turns up
        # somewhere it was not expected.
        regulated_data_is_finding: true
        finding_severity: non_production
        restore_testing: false
        canary_required: false
        backup_policy: reduced

      production_equivalent:
        compliance_scope: in
        retention_floor: full
        regulated_data_expected: true
        # prompt 13.1: "regulated data in UAT must NOT trigger the
        # scope-change finding that applies to dev and test. UAT is in scope
        # from the outset." Real users bring real data -- design 14 calls this
        # "not misconduct, it is how UAT works" -- and a control that fires on
        # the expected case trains people to close it without reading.
        regulated_data_is_finding: false
        finding_severity: production
        # design 14: "An environment holding regulated data with an untested
        # restore path is an audit finding regardless of its SLA status."
        restore_testing: true
        canary_required: true
        # design 14 gives UAT "Full policy, reduced frequency". The POLICY
        # follows the data -- an environment holding regulated data is backed
        # up the same way production is -- while the FREQUENCY follows the
        # resilience axis below. The two halves of one row landing on
        # different axes is the clearest illustration in the file of why
        # there are two.
        backup_policy: full

      production:
        compliance_scope: in
        retention_floor: full
        regulated_data_expected: true
        regulated_data_is_finding: false
        finding_severity: production
        restore_testing: true
        canary_required: true
        backup_policy: full

  # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # Resilience — what the environment PROMISES
  # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # Drives availability, SLA, backup frequency, paging and whether the thing
  # may be switched off at night. None of this is affected by how sensitive
  # the data is.
  resilience:
    attributes:
      - availability_zones
      - sla_commitment
      - backup_frequency
      - pagerduty_routing
      - schedulable
      - multi_az_required

    values:
      non_production:
        availability_zones: single
        sla_commitment: false
        backup_frequency: reduced
        # No paging. NOT no alerting -- see D-018 and alarm_routing below.
        pagerduty_routing: false
        schedulable: true
        multi_az_required: false

      production:
        availability_zones: multi
        sla_commitment: true
        backup_frequency: full
        pagerduty_routing: true
        # design 14 marks production "No" for HOOPs, and prompt 13.2 says to
        # "enforce that, do not rely on configuration". This value is what the
        # scheduler checks; the enforcement is that it refuses regardless.
        schedulable: false
        multi_az_required: true

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The tiers, as positions
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Note what is NOT here: no tier sets compliance_scope, retention_floor or any
# other axis attribute. UAT differs from test in exactly one character of this
# file, which is the whole point.

tiers:

  dev:
    purpose: Where developers build. Things break.
    data_handling: non_production
    resilience: non_production
    provisioned_by_default: true

  test:
    purpose: QA verifies function against specification.
    data_handling: non_production
    resilience: non_production
    provisioned_by_default: true

  uat:
    purpose: Do the users accept this, or are adjustments needed?
    # The divergence. Real users bring real data; the infrastructure behind it
    # is still non-production.
    data_handling: production_equivalent
    resilience: non_production
    # design 14: "UAT is optional and opt-in. It is not provisioned by
    # default, because it raises the customer's AWS cost and not every
    # customer runs a formal acceptance stage." Opt-in rather than opt-out so
    # that a customer who never uses UAT does not have to notice it in order
    # to stop paying for it.
    provisioned_by_default: false

  prod:
    purpose: Production.
    data_handling: production
    resilience: production
    provisioned_by_default: true

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Attributes that follow NEITHER axis
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Kept separate and kept short. Everything here is an assertion that the value
# depends on which tier this is rather than on what the tier IS, and each one
# carries its reason so the assertion can be argued with.
#
# If this section grows, the axis model is wrong and should be fixed rather
# than worked around.

tier_specific:

  monitoring_depth:
    reason: >-
      A gradient rather than a consequence of either axis. design 14's matrix
      lists four distinct values, and UAT's "moderate" is neither the
      non-production nor the production setting.
    dev: light
    test: light
    uat: moderate
    prod: pervasive

  alarm_routing:
    reason: >-
      Follows resilience for the PAGING half and data handling for the rest,
      so it belongs to both axes and therefore to neither. UAT reaches Jira
      and the commercial channel without paging anybody, which is exactly the
      combination that has no single axis to inherit from.
    dev: digest
    test: digest_and_jira
    uat: jira_and_commercial
    prod: pagerduty

  developer_console_access:
    reason: >-
      Follows design 11's access model, which is about blast radius rather
      than about data or resilience. Test is more open than UAT despite both
      being non-production for resilience.
    dev: full_within_guardrails
    test: read_and_limited_ops
    uat: read_only
    prod: read_only

  path_to_change:
    reason: >-
      Direct access in dev only. Everything else goes through AppDeployer,
      which is a deployment-mechanism decision rather than a tier property.
    dev: direct
    test: app_deployer
    uat: app_deployer
    prod: app_deployer

  change_reconciliation:
    reason: >-
      Follows path_to_change rather than either axis. design 14 has test at
      Yes despite test being non-production on BOTH axes -- reconciliation
      exists wherever deployment goes through AppDeployer, which is everywhere
      except dev's direct access. Deriving this from the data axis would have
      silently turned test's reconciliation off.
    dev: false
    test: true
    uat: true
    prod: true

  hoop_aggressiveness:
    reason: >-
      All three non-production tiers are schedulable -- that comes from the
      resilience axis -- but how hard they are scheduled does not. design 14
      distinguishes "aggressive" from "conservative": UAT may have real users
      in it at unpredictable hours, and switching it off underneath an
      acceptance session is a different kind of wrong from switching off an
      idle dev box.
    dev: aggressive
    test: aggressive
    uat: conservative
    prod: none
files.vesting/derivation-rules.yaml:
# AltDigital Managed Platform — vesting derivation rules
#
# ===========================================================================
# THIS FILE IS CONFIGURATION, NOT CODE. IT IS MEANT TO BE EDITED.
# ===========================================================================
#
# The onboarding questionnaire marks fields [A] asked, [D] derived, or [P]
# placeholder. Prompt 3.1 is explicit that every [D] field must be COMPUTED by
# the pipeline rather than typed by whoever is filling the form. This file is
# how they are computed.
#
# It is a data document on purpose. The same instruction appears in prompt 4.1
# for the instrumentation Lambda — "a configuration document, not a switch
# statement" — and the reason is identical: adding a framework, changing a
# retention floor, or re-tiering an environment should be a reviewable diff
# that a non-programmer can read, not a code change.
#
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# What is deliberately NOT here
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Anything that is a judgement call at onboarding time stays an [A] question.
# The test for belonging here is: given the answers, is there exactly one
# correct output, and would a human deriving it by hand ever legitimately
# disagree? If they could disagree, it is not derived — it is a decision, and
# burying a decision in a rules file makes it invisible.

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2.7 — Conformance packs, derived from 2.1 frameworks in scope
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# UNVERIFIED NAMES. These are AWS sample conformance pack template names and
# AWS renames and re-versions them (PCI 3.2.1 -> 4.0 being the obvious one
# coming). scripts/derive-vesting.py does NOT assume they resolve; it warns,
# and the vesting pipeline checks them against the account before deploying.
#
# Verify with the AWS samples repository or:
#   aws configservice describe-conformance-packs
#
# A pack name that does not resolve fails the deploy, not the derivation —
# which is the right order, because a typo here should not block a
# questionnaire review.
conformance_packs:
  hipaa:
    - Operational-Best-Practices-for-HIPAA-Security
  pci-dss:
    - Operational-Best-Practices-for-PCI-DSS-3.2.1
  soc2:
    - Operational-Best-Practices-for-SOC-2
  # "other" deliberately maps to nothing. A framework nobody has named cannot
  # have a pack derived for it, and silently applying a default would be worse
  # than applying none — it would look like coverage.
  other: []

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2.8 — Log retention floor, derived from 2.1
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The questionnaire says "union of applicable frameworks". Union of retention
# periods means the LONGEST, not the sum and not the most common.
#
# These are floors in DAYS and they set an Object Lock COMPLIANCE retention,
# which cannot be shortened by anyone including account root. Raising a number
# here is cheap; lowering it does nothing for data already written under the
# old value. Treat every increase as permanent for six years of billing.
#
#   hipaa    2190  six years. HIPAA §164.316(b)(2)(i) requires documentation
#                  retention for six years from creation or last effective
#                  date. Applied to logs as the platform's reading of
#                  "documentation", which is conservative — see D-010.
#   pci-dss   365  one year, with three months immediately available.
#                  Requirement 10.7 (10.5.1 in 3.2.1).
#   soc2      365  no statutory period exists. SOC 2 requires evidence
#                  covering the audit period, typically twelve months. This is
#                  a house number, not a citation, and is marked as such.
#   other     365  the platform default, applied when a framework is named
#                  that this file does not know.
retention_floor_days:
  hipaa: 2190
  pci-dss: 365
  soc2: 365
  other: 365
default: 365

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3.1 — Primary region
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Derived, with one gate. 2.2 asks whether any data relates to NON-US
# individuals — note the questionnaire's own emphasis that this is about data
# SUBJECTS, not where the customer is headquartered.
#
# If yes, the pipeline does NOT pick a region. It stops. Choosing an EU or UK
# region on a customer's behalf implies a residency and transfer position
# (GDPR Article 44 onward) that is a legal determination, not a config value.
# The platform's allowed region list is US-only today, so "yes" means the
# answer is outside what this platform can currently provide.
primary_region:
  default: us-east-2
  non_us_data_subjects: HALT

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 7.7 — Monitoring tier, derived from environment
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Design doc 14 (Environment Tiers) is NOT present in the design package, so
# these tiers are derived from what the questionnaire itself states rather than
# from 14. The questionnaire is unambiguous on the load-bearing point (3a.9):
# UAT is "always production-equivalent for data handling", because real users
# bring real data. So UAT is NOT a lower tier than production for anything
# touching data.
#
# The distinction below is about alerting volume and response expectation, not
# about controls. Controls are identical everywhere; nobody is paged at 3am for
# a dev box.
monitoring_tier:
  prod: full
  uat: production-equivalent
  test: reduced
  dev: reduced

# Which environments page a human out of hours. Separate from tier because
# "monitored thoroughly" and "wakes someone up" are different decisions and
# conflating them is how alert fatigue starts.
pages_out_of_hours:
  prod: true
  uat: false
  test: false
  dev: false

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 6.4 — Dedicated Host requirement, derived from 6.1
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Licensing, NOT security. Questionnaire section 6 is about customer-owned
# licences; the security-motivated dedicated-infrastructure question is 5.9,
# added separately (see docs/isolation-tiers.md). Conflating them produces a
# client paying a tenancy premium for a reason nobody can later explain.
#
# Windows Server and SQL Server BYOL under most Microsoft agreements require
# dedicated hardware with visible physical cores. Other licences generally do
# not.
dedicated_host_required_for_licences:
  - sql-server
  - windows-server

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2.3 — Egress profile default, derived from data classification
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# A DEFAULT, not a determination. 3.2 asks the customer directly, and their
# answer wins. This is what to pre-fill and what to argue from.
#
# Note 'regulated' maps to `isolated` rather than `locked`. That is deliberate
# and is the analysis in docs/isolation-tiers.md: `isolated` has no NAT and no
# internet path at all, which is both cheaper AND more restrictive than the
# Network Firewall profile. `locked` is not implemented (B-010), and defaulting
# to an unimplemented profile would fail vesting at the network step.
egress_profile_default:
  regulated: isolated
  confidential: controlled
  internal: controlled
  public: public-facing
default_egress_profile: controlled

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4.1 / 4.2 — Resilience defaults
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The questionnaire states these defaults inline. Repeated here so the pipeline
# has one source and a reviewer can see them without cross-referencing.
resilience_defaults:
  rto_hours: 4
  rpo_hours: 2
  sla_tier: standard

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Environments vested
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Three always; UAT is opt-in per 3a.1 and raises cost.
environments_always: [dev, test, prod]
environments_optional: [uat]
files.vesting/questionnaire.example.yaml:
# Example completed questionnaire. Placeholder contacts only.
#
# A REAL completed questionnaire must never be committed: it carries named
# contacts with direct email addresses, which the repository rules treat as
# personal data the same way as config/contacts.env. Enforced in .gitignore
# and the pre-commit hook. Name real ones *.questionnaire.yaml.
#
# Shaped on the OEight / Arc8 relationship for realism. The values here are
# illustrative and are NOT Arc8's actual contract terms.

schema_version: 1

identity:
  partner: oeight
  client_name: "OEight"
  client_slug: oeight
  application_name: "Arc8"
  application_code: arc8
  service_model: B
  partner_is_application_owner: true    # OEight owns the Arc8 IP
  technical_contact:  { name: "Placeholder Tech",   email: "tech@example.com" }
  escalation_contact: { name: "Placeholder Esc",    email: "esc@example.com" }
  change_approver:    { name: "Placeholder Appr",   email: "appr@example.com" }
  billing_contact:    { name: "Placeholder Bill",   email: "bill@example.com" }

compliance:
  frameworks: [hipaa, soc2]
  non_us_data_subjects: false
  data_classification: regulated
  cardholder_data: false
  phi: true
  baa_window_partner_to_client_hours: 48

network:
  egress_profile: isolated
  internet_exposure: outbound
  inbound_cross_tenant_api: false
  outbound_allowlist: []

environments:
  uat_required: false
  timezone: America/Chicago
  hoop:
    dev:  { always_on: false, days: [mon, tue, wed, thu, fri], start: "07:00", end: "19:00" }
    test: { always_on: false, days: [mon, tue, wed, thu, fri], start: "07:00", end: "19:00" }
  manual_turnup_authorised: ["OEight engineering leads"]

resilience:
  rto_hours: 4
  rpo_hours: 2
  sla_tier: standard
  # null takes the platform default of 35 days. A client wanting longer says so
  # here; 35 is a floor rather than a starting point, because the copy vault's
  # Vault Lock rejects anything shorter.
  backup_retention_days: null
  maintenance_window: { days: [tue], start: "08:00", end: "10:00" }

security:
  dedicated_kms_key: false
  fips_or_cloudhsm: false
  external_key_material: false
  migrating_secrets: false
  customer_staff_need_access: true
  no_regulated_data_in_lower_envs_ack: true
  developer_manager: { name: "Placeholder Mgr", email: "mgr@example.com" }

  dedicated_infrastructure_control_ref: null

licensing:

monitoring:
