  endpoints: ["https://arc8.example.com/health"]
  success_condition: "HTTP 200 and body contains \"ok\""
  acceptable_response_ms: 2000
  existing_test_suite: none
  journey_requires_auth: true

change:
  cicd_tooling: "GitHub Actions"
  deployment_frequency: weekly
  customer_escalation_contacts: []

exit:
  ip_boundary_ack: true
  post_exit_governance_loss_ack: true
  truveon_retention_desired: false
files.alerting/10-alert-topic.yaml:
AWSTemplateFormatVersion: '2010-09-09'

Description: >-
  AltDigital Managed Platform — the single alerting destination. An SNS topic
  in the Audit account that every platform and member alarm publishes to, and
  which forwards to PagerDuty. Deployed once per region, into the Audit
  account.

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Why one topic in one account rather than a topic per account
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The obvious design is a topic in every account, each subscribed to
# PagerDuty. It is worse in the way that matters: the PagerDuty routing key is
# a credential, and that design copies it into every account in the
# Organization — including member accounts, which are the ones most likely to
# be compromised. Rotating it then means touching every account.
#
# CloudWatch alarms can publish cross-account when the topic policy allows it,
# so the key lives in exactly one account, rotates in one place, and a member
# account holds nothing but permission to publish.
#
# Design doc 02 puts Security Hub, Config and GuardDuty aggregation in the
# Audit account. Alerting converges to the same place for the same reason.
#
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# This topic is regional, and that is a real limitation
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# CloudWatch is regional, so alarms in us-east-2 can only be evaluated by
# us-east-2. A second topic in us-west-2 does not make us-east-2's alarms
# survive a us-east-2 outage — it only helps alarms that live in us-west-2,
# and there are none yet.
#
# So this is deployed to the home region only, and the replica region gets a
# copy when it gets alarms. Recorded as B-017 rather than left as an unstated
# assumption, because "alerting is multi-region" is exactly the sort of thing
# that gets believed without being true.

Parameters:

  OrganizationId:
    Type: String
    Description: >-
      Organization id (o-xxxx). Scopes who may publish. Every account in the
      Organization may publish; nothing outside it may.
    AllowedPattern: '^o-[a-z0-9]{10,32}$'

  PagerDutySecretName:
    Type: String
    Default: ''
    Description: >-
      Secrets Manager secret holding the PagerDuty CloudWatch routing key,
      under the key `integration_key`. Written by
      scripts/sync-pagerduty-secrets.sh from the Terraform output.

      Empty deploys the topic with NO subscription. That is a deliberate and
      useful state: the cross-account publish path can be proved before any
      credential exists, by pushing an alarm to ALARM and reading the topic's
      NumberOfMessagesPublished metric. An unsubscribed topic that accepts
      publishes is a known-good half; a subscribed topic that silently drops
      them is not distinguishable from a working one.

  LowUrgencySecretName:
    Type: String
    Default: ''
    Description: >-
      Secrets Manager secret holding the routing key for the LOW-URGENCY
      PagerDuty service, under the key `integration_key`.

      A second service and a second topic, because urgency in PagerDuty is a
      property of the service rather than of the individual alert, and the
      CloudWatch vendor integration does not populate an alert severity field
      that a single service could derive urgency from.

      Empty leaves dev and test alarms actionless, which was their state before
      this existed.

Conditions:
  HasPagerDuty: !Not [!Equals [!Ref PagerDutySecretName, '']]
  HasLowUrgency: !Not [!Equals [!Ref LowUrgencySecretName, '']]

Resources:

  # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # Encryption
  # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # The payload is alarm names, descriptions, account ids and state
  # transitions — not regulated data. Encrypting it is a posture decision, not
  # a control that protects anything specific, and it carries a genuine cost:
  # a cross-account publisher needs KMS access as well as SNS access, and the
  # KMS grant is the half that fails silently.
  #
  # Done anyway, because "everything at rest is encrypted with a
  # platform-managed key" is a sentence AltDigital says to clients, and an
  # exception that exists only in a template comment is an exception nobody
  # will remember when an auditor asks.
  AlertsKey:
    Type: AWS::KMS::Key
    DeletionPolicy: Retain
    UpdateReplacePolicy: Retain
    Properties:
      Description: Encrypts the platform alerting topic
      EnableKeyRotation: true
      PendingWindowInDays: 30
      KeyPolicy:
        Version: '2012-10-17'
        Statement:
          - Sid: EnableIAMPolicyDelegation
            Effect: Allow
            Principal: { AWS: !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:iam::${AWS::AccountId}:root' }
            Action: 'kms:*'
            Resource: '*'

          # CloudWatch in a MEMBER account calls KMS in THIS account to encrypt
          # the message it is publishing. The caller is the service principal
          # cloudwatch.amazonaws.com, which belongs to no account, so
          # aws:PrincipalOrgID can never match — that mistake cost a working
          # day on the CloudTrail key in security/10-log-archive.yaml.
          #
          # aws:SourceOrgID is the correct condition for a service principal:
          # it describes the organization of the resource the service is acting
          # for, not the caller.
          #
          # VERIFIED 2026-09-17, not assumed. An alarm in the Log Archive
          # account (868150784436) was driven to ALARM and the Audit account's
          # NumberOfMessagesPublished went 0 -> 1, which is only possible if
          # both this key policy and the topic policy admitted the publish.
          # Re-check with scripts/test-alert-path.sh after any edit to either.
          #
          # This was worth testing rather than asserting: aws:SourceOrgID is
          # confirmed for config.amazonaws.com and delivery.logs.amazonaws.com
          # elsewhere in this repository, but "confirmed for two service
          # principals" is not "confirmed for service principals", and the
          # failure mode is a policy that can never match.
          - Sid: AllowCloudWatchToEncrypt
            Effect: Allow
            Principal:
              Service:
                - cloudwatch.amazonaws.com
                - events.amazonaws.com
            Action:
              - 'kms:GenerateDataKey*'
              - 'kms:Decrypt'
            Resource: '*'
            Condition:
              StringEquals:
                'aws:SourceOrgID': !Ref OrganizationId

          # CloudWatch Logs, for the routing layer's log group. Added
          # 2026-09-18 when alerting/20-router.yaml failed to create with
          # "The specified KMS key does not exist or is not allowed to be used"
          # — a message that names neither the key policy nor the missing
          # principal, and reads like the key ARN is wrong.
          #
          # Three things differ from the statement above and all three are
          # required:
          #
          #   the principal is REGIONAL — logs.us-east-2.amazonaws.com, not
          #   logs.amazonaws.com, which is silently never matched
          #
          #   kms:Describe* is needed as well as encrypt and decrypt; Logs
          #   validates the key before it will attach it
          #
          #   the condition is the log-group encryption context rather than
          #   aws:SourceOrgID, which Logs does not send. Scoped to this
          #   account's log groups so the grant is not open-ended.
          - Sid: AllowCloudWatchLogs
            Effect: Allow
            Principal:
              Service: !Sub 'logs.${AWS::Region}.amazonaws.com'
            Action:
              - 'kms:Encrypt*'
              - 'kms:Decrypt*'
              - 'kms:ReEncrypt*'
              - 'kms:GenerateDataKey*'
              - 'kms:Describe*'
            Resource: '*'
            Condition:
              ArnLike:
                'kms:EncryptionContext:aws:logs:arn': !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:logs:${AWS::Region}:${AWS::AccountId}:log-group:*'

          # Publishing to an ENCRYPTED topic needs the key as well as the
          # topic, and the two are separate grants that fail at different
          # layers. Admitting a principal to the topic policy alone produces
          # KMSAccessDenied on publish — an error that names KMS while the
          # thing you just edited was SNS.
          #
          # Both roles publish as IAM principals rather than as service
          # principals, so aws:PrincipalArn is the right condition here where
          # aws:SourceOrgID is right above. Getting that backwards is the
          # mistake that cost a day on the CloudTrail key.
          #
          # NOTE: PlatformEventBridgeDelivery was added at the same time as
          # PlatformResponseAutomation, having been missed when the event rules
          # were built. The rules had targets attached and had never delivered
          # an event, so the gap was invisible — wiring that looks complete and
          # fails on first use.
          - Sid: AllowPlatformRolesToEncrypt
            Effect: Allow
            Principal: { AWS: '*' }
            Action:
              - 'kms:GenerateDataKey*'
              - 'kms:Decrypt'
            Resource: '*'
            Condition:
              StringEquals:
                'aws:PrincipalOrgID': !Ref OrganizationId
              ArnLike:
                'aws:PrincipalArn':
                  - !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:iam::*:role/PlatformEventBridgeDelivery'
                  - !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:iam::*:role/PlatformResponseAutomation'
      Tags:
        - { Key: platform-managed, Value: 'true' }

  AlertsKeyAlias:
    Type: AWS::KMS::Alias
    Properties:
      AliasName: alias/platform-alerts
      TargetKeyId: !Ref AlertsKey

  # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # The topic
  # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  AlertsTopic:
    Type: AWS::SNS::Topic
    Properties:
      TopicName: platform-alerts
      DisplayName: AltDigital Platform Alerts
      KmsMasterKeyId: !Ref AlertsKey
      Tags:
        - { Key: platform-managed, Value: 'true' }

  AlertsTopicPolicy:
    Type: AWS::SNS::TopicPolicy
    Properties:
      Topics:
        - !Ref AlertsTopic
      PolicyDocument:
        Version: '2012-10-17'
        Statement:
          # Publish is granted to the CloudWatch service principal, scoped to
          # the Organization — not to account principals. An alarm publishes as
          # the service, never as a role, so a grant to member account roles
          # would be both useless and an unnecessary widening.
          - Sid: AllowOrganizationAlarmsToPublish
            Effect: Allow
            Principal:
              Service:
                - cloudwatch.amazonaws.com
                - events.amazonaws.com
            Action: 'sns:Publish'
            Resource: !Ref AlertsTopic
            Condition:
              StringEquals:
                'aws:SourceOrgID': !Ref OrganizationId
          # EventBridge RULES, unlike CloudWatch alarms, publish cross-account
          # as an assumed ROLE rather than as a service principal — so the
          # statement above cannot admit them and PutTargets fails with
          # "RoleArn is required for target".
          #
          # Admitted by role NAME rather than by organization membership alone.
          # aws:PrincipalOrgID on its own would let any principal in any member
          # account publish to the channel every page travels through, which is
          # a poor trade for four event rules.
          - Sid: AllowPlatformEventDeliveryRole
            Effect: Allow
            Principal: { AWS: '*' }
            Action: 'sns:Publish'
            Resource: !Ref AlertsTopic
            Condition:
              StringEquals:
                'aws:PrincipalOrgID': !Ref OrganizationId
              ArnLike:
                # Two roles publish here as IAM principals rather than as
                # service principals, and both had to be added the hard way
                # after a deploy failed:
                #
                #   PlatformEventBridgeDelivery   event rules, which cannot
                #                                 target a cross-account topic
                #                                 as a service principal
                #   PlatformResponseAutomation    the response engine's stage 4,
                #                                 publishing the incident dossier
                #
                # Named individually rather than matched as Platform*. A
                # wildcard would admit every future platform role in every
                # member account to the channel every page travels through, and
                # the next role added would gain publish rights silently.
                'aws:PrincipalArn':
                  - !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:iam::*:role/PlatformEventBridgeDelivery'
                  - !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:iam::*:role/PlatformResponseAutomation'

          # Subscribing is a separate and much more dangerous permission than
          # publishing: a subscriber reads every alarm in the platform,
          # including the resource names in the descriptions. Restricted to
          # this account, which is where the PagerDuty subscription is created.
          #
          # sns:Subscribe alone, not sns:Subscribe + sns:Receive. cfn-lint
          # rejects sns:Receive: it appears in older AWS documentation but is
          # absent from the current service authorization reference, so a deny
          # naming it is a deny on an action that may not exist. Subscribe is
          # the real control regardless — nothing receives without having
          # subscribed first.
          - Sid: DenySubscribeFromOutsideThisAccount
            Effect: Deny
            Principal: { AWS: '*' }
            Action: 'sns:Subscribe'
            Resource: !Ref AlertsTopic
            Condition:
              StringNotEquals:
                'aws:PrincipalAccount': !Ref AWS::AccountId

          - Sid: DenyInsecureTransport
            Effect: Deny
            Principal: { AWS: '*' }
            Action: 'sns:Publish'
            Resource: !Ref AlertsTopic
            Condition:
              Bool:
                'aws:SecureTransport': 'false'

  # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # PagerDuty
  # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # The routing key is read with a dynamic reference, so it is resolved at
  # deploy time and never becomes a stack parameter. A NoEcho parameter would
  # have been simpler and would have put the key in the changeset, where it is
  # readable by anyone who can describe the stack.
  #
  # The vendor endpoint is the v1 CloudWatch integration URL, not Events API
  # v2. That is deliberate: PagerDuty's CloudWatch vendor integration parses
  # the SNS envelope and renders the alarm name as the incident title and the
  # alarm description as the body. Events v2 would accept the same POST and
  # produce an incident whose body is an unparsed JSON blob.
  PagerDutySubscription:
    Type: AWS::SNS::Subscription
    Condition: HasPagerDuty
    Properties:
      TopicArn: !Ref AlertsTopic
      Protocol: https
      Endpoint: !Sub
        - 'https://events.pagerduty.com/integration/${Key}/enqueue'
        - Key: !Sub '{{resolve:secretsmanager:${PagerDutySecretName}:SecretString:integration_key}}'
      # PagerDuty confirms the subscription automatically. If this sits in
      # PendingConfirmation, the key is wrong — a bad key returns 200 to the
      # confirmation POST and then discards everything, which is the single
      # most misleading failure in this whole path.
      DeliveryPolicy:
        healthyRetryPolicy:
          numRetries: 10
          minDelayTarget: 10
          maxDelayTarget: 300
          numMinDelayRetries: 3
          numMaxDelayRetries: 3
          backoffFunction: exponential

  # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # Alerting on the alerting
  # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # If delivery to PagerDuty fails, every other alarm in the platform becomes
  # silent and nothing says so. This alarm cannot page through the path it is
  # monitoring, so it is the one place where a second channel is not optional.
  # It currently has no action either — B-015 — but it is the first one that
  # should get a non-PagerDuty destination.
  NotificationFailureAlarm:
    Type: AWS::CloudWatch::Alarm
    Condition: HasPagerDuty
    Properties:
      AlarmName: platform-alert-delivery-failed
      AlarmDescription: >-
        SNS could not deliver a platform alarm to PagerDuty. Every alarm in the
        platform routes through this topic, so while this is firing the
        platform is not alerting at all — treat it as the highest-severity
        condition here, above whatever alarm failed to deliver.
        Check the subscription is Confirmed rather than PendingConfirmation,
        then the routing key in Secrets Manager.
      Namespace: AWS/SNS
      MetricName: NumberOfNotificationsFailed
      Dimensions:
        - Name: TopicName
          Value: !GetAtt AlertsTopic.TopicName
      Statistic: Sum
      Period: 300
      EvaluationPeriods: 1
      Threshold: 1
      ComparisonOperator: GreaterThanOrEqualToThreshold
      TreatMissingData: notBreaching

  # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # Low-urgency path
  # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # Same key policy and topic policy shape as the main topic — it reuses
  # AlertsKey and grants the same org-scoped publish — because the difference
  # between these two paths is entirely about what PagerDuty does on receipt,
  # not about who may publish.
  #
  # A separate TOPIC rather than a second subscription on the first, because an
  # SNS topic fans out to every subscriber: one topic with both integrations
  # attached would deliver every alarm to both services, and every dev alarm
  # would page after all.
  LowUrgencyTopic:
    Type: AWS::SNS::Topic
    Condition: HasLowUrgency
    Properties:
      TopicName: platform-alerts-low
      DisplayName: AltDigital Platform Alerts (low urgency)
      KmsMasterKeyId: !Ref AlertsKey
      Tags:
        - { Key: platform-managed, Value: 'true' }

  LowUrgencyTopicPolicy:
    Type: AWS::SNS::TopicPolicy
    Condition: HasLowUrgency
    Properties:
      Topics:
        - !Ref LowUrgencyTopic
      PolicyDocument:
        Version: '2012-10-17'
        Statement:
          - Sid: AllowOrganizationAlarmsToPublish
            Effect: Allow
            Principal:
              Service:
                - cloudwatch.amazonaws.com
                - events.amazonaws.com
            Action: 'sns:Publish'
            Resource: !Ref LowUrgencyTopic
            Condition:
              StringEquals:
                'aws:SourceOrgID': !Ref OrganizationId
          # EventBridge RULES, unlike CloudWatch alarms, publish cross-account
          # as an assumed ROLE rather than as a service principal — so the
          # statement above cannot admit them and PutTargets fails with
          # "RoleArn is required for target".
          #
          # Admitted by role NAME rather than by organization membership alone.
          # aws:PrincipalOrgID on its own would let any principal in any member
          # account publish to the channel every page travels through, which is
          # a poor trade for four event rules.
          - Sid: AllowPlatformEventDeliveryRole
            Effect: Allow
            Principal: { AWS: '*' }
            Action: 'sns:Publish'
            Resource: !Ref LowUrgencyTopic
            Condition:
              StringEquals:
                'aws:PrincipalOrgID': !Ref OrganizationId
              ArnLike:
                # Two roles publish here as IAM principals rather than as
                # service principals, and both had to be added the hard way
                # after a deploy failed:
                #
                #   PlatformEventBridgeDelivery   event rules, which cannot
                #                                 target a cross-account topic
                #                                 as a service principal
                #   PlatformResponseAutomation    the response engine's stage 4,
                #                                 publishing the incident dossier
                #
                # Named individually rather than matched as Platform*. A
                # wildcard would admit every future platform role in every
                # member account to the channel every page travels through, and
                # the next role added would gain publish rights silently.
                'aws:PrincipalArn':
                  - !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:iam::*:role/PlatformEventBridgeDelivery'
                  - !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:iam::*:role/PlatformResponseAutomation'
          - Sid: DenySubscribeFromOutsideThisAccount
            Effect: Deny
            Principal: { AWS: '*' }
            Action: 'sns:Subscribe'
            Resource: !Ref LowUrgencyTopic
            Condition:
              StringNotEquals:
                'aws:PrincipalAccount': !Ref AWS::AccountId
          - Sid: DenyInsecureTransport
            Effect: Deny
            Principal: { AWS: '*' }
            Action: 'sns:Publish'
            Resource: !Ref LowUrgencyTopic
            Condition:
              Bool:
                'aws:SecureTransport': 'false'

  LowUrgencySubscription:
    Type: AWS::SNS::Subscription
    Condition: HasLowUrgency
    Properties:
      TopicArn: !Ref LowUrgencyTopic
      Protocol: https
      Endpoint: !Sub
        - 'https://events.pagerduty.com/integration/${Key}/enqueue'
        - Key: !Sub '{{resolve:secretsmanager:${LowUrgencySecretName}:SecretString:integration_key}}'
      DeliveryPolicy:
        healthyRetryPolicy:
          numRetries: 10
          minDelayTarget: 10
          maxDelayTarget: 300
          numMinDelayRetries: 3
          numMaxDelayRetries: 3
          backoffFunction: exponential

  # Deliberately NO delivery-failure alarm on this topic.
  #
  # The production topic has one because losing it means losing every page. If
  # the low-urgency path breaks, dev and test alarms stop arriving in a queue
  # nobody watches urgently — which is worth knowing and is not worth its own
  # alarm, since the alarm would itself be low urgency and land in the same
  # queue that is not being delivered.

Outputs:

  LowUrgencyTopicArn:
    Condition: HasLowUrgency
    Description: Dev and test alarms publish here. Low urgency; does not page.
    Value: !Ref LowUrgencyTopic

  AlertsTopicArn:
    Description: Publish platform alarms here. Referenced cross-account by alarm stacks.
    Value: !Ref AlertsTopic

  AlertsKeyArn:
    Description: Key encrypting the alerting topic
    Value: !GetAtt AlertsKey.Arn

  SubscriptionState:
    Description: Whether a PagerDuty subscription was created
    Value: !If [HasPagerDuty, 'subscribed', 'no-subscription-topic-only']
files.alerting/20-router.yaml:
AWSTemplateFormatVersion: '2010-09-09'

Description: >-
  AltDigital Managed Platform — the routing layer. A central event bus every
  member account forwards to, a router that decides by severity and
  environment, and the four destinations design/06 names. Deploys to the Audit
  account alongside the alert topics.

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Why one central bus rather than routing in each member account
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Member accounts already deliver cross-account to the Audit SNS topics, so a
# per-account router would have been less new machinery. It is the wrong shape
# for three reasons:
#
#   The PagerDuty routing key would have to exist in every member account. It
#   is a credential that can raise an incident on the platform's service, and
#   the accounts that would hold it are the ones a tenant's workload runs in.
#
#   Routing policy would be deployed N times and drift N ways. "Why was I not
#   paged" is already hard to answer; it becomes unanswerable when the answer
#   depends on which account the alarm was in.
#
#   Correlation would be impossible. The dossier that merges with a raw alarm
#   arrives from the same account, but a future cross-account correlation — one
#   incident spanning a tenant's dev and prod, or a partner's whole book — has
#   nowhere to happen if each account routes alone.
#
# The cost is a single point of failure for alerting. That is why the
# CloudWatch SNS subscription in 10-alert-topic.yaml is retained rather than
# replaced: if this bus or this Lambda is broken, alarms still reach PagerDuty
# by the old path, unenriched but delivered. Degraded beats silent.
#
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Jira does not exist yet
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Prompt 12.3 provisions it. Until then the Jira destination is a durable queue
# of ticket intents rather than a Jira integration, and this template does not
# pretend otherwise: the queue has a 14-day retention so the backlog that
# accumulates before 12.3 is drainable rather than lost, and an alarm fires if
# it grows past the point where draining by hand is realistic.
#
# The alternative — dropping non-paging events until Jira exists — would mean
# every `digest_and_jira` alarm in dev and test going nowhere, which is the
# state 5.3 exists to end.

Parameters:

  OrganizationId:
    Type: String
    AllowedPattern: '^o-[a-z0-9]{10,32}$'
    Description: >-
      Only accounts in this organization may put events on the bus. An event
      bus without this is an open door to raising incidents on our own pager.

  PagerDutySecretName:
    Type: String
    Default: platform/pagerduty
    Description: >-
      Holds events_v2_routing_key. Written by
      scripts/sync-pagerduty-secrets.sh from the Terraform output; never a
      stack parameter, so it never appears in a changeset.

  PagerDutySecretNameLow:
    Type: String
    Default: platform/pagerduty-low
    Description: 'Routing key for the dev/test service.'

  AlertsKeyArn:
    Type: String
    Description: 'KMS key from 10-alert-topic.yaml, reused for the queues.'

  AlertsTopicArn:
    Type: String
    Description: >-
      Where the router's OWN failures go. Passed rather than imported: an
      Export cannot be changed while anything imports it, which would freeze
      10-alert-topic.yaml against a stack it does not know about.

  LowUrgencyTopicArn:
    Type: String
    Default: ''
    Description: 'Backlog warnings that are not incidents.'

  RouterCodeBucket:
    Type: String

  RouterCodeKey:
    Type: String

Conditions:
  HasLowUrgency: !Not [!Equals [!Ref LowUrgencyTopicArn, '']]

Resources:

  # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # The bus
  # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  PlatformBus:
    Type: AWS::Events::EventBus
    Properties:
      Name: platform-alerts

  PlatformBusPolicy:
    Type: AWS::Events::EventBusPolicy
    Properties:
      EventBusName: !Ref PlatformBus
      StatementId: AllowOrganizationPutEvents
      Statement:
        Effect: Allow
        # Any principal, narrowed by the org condition — the documented pattern
        # for an organization bus, because the member-side forwarding roles are
        # created per account and cannot be enumerated here.
        Principal: '*'
        Action: 'events:PutEvents'
        Resource: !GetAtt PlatformBus.Arn
        Condition:
          StringEquals:
            'aws:PrincipalOrgID': !Ref OrganizationId

  # Events the router could not process. Retained rather than discarded: a
  # routing failure means something asked for attention and did not get it, and
  # the event is the only record of what it was.
  RouterDlq:
    Type: AWS::SQS::Queue
    # Delete, after this was written as Retain and the trap fired on the very
    # first deploy: the stack rolled back on an unrelated KMS policy error, the
    # queue was kept, and the retry failed with "queue already exists".
    #
    # The Retain argument was that this is the only record of events the router
    # never managed to log. True, and beside the point — at the moment a stack
    # rolls back the queue is empty, so Retain protected nothing and cost the
    # ability to deploy at all. The contents are short-lived by design in any
    # case: RouterDlqAlarm fires on a single visible message precisely so this
    # is drained rather than accumulated.
    #
    # canaries/00-canary-artifacts.yaml documents the same trap for S3, and the
    # rule that generalises is: Retain is for state that has accumulated value,
    # not for a resource that merely could. Retaining an empty thing only makes
    # the stack unretryable.
    DeletionPolicy: Delete
    UpdateReplacePolicy: Delete
    Properties:
      QueueName: platform-router-dlq
      MessageRetentionPeriod: 1209600
      KmsMasterKeyId: !Ref AlertsKeyArn
      SqsManagedSseEnabled: false

  # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # Destinations
  # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  JiraQueue:
    Type: AWS::SQS::Queue
    # Delete, not Retain. Every message here was written after a routing
    # decision that is itself recorded in the routing log group with a year's
    # retention, so the contents are reconstructible — and Retain would make a
    # failed stack unretryable for no gain.
    DeletionPolicy: Delete
    UpdateReplacePolicy: Delete
    Properties:
      QueueName: platform-jira-intents
      MessageRetentionPeriod: 1209600
      VisibilityTimeout: 300
      KmsMasterKeyId: !Ref AlertsKeyArn
      SqsManagedSseEnabled: false
      RedrivePolicy:
        deadLetterTargetArn: !GetAtt DestinationDlq.Arn
        maxReceiveCount: 5

  ReviewQueue:
    Type: AWS::SQS::Queue
    # Delete, not Retain. Every message here was written after a routing
    # decision that is itself recorded in the routing log group with a year's
    # retention, so the contents are reconstructible — and Retain would make a
    # failed stack unretryable for no gain.
    DeletionPolicy: Delete
    UpdateReplacePolicy: Delete
    Properties:
      QueueName: platform-review-queue
      MessageRetentionPeriod: 1209600
      VisibilityTimeout: 300
      KmsMasterKeyId: !Ref AlertsKeyArn
      SqsManagedSseEnabled: false
      RedrivePolicy:
        deadLetterTargetArn: !GetAtt DestinationDlq.Arn
        maxReceiveCount: 5

  # design/12's destination: "defined by who needs to have a conversation, not
  # by severity". 06a routes uat that way by default, so this is not
  # speculative — it is load-bearing for every UAT alarm today.
  CommercialQueue:
    Type: AWS::SQS::Queue
    # Delete, not Retain. Every message here was written after a routing
    # decision that is itself recorded in the routing log group with a year's
    # retention, so the contents are reconstructible — and Retain would make a
    # failed stack unretryable for no gain.
    DeletionPolicy: Delete
    UpdateReplacePolicy: Delete
    Properties:
      QueueName: platform-commercial-events
      MessageRetentionPeriod: 1209600
      VisibilityTimeout: 300
      KmsMasterKeyId: !Ref AlertsKeyArn
      SqsManagedSseEnabled: false
      RedrivePolicy:
        deadLetterTargetArn: !GetAtt DestinationDlq.Arn
        maxReceiveCount: 5

  DestinationDlq:
    Type: AWS::SQS::Queue
    # Delete, not Retain. Every message here was written after a routing
    # decision that is itself recorded in the routing log group with a year's
    # retention, so the contents are reconstructible — and Retain would make a
    # failed stack unretryable for no gain.
    DeletionPolicy: Delete
    UpdateReplacePolicy: Delete
    Properties:
      QueueName: platform-destination-dlq
      MessageRetentionPeriod: 1209600
      KmsMasterKeyId: !Ref AlertsKeyArn
      SqsManagedSseEnabled: false

  # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # The router
  # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  RouterRole:
    Type: AWS::IAM::Role
    Properties:
      AssumeRolePolicyDocument:
        Version: '2012-10-17'
        Statement:
          - Effect: Allow
            Principal: { Service: lambda.amazonaws.com }
            Action: sts:AssumeRole
      ManagedPolicyArns:
        - !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:iam::aws:policy/service-role/AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole'
      Policies:
        - PolicyName: Route
          PolicyDocument:
            Version: '2012-10-17'
            Statement:
              - Effect: Allow
                Action: 'sqs:SendMessage'
                Resource:
                  - !GetAtt JiraQueue.Arn
                  - !GetAtt ReviewQueue.Arn
                  - !GetAtt CommercialQueue.Arn
                  # The function's own DeadLetterConfig. Lambda validates this
                  # at CREATE and refuses the function outright — "The provided
                  # execution role does not have permissions to call SendMessage
                  # on SQS" — rather than failing later when a DLQ write is
                  # actually needed. Which is the right behaviour: a
                  # dead-letter queue the function cannot write to is a silent
                  # hole exactly where the guarantees are supposed to be.
                  - !GetAtt RouterDlq.Arn
              - Effect: Allow
                Action: 'secretsmanager:GetSecretValue'
                Resource:
                  - !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:secretsmanager:${AWS::Region}:${AWS::AccountId}:secret:${PagerDutySecretName}-*'
                  - !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:secretsmanager:${AWS::Region}:${AWS::AccountId}:secret:${PagerDutySecretNameLow}-*'
              - Effect: Allow
                Action: ['kms:GenerateDataKey', 'kms:Decrypt']
                Resource: !Ref AlertsKeyArn
              - Effect: Allow
                # The account -> tier map. Without it the router assumed prod
                # for anything carrying no tier of its own, so a CRITICAL
                # finding in a dev sandbox would have paged as production.
                # Written by scripts/sync-account-tiers.sh.
                Action: 'ssm:GetParameter'
                Resource: !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:ssm:${AWS::Region}:${AWS::AccountId}:parameter/platform/routing/*'
              # No CloudWatch permissions, deliberately.
              #
              # This granted cross-account ListTagsForResource so the router
              # could read the routing class off the alarm's tags. It cannot
              # work: CloudWatch alarms have no resource-based policy, so an
              # IAM grant in this account is only half of a permission that
              # needs two halves. Every alarm routed to review with
              # "could not read alarm tags".
              #
              # The instrumentation Lambda now writes the routing class into the
              # AlarmDescription, which travels inside the event, so the router
              # needs no AWS call at all on the path that pages people.

  RouterFunction:
    Type: AWS::Lambda::Function
    Properties:
      FunctionName: platform-router
      Runtime: python3.12
      Handler: router.handler
      Role: !GetAtt RouterRole.Arn
      Timeout: 60
      MemorySize: 256
      # No ReservedConcurrentExecutions, and not by choice.
      #
      # A cap belongs here: the router POSTs to PagerDuty, and an alarm storm
      # across many accounts should queue rather than arrive as a thousand
      # simultaneous incidents. But the Audit account's total Lambda
      # concurrency is 10 — AWS's default for an account that has not used
      # Lambda much — and reserving ANY amount leaves fewer than the 10
      # unreserved executions AWS requires, so the reservation is rejected
      # outright rather than clamped.
      #
      # The consequence is worse than a missing cap: with a ceiling of 10 the
      # whole account throttles under a storm, and a throttled router
      # dead-letters the events it cannot take. B-040 carries the quota
      # increase, which has to happen before this is trusted in production.
      Code:
        S3Bucket: !Ref RouterCodeBucket
        S3Key: !Ref RouterCodeKey
      DeadLetterConfig:
        TargetArn: !GetAtt RouterDlq.Arn
      Environment:
        Variables:
          PAGERDUTY_SECRET_NAME: !Ref PagerDutySecretName
          PAGERDUTY_SECRET_NAME_LOW: !Ref PagerDutySecretNameLow
          JIRA_QUEUE_URL: !Ref JiraQueue
          REVIEW_QUEUE_URL: !Ref ReviewQueue
          COMMERCIAL_QUEUE_URL: !Ref CommercialQueue

  RouterLogGroup:
    Type: AWS::Logs::LogGroup
    DeletionPolicy: Delete
    UpdateReplacePolicy: Delete
    Properties:
      LogGroupName: /aws/lambda/platform-router
      # A year. These records answer "why was I not paged about this", which is
      # asked long after the fact and is the question an auditor asks too.
      RetentionInDays: 365
      KmsKeyId: !Ref AlertsKeyArn

  # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # What reaches the router
  # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # One rule per source rather than one catch-all, so an unexpected event type
  # on the bus is visibly unrouted rather than quietly matched. The router has
  # its own else for shapes it does not recognise; this is the layer before it.
  AlarmRule:
    Type: AWS::Events::Rule
    Properties:
      Name: platform-route-alarms
      EventBusName: !Ref PlatformBus
      EventPattern:
        detail-type: ['CloudWatch Alarm State Change']
      State: ENABLED
      Targets:
        - Id: router
          Arn: !GetAtt RouterFunction.Arn
          DeadLetterConfig:
            Arn: !GetAtt RouterDlq.Arn
          RetryPolicy:
            MaximumRetryAttempts: 4
            MaximumEventAgeInSeconds: 3600

  FindingsRule:
    Type: AWS::Events::Rule
    Properties:
      Name: platform-route-findings
      EventBusName: !Ref PlatformBus
      EventPattern:
        detail-type:
          - 'Security Hub Findings - Imported'
          - 'GuardDuty Finding'
          - 'Config Rules Compliance Change'
      State: ENABLED
      Targets:
        - Id: router
          Arn: !GetAtt RouterFunction.Arn
          DeadLetterConfig:
            Arn: !GetAtt RouterDlq.Arn
          RetryPolicy:
            MaximumRetryAttempts: 4
            MaximumEventAgeInSeconds: 3600

  DossierRule:
    Type: AWS::Events::Rule
    Properties:
      Name: platform-route-dossiers
      EventBusName: !Ref PlatformBus
      EventPattern:
        # Two emitters, one shape. platform.recovery is the restore workflow
        # (recovery/src/worker.py), which emits a dossier rather than routing
        # for itself — prompt 6.2: "DO NOT build a second routing path".
        #
        # Listed explicitly rather than matched on the detail-type alone,
        # because the pattern is also the list of things allowed to raise an
        # incident on this platform's pager, and that list should be readable.
        # platform.security is containment (prompt 7.1). Unlike the other two
        # it runs IN this account and puts straight onto this bus, so it never
        # passes through baseline/70-event-forwarding.yaml — which is why that
        # template's matching rule lists only the two member-side sources.
        source: ['platform.response', 'platform.recovery', 'platform.security',
                 'platform.change']
        detail-type: ['Platform Incident Dossier']
      State: ENABLED
      Targets:
        - Id: router
          Arn: !GetAtt RouterFunction.Arn
          DeadLetterConfig:
            Arn: !GetAtt RouterDlq.Arn
          RetryPolicy:
            MaximumRetryAttempts: 4
            MaximumEventAgeInSeconds: 3600

  # A dossier from a source this template does not know about.
  #
  # This closes a hole in the else below, found by deploying prompt 7.1. The
  # UnmatchedRule excludes by DETAIL-TYPE alone, and DossierRule is the only
  # rule that also filters on SOURCE — so a "Platform Incident Dossier" from an
  # unrecognised source matched neither: not DossierRule, because the source
  # was not listed, and not UnmatchedRule, because the detail-type was. It went
  # nowhere at all, silently, which is the exact failure the else exists to
  # prevent.
  #
  # It surfaced when containment began emitting as platform.security before
  # this template had been redeployed to expect it: a full security incident,
  # contained correctly, and no routing decision recorded anywhere.
  UnmatchedDossierRule:
    Type: AWS::Events::Rule
    Properties:
      Name: platform-route-unmatched-dossiers
      EventBusName: !Ref PlatformBus
      EventPattern:
        detail-type: ['Platform Incident Dossier']
        source:
          - anything-but:
              - platform.response
              - platform.recovery
              - platform.security
              - platform.change
      State: ENABLED
      Targets:
        - Id: router
          Arn: !GetAtt RouterFunction.Arn
          DeadLetterConfig:
            Arn: !GetAtt RouterDlq.Arn

  # Everything else on the bus. Not a no-op: it is how an event nobody planned
  # for becomes visible instead of vanishing, which is the same else rule the
  # response engine follows.
  UnmatchedRule:
    Type: AWS::Events::Rule
    Properties:
      Name: platform-route-unmatched
      EventBusName: !Ref PlatformBus
      EventPattern:
        detail-type:
          - anything-but:
              - 'CloudWatch Alarm State Change'
              - 'Security Hub Findings - Imported'
              - 'GuardDuty Finding'
              - 'Config Rules Compliance Change'
              - 'Platform Incident Dossier'
      State: ENABLED
      Targets:
        - Id: router
          Arn: !GetAtt RouterFunction.Arn
          DeadLetterConfig:
            Arn: !GetAtt RouterDlq.Arn

  RouterInvokePermission:
    Type: AWS::Lambda::Permission
    Properties:
      FunctionName: !GetAtt RouterFunction.Arn
      Action: lambda:InvokeFunction
      Principal: events.amazonaws.com
      SourceAccount: !Ref AWS::AccountId

  # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # Alarming on the alerting
  # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # These cannot page through the path they monitor, so they go to the SNS
  # topic directly — the old CloudWatch integration, which is exactly the
  # fallback this template kept for the purpose.
  RouterErrorsAlarm:
    Type: AWS::CloudWatch::Alarm
    Properties:
      AlarmName: platform-router-errors
      AlarmDescription: >-
        The routing layer is failing. Events are landing in
        platform-router-dlq and nothing is being paged, ticketed or queued
        through the router. Alarms still reach PagerDuty by the direct SNS
        subscription, unenriched.
      Namespace: AWS/Lambda
      MetricName: Errors
      Dimensions:
        - Name: FunctionName
          Value: !Ref RouterFunction
      Statistic: Sum
      Period: 300
      EvaluationPeriods: 1
      Threshold: 1
      ComparisonOperator: GreaterThanOrEqualToThreshold
      TreatMissingData: notBreaching
      AlarmActions:
        - !Ref AlertsTopicArn

  RouterDlqAlarm:
    Type: AWS::CloudWatch::Alarm
    Properties:
      AlarmName: platform-router-dlq-not-empty
      AlarmDescription: >-
        An event asked for attention and the router could not deliver it. The
        message body in platform-router-dlq is the only record of what it was.
      Namespace: AWS/SQS
      MetricName: ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible
      Dimensions:
        - Name: QueueName
          Value: !GetAtt RouterDlq.QueueName
      Statistic: Maximum
      Period: 300
      EvaluationPeriods: 1
      Threshold: 0
      ComparisonOperator: GreaterThanThreshold
      TreatMissingData: notBreaching
      AlarmActions:
        - !Ref AlertsTopicArn

  # The Jira backlog, which by design has no consumer until prompt 12.3. This
  # alarm is not about Jira being down — it is the point at which "we will
  # drain it when Jira exists" stops being true.
  JiraBacklogAlarm:
    Type: AWS::CloudWatch::Alarm
    Properties:
      AlarmName: platform-jira-intents-backlog
      AlarmDescription: >-
        Ticket intents are accumulating faster than expected and Jira does not
        exist yet (prompt 12.3). Retention is 14 days; past that the backlog is
        silently discarded. Either 12.3 is now urgent or something is routing
        far more to Jira than intended.
      Namespace: AWS/SQS
      MetricName: ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible
      Dimensions:
        - Name: QueueName
          Value: !GetAtt JiraQueue.QueueName
      Statistic: Maximum
      Period: 3600
      EvaluationPeriods: 1
      Threshold: 500
      ComparisonOperator: GreaterThanThreshold
      TreatMissingData: notBreaching
      AlarmActions:
        - !If [HasLowUrgency, !Ref LowUrgencyTopicArn, !Ref AlertsTopicArn]

Outputs:
  BusArn:
    Description: 'Member accounts forward here.'
    Value: !GetAtt PlatformBus.Arn
    Export:
      Name: !Sub '${AWS::StackName}-BusArn'
  JiraQueueUrl:
    Value: !Ref JiraQueue
  ReviewQueueUrl:
    Value: !Ref ReviewQueue
  CommercialQueueUrl:
    Value: !Ref CommercialQueue
files.alerting/30-runaway.yaml:
AWSTemplateFormatVersion: '2010-09-09'

Description: >-
  AltDigital Managed Platform — runaway detection. Account-wide rate alarms
  that catch a feedback loop before its cost becomes the thing that reports it.

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Why this exists
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# B-116. The commercial router emitted an event that matched the rule which
# triggered it, and fed itself 190,672 times in 24 hours before anybody looked.
# Nothing alarmed, because nothing was broken in any way the platform measures:
#
#   Errors          zero. Every invocation succeeded.
#   Throttles       zero. 475/minute is nowhere near a concurrency limit.
#   Duration        normal. The function did its small job correctly.
#   DLQ depth       zero. Nothing failed, so nothing was dead-lettered.
#
# Every alarm design 06a defines for a Lambda function asks "is this function
# working". A runaway is a function working perfectly, extremely often. The
# only signal it produces is RATE, and rate was not being watched.
#
# It cost about a dollar a day and was discovered by accident while tracing an
# unrelated chain. The next one is not guaranteed to be a cheap function: the
# same loop around a Bedrock call, a cross-region replication or a Textract
# job is three orders of magnitude more expensive per iteration, and would
# still produce no errors, no throttles and no dead letters.
#
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# ACCOUNT-WIDE metrics, deliberately, with no dimensions
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The obvious design is an invocation alarm per function. It is the wrong one,
# because it has to be remembered: every new Lambda needs somebody to add an
# alarm for it, and the gap that let B-116 run for a day was exactly that
# nobody had. A control whose coverage depends on being extended by hand is a
# control with holes shaped like whatever was built most recently.
#
# Account-wide Invocations has no dimensions and therefore no enumeration.
# It covers every function that exists now and every function added later,
# including ones written by somebody who has never read this file.
#
# The same reasoning applies to the EventBridge metrics, and there it is not
# even a choice: `PutEventsEntriesCount` and `TriggeredRules` publish ONLY at
# account level. Measured on the live account, the EventBusName dimension
# returns no data at all — so a per-bus alarm would have been permanently
# inert, which is the B-100 shape.
#
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Thresholds, measured rather than guessed
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Taken from the Audit account either side of the B-116 fix:
#
#   metric                        normal / 5min     during the loop / 5min
#   Lambda Invocations            1 - 6             ~5,000
#   Events TriggeredRules         low single digits ~4,967
#   Events PutEventsEntriesCount  low single digits ~2,604
#
# Three orders of magnitude apart, so the threshold is not a fine judgement.
# 500 sits roughly 100x above normal and 5-10x below the observed runaway: far
# enough above routine work to stay quiet through a busy sweep, far enough
# below a loop to fire within two periods of one starting.
#
# The threshold is a FIXED number and the estate will grow into it. That is
# accepted rather than solved: anomaly detection adapts but needs weeks of
# history and fails oddly on spiky workloads, and a band that widens on its own
# would have widened around B-116 given long enough. Revisit trigger is tenant
# count, not a date — see the AlarmDescription, which is what somebody reads
# when this fires.

Parameters:

  AlertsTopicArn:
    Type: String
    Description: >-
      High-urgency SNS topic. Targeted DIRECTLY rather than through the
      routing layer: the router is itself a Lambda, and a runaway involving it
      would be a runaway whose alarm depended on the thing running away. The
      topic's direct PagerDuty subscription is the fallback path that survives
      the router being broken or overwhelmed.

  InvocationThreshold:
    Type: Number
    Default: 500
    Description: >-
      Lambda invocations per 5-minute period, account-wide, above which this is
      a runaway rather than work. See the header for the measurements behind
      this number.

  EventThreshold:
    Type: Number
    Default: 500
    Description: Events published or rules triggered per 5-minute period, account-wide.

Resources:

  # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # Lambda: the direct compute cost
  # -------------------------------------------------------------------------

  LambdaInvocationRunawayAlarm:
    Type: AWS::CloudWatch::Alarm
    Properties:
      AlarmName: platform-lambda-invocation-runaway
      # Capped at 1024 characters by CloudFormation, which is why the detail
      # lives in docs/runbooks and this says only what a woken person needs in
      # the first minute.
      AlarmDescription: >-
        Account-wide Lambda invocations exceeded the runaway threshold for ten
        minutes. Almost certainly a feedback loop, not load: a function whose
        output matches the rule that triggers it, or a retry storm with no
        backoff.

        Nothing else will alarm. A loop has no errors, no throttles and no dead
        letters, because every invocation succeeds at doing a small thing it
        should not be doing at all.

        FIND: CloudWatch Metrics, AWS/Lambda Invocations by FunctionName, last
        hour. Obvious by magnitude. Then check whether that function's own
        output matches its triggering rule's pattern - that was B-116.

        STOP: disable the triggering EventBridge rule, not the function. Halts
        it immediately and preserves everything needed to understand it.

        Runbook: docs/runbooks/runaway.md
      Namespace: AWS/Lambda
      MetricName: Invocations
      # No Dimensions, on purpose. See the header: an alarm that must be
      # extended per function is an alarm with holes shaped like the newest
      # code.
      Statistic: Sum
      Period: 300
      EvaluationPeriods: 2
      Threshold: !Ref InvocationThreshold
      ComparisonOperator: GreaterThanThreshold
      # A period with no invocations is a quiet platform, not a broken one.
      TreatMissingData: notBreaching
      ActionsEnabled: true
      AlarmActions:
        - !Ref AlertsTopicArn
      OKActions:
        - !Ref AlertsTopicArn

  # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # EventBridge: the cost that is easy to miss
  # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # Separate from the Lambda alarm rather than folded into it, because a loop
  # can run entirely between rules and targets that are not Lambdas — a rule
  # forwarding to another bus, to SQS, to Step Functions — and would move these
  # metrics while leaving Invocations flat.

  EventPublishRunawayAlarm:
    Type: AWS::CloudWatch::Alarm
    Properties:
      AlarmName: platform-eventbridge-publish-runaway
      AlarmDescription: >-
        Account-wide EventBridge publishing exceeded the runaway threshold for
        ten minutes. Custom events bill per million published, so this is a
        cost signal as much as a correctness one.

        A loop running between rules and non-Lambda targets moves this and
        leaves Lambda invocations flat, which is why this alarm is separate.

        FIND: AWS/Events TriggeredRules by RuleName, last hour, then read that
        rule's event pattern against what its target emits.

        STOP: disable the rule, not the target.

        Runbook: docs/runbooks/runaway.md
      Namespace: AWS/Events
      MetricName: PutEventsEntriesCount
      # Measured: the EventBusName dimension publishes no data on this account,
      # so a per-bus alarm would never evaluate. Account level is the only
      # level that carries the signal.
      Statistic: Sum
      Period: 300
      EvaluationPeriods: 2
      Threshold: !Ref EventThreshold
      ComparisonOperator: GreaterThanThreshold
      TreatMissingData: notBreaching
      ActionsEnabled: true
      AlarmActions:
        - !Ref AlertsTopicArn
      OKActions:
        - !Ref AlertsTopicArn

  RuleTriggerRunawayAlarm:
    Type: AWS::CloudWatch::Alarm
    Properties:
      AlarmName: platform-eventbridge-rule-runaway
      AlarmDescription: >-
        Account-wide EventBridge rule triggers exceeded the runaway threshold
        for ten minutes.

        This is the EARLIEST of the three signals for a self-feeding rule: the
        rule matches its own target's output and triggers before anything
        downstream runs, so it moves first and by the largest margin. During
        B-116 it peaked near 5,000 per five minutes against a normal of low
        single digits.

        FIND and STOP: as for platform-eventbridge-publish-runaway.

        Runbook: docs/runbooks/runaway.md
      Namespace: AWS/Events
      MetricName: TriggeredRules
      Statistic: Sum
      Period: 300
      EvaluationPeriods: 2
      Threshold: !Ref EventThreshold
      ComparisonOperator: GreaterThanThreshold
      TreatMissingData: notBreaching
      ActionsEnabled: true
      AlarmActions:
        - !Ref AlertsTopicArn
      OKActions:
        - !Ref AlertsTopicArn

Outputs:

  LambdaAlarmName:
    Description: Account-wide Lambda invocation runaway alarm.
    Value: !Ref LambdaInvocationRunawayAlarm

  EventPublishAlarmName:
    Description: Account-wide EventBridge publish runaway alarm.
    Value: !Ref EventPublishRunawayAlarm

  RuleTriggerAlarmName:
    Description: Account-wide EventBridge rule trigger runaway alarm.
    Value: !Ref RuleTriggerRunawayAlarm
files.alerting/40-cadence.yaml:
AWSTemplateFormatVersion: '2010-09-09'

Description: >-
  AltDigital Managed Platform — cadence sweep. Is each scheduled component
  running, at roughly the rate it declared? Both directions.

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The other half of runaway detection
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# alerting/30-runaway.yaml catches something running at a gross multiple of
# normal. This catches the opposite, which is worse: something that should be
# running and is not.
#
# A runaway at least leaves a trace — invocations, log lines, a bill. A
# component that stops produces nothing at all, and nothing is exactly what an
# estate with no problems produces. That is B-086, B-089, B-092 and B-100:
# every one of them a thing not running, reporting success.
#
# design 06a states the principle for telemetry streams, and it generalises:
#
#   "CloudWatch Logs does not alarm on absence natively. Absence is only
#    detectable against a DECLARED EXPECTATION."
#
# The declaration is the rule's own ScheduleExpression, read from the deployed
# infrastructure rather than from a list maintained beside it. See
# alerting/src/cadence.py on why a second copy would drift.
#
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Who watches this
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The sweep is itself a scheduled component, and it cannot report its own
# absence: if it stops, it simply stops emitting findings, which reads exactly
# like an estate with nothing wrong.
#
# So it publishes a heartbeat metric on every run, and CadenceSweepStalled
# alarms on the ABSENCE of that metric — TreatMissingData: breaching, which is
# the inverse of every other alarm in the platform. It is the one alarm that
# fires because nothing arrived.
#
# That alarm is the end of the chain. Nothing watches IT, and that is a
# deliberate stopping point rather than an oversight: the regress has to end,
# and it ends at a CloudWatch alarm, which is the most reliable component in
# the path and the only one with no code of ours in it.

Parameters:

  ArtifactBucket:
    Type: String

  ArtifactKey:
    Type: String

  AlertBusName:
    Type: String
    Default: platform-alerts

  AlertsTopicArn:
    Type: String
    Description: >-
      High-urgency topic for the dead man's switch only. Findings from the
      sweep itself route through the alert bus as digest_and_jira — a
      scheduled job that missed a window needs looking at today, not at 3am.
      The sweep having stopped is different, because it blinds every other
      absence check.

  SweepSchedule:
    Type: String
    Default: rate(1 hour)
    Description: >-
      Hourly. Frequent enough that a stopped component is caught within a
      working day, infrequent enough that the sweep is not itself a
      significant source of the invocations it measures.

  LogsKeyArn:
    Type: String
    Default: ''

Conditions:

  UseDefaultLogsKey: !Equals [!Ref LogsKeyArn, '']

Resources:

  CadenceRole:
    Type: AWS::IAM::Role
    Properties:
      RoleName: PlatformCadenceSweep
      AssumeRolePolicyDocument:
        Version: '2012-10-17'
        Statement:
          - Effect: Allow
            Principal: { Service: lambda.amazonaws.com }
            Action: sts:AssumeRole
      ManagedPolicyArns:
        - !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:iam::aws:policy/service-role/AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole'

  CadencePolicy:
    Type: AWS::IAM::Policy
    Properties:
      PolicyName: SweepScheduledCadence
      Roles: [!Ref CadenceRole]
      PolicyDocument:
        Version: '2012-10-17'
        Statement:
          # Read-only over EventBridge. This inspects schedules; it never
          # changes one. Stopping a runaway by disabling a rule is a human
          # action with a runbook, not something this role can do -- CLAUDE.md
          # keeps automation additive, and a sweep that could disable rules on
          # a rate signal would eventually disable the platform during a
          # legitimate burst.
          - Sid: ReadSchedules
            Effect: Allow
            Action:
              - events:ListEventBuses
              - events:ListRules
              - events:DescribeRule
            Resource: '*'
          - Sid: ReadRuleMetrics
            Effect: Allow
            # GetMetricStatistics takes no resource-level permissions.
            Action: cloudwatch:GetMetricStatistics
            Resource: '*'
          - Sid: PublishHeartbeat
            Effect: Allow
            Action: cloudwatch:PutMetricData
            Resource: '*'
            Condition:
              StringEquals:
                cloudwatch:namespace: Platform/Cadence
          - Sid: EmitFindings
            Effect: Allow
            Action: events:PutEvents
            Resource: !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:events:${AWS::Region}:${AWS::AccountId}:event-bus/${AlertBusName}'

  CadenceLogGroup:
    Type: AWS::Logs::LogGroup
    DeletionPolicy: Retain
    UpdateReplacePolicy: Retain
    Properties:
      LogGroupName: /aws/lambda/platform-cadence-sweep
      RetentionInDays: 365
      KmsKeyId: !If
        - UseDefaultLogsKey
        - !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:kms:${AWS::Region}:${AWS::AccountId}:alias/platform-logs'
        - !Ref LogsKeyArn

  CadenceFunction:
    Type: AWS::Lambda::Function
    DependsOn: CadenceLogGroup
    Properties:
      FunctionName: platform-cadence-sweep
      Runtime: python3.12
      Handler: cadence.handler
      Role: !GetAtt CadenceRole.Arn
      # Generous: one GetMetricStatistics call per scheduled rule, serially.
      # At 100 rules that is 100 round trips.
      Timeout: 300
      MemorySize: 256
      Code:
        S3Bucket: !Ref ArtifactBucket
        S3Key: !Ref ArtifactKey
      Environment:
        Variables:
          ALERT_BUS_NAME: !Ref AlertBusName

  CadenceSchedule:
    Type: AWS::Events::Rule
    Properties:
      Name: platform-cadence-sweep
      Description: >-
        Hourly check that every scheduled rule is firing at its declared rate.
        This rule is itself covered by the sweep it triggers.
      ScheduleExpression: !Ref SweepSchedule
      State: ENABLED
      Targets:
        - Id: sweep
          Arn: !GetAtt CadenceFunction.Arn

  CadencePermission:
    Type: AWS::Lambda::Permission
    Properties:
      FunctionName: !GetAtt CadenceFunction.Arn
      Action: lambda:InvokeFunction
      Principal: events.amazonaws.com
      SourceArn: !GetAtt CadenceSchedule.Arn

  # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # The dead man's switch
  # -------------------------------------------------------------------------

  CadenceSweepStalledAlarm:
    Type: AWS::CloudWatch::Alarm
    Properties:
      AlarmName: platform-cadence-sweep-stalled
      AlarmDescription: >-
        The cadence sweep has not reported for three hours. It is the control
        that notices when scheduled components stop running, so while it is
        down the platform cannot tell a quiet estate from a stopped one.

        This alarm fires on ABSENCE, not on a value. It is the inverse of every
        other alarm here and it is the end of the chain: nothing watches this,
        deliberately, because the regress has to stop somewhere and a
        CloudWatch alarm is the most reliable link in it.

        CHECK: /aws/lambda/platform-cadence-sweep for an error, then whether
        the platform-cadence-sweep rule is still ENABLED. A rule disabled to
        stop an incident and never re-enabled is the likeliest cause.
      Namespace: Platform/Cadence
      MetricName: SweepCompleted
      Statistic: Sum
      Period: 3600
      EvaluationPeriods: 3
      Threshold: 1
      ComparisonOperator: LessThanThreshold
      # The whole point. Every other alarm treats missing data as "nothing to
      # report"; here, nothing arriving IS the report.
      TreatMissingData: breaching
      ActionsEnabled: true
      AlarmActions:
        - !Ref AlertsTopicArn
      OKActions:
        - !Ref AlertsTopicArn

Outputs:

  FunctionName:
    Description: The cadence sweep.
    Value: !Ref CadenceFunction

  StalledAlarmName:
    Description: Fires when the sweep itself stops reporting.
    Value: !Ref CadenceSweepStalledAlarm
files.scheduling/10-hoop.yaml:
AWSTemplateFormatVersion: '2010-09-09'

Description: >-
  AltDigital Managed Platform — HOOP scheduler (prompt 13.2) and its
  turndown/turnup verification (13.3). Deploys INTO the account it schedules.

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Deployed into the account it acts on, deliberately
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The alternative is a central scheduler assuming a role into each member
# account, and it is worse here for one reason: the blast radius of a bug.
#
# A central scheduler holds stop permissions across every account in the
# estate. A bug in its account-selection logic stops the wrong environment,
# and the wrong environment could be anybody's. This stack has permission in
# exactly one account and none anywhere else, so the same bug stops the
# environment it was already allowed to stop.
#
# That is the second layer of the enforcement hoop.py describes: the code
# refuses production, and the deployment never puts the code where production
# is. Neither layer alone would be enough -- a check is one edit from removal,
# and a permission boundary is one StackSet target from being widened.
#
# A third layer sits above both: AccountTier does not accept `prod` as a
# value, so CloudFormation rejects the stack before any code runs. It is the
# only one of the four refusals that does not require the Lambda to execute.
#
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Two functions, one package
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
#   hoop.handler    turndown and turnup, scheduled or manual, one code path
#   cycle.handler   verifies what just happened, and routes a failure
#
# Separate functions rather than one, because they have different failure
# modes and the verification must be able to run when the scheduler did not.
# A turnup that timed out leaves an environment nobody has checked, and the
# check is the thing that says so.

Parameters:

  ArtifactBucket:
    Type: String

  ArtifactKey:
    Type: String

  AccountId:
    Type: String
    Description: >-
      The account this stack schedules — its own. Passed explicitly rather
      than read from AWS::AccountId so that the value in the schedule payload
      is visible in the template and in the stack's parameters, where somebody
      auditing what may be turned down can read it without inspecting code.

  AccountTier:
    Type: String
    AllowedValues: [dev, test, uat]
    Description: >-
      This account's environment tier, read from the registry by the deploy
      script and fixed here at deploy time.

      `prod` is not an allowed value. CloudFormation refuses the stack before
      any code runs — which is the earliest of the four places production is
      refused, and the only one that does not require the Lambda to execute.

  AccountKind:
    Type: String
    Default: tenant
    AllowedValues: [tenant, shared]
    Description: >-
      Whether this is a customer environment or one of AltDigital's own. A
      `shared` account is refused unless it is the single designated exercise
      account: found while deploying this, because both sandboxes are
      registered `dev` and the scheduler would otherwise have turned down the
      account the canaries run in.

  ManifestParam:
    Type: String
    Default: /platform/hoop/manifest
    Description: >-
      Where turndown records what it stopped. Read by the turnup verification
      to assert the full expected set rather than merely the absence of errors.

  StateParam:
    Type: String
    Default: /platform/hoop/state
    Description: >-
      Whether this environment is scheduled down. Published by the scheduler
      and read by everything else that needs to know, rather than each system
      computing the window itself — see scheduling/src/state.py on why eight
      independent readings of one HOOP disagree.

  AlertBusName:
    Type: String
    Default: platform-alerts

  AlertBusArn:
    Type: String
    Description: Cross-account ARN of the alert bus, for findings.

  HoopConfig:
    Type: String
    Default: '{}'
    Description: >-
      The HOOP as JSON — timezone and windows. questionnaire 3a.7 supplies the
      timezone and it is NEVER defaulted: an empty config means this
      environment is not scheduled, which is a legitimate state, and the
      scheduler refuses rather than assuming UTC.

  ExerciseAccountId:
    Type: String
    Default: ''
    Description: >-
      Set ONLY in the exercise deployment. Names the single platform-owned
      account whose environment may be cycled to prove the path works. Empty
      in every tenant deployment, which is what makes it an absent capability
      rather than a guarded one.

  ScheduleExpression:
    Type: String
    Default: rate(15 minutes)
    Description: >-
      How often the window is evaluated, NOT the HOOP itself. The scheduler
      asks "should this be up now" and acts on the answer, so a 15-minute
      evaluation means an environment comes up within 15 minutes of its window
      opening. Finer costs more invocations; coarser makes somebody wait.

  LogsKeyArn:
    Type: String
    Default: ''

Conditions:

  UseDefaultLogsKey: !Equals [!Ref LogsKeyArn, '']
  IsExercise: !Not [!Equals [!Ref ExerciseAccountId, '']]

Resources:

  SchedulerRole:
    Type: AWS::IAM::Role
    Properties:
      RoleName: PlatformHoopScheduler
      AssumeRolePolicyDocument:
        Version: '2012-10-17'
        Statement:
          - Effect: Allow
            Principal: { Service: lambda.amazonaws.com }
            Action: sts:AssumeRole
      ManagedPolicyArns:
        - !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:iam::aws:policy/service-role/AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole'

  SchedulerPolicy:
    Type: AWS::IAM::Policy
    Properties:
      PolicyName: HoopSchedule
      Roles: [!Ref SchedulerRole]
      PolicyDocument:
        Version: '2012-10-17'
        Statement:
          # Reads are broad because the scheduler has to find what exists.
          - Sid: Discover
            Effect: Allow
            Action:
              - ec2:DescribeInstances
              - ec2:DescribeVolumes
              - rds:DescribeDBInstances
              - rds:DescribeDBClusters
              - rds:ListTagsForResource
              - ecs:ListClusters
              - ecs:ListServices
              - ecs:DescribeServices
              - autoscaling:DescribeAutoScalingGroups
            Resource: '*'

          # Writes are narrow in KIND rather than in resource: stop and start,
          # never terminate, never delete. There is no ec2:TerminateInstances,
          # no rds:DeleteDBInstance and no autoscaling:DeleteAutoScalingGroup
          # here, so CLAUDE.md's rule is enforced by the role and not only by
          # the code. A bug cannot destroy what the role cannot call.
          - Sid: StopAndStart
            Effect: Allow
            Action:
              - ec2:StartInstances
              - ec2:StopInstances
              - ec2:CreateTags
              - rds:StartDBInstance
              - rds:StopDBInstance
              - rds:StartDBCluster
              - rds:StopDBCluster
              - rds:AddTagsToResource
              - ecs:UpdateService
              - ecs:TagResource
              - autoscaling:UpdateAutoScalingGroup
              - autoscaling:CreateOrUpdateTags
            Resource: '*'

          # The manifest, in THIS account's parameter store. Scoped to the
          # one path. The scheduler needs no access to the platform registry
          # at all, which is the point: a cross-account role able to write the
          # registry from every scheduled account in the estate is a large
          # trust relationship to buy one lookup.
          - Sid: ManifestAndState
            Effect: Allow
            Action:
              - ssm:GetParameter
              - ssm:PutParameter
            Resource:
              - !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:ssm:${AWS::Region}:${AWS::AccountId}:parameter${ManifestParam}'
              # The published state, read by alarm suppression, the telemetry
              # gap detector and cost reporting (prompt 13.4). Two parameters
              # named individually rather than a path wildcard: the scheduler
              # writes exactly these two and nothing else under /platform.
              - !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:ssm:${AWS::Region}:${AWS::AccountId}:parameter${StateParam}'

          - Sid: EmitFindings
            Effect: Allow
            Action: events:PutEvents
            Resource: !Ref AlertBusArn

          - Sid: PublishDuration
            Effect: Allow
            Action: cloudwatch:PutMetricData
            Resource: '*'
            Condition:
              StringEquals:
                cloudwatch:namespace: Platform/HOOP

  SchedulerLogGroup:
    Type: AWS::Logs::LogGroup
    DeletionPolicy: Retain
    UpdateReplacePolicy: Retain
    Properties:
      LogGroupName: /aws/lambda/platform-hoop-scheduler
      # A year. What was stopped and when is the answer to "why was the
      # environment down" and to "why is this month's bill different".
      RetentionInDays: 365
      KmsKeyId: !If
        - UseDefaultLogsKey
        - !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:kms:${AWS::Region}:${AWS::AccountId}:alias/platform-logs'
        - !Ref LogsKeyArn

  SchedulerFunction:
    Type: AWS::Lambda::Function
    DependsOn: SchedulerLogGroup
    Properties:
      FunctionName: platform-hoop-scheduler
      Runtime: python3.12
      Handler: hoop.handler
      Role: !GetAtt SchedulerRole.Arn
      # A turndown walks every ASG, service, database and instance in the
      # account. Five minutes is generous for a non-production environment and
      # cheap to leave generous.
      Timeout: 300
      MemorySize: 256
      Code:
        S3Bucket: !Ref ArtifactBucket
        S3Key: !Ref ArtifactKey
      Environment:
        Variables:
          HOOP_ACCOUNT_TIER: !Ref AccountTier
          HOOP_ACCOUNT_KIND: !Ref AccountKind
          HOOP_MANIFEST_PARAM: !Ref ManifestParam
          HOOP_STATE_PARAM: !Ref StateParam
          ALERT_BUS_NAME: !Ref AlertBusName
          HOOP_EXERCISE_ACCOUNT_ID: !Ref ExerciseAccountId

  VerifyLogGroup:
    Type: AWS::Logs::LogGroup
    DeletionPolicy: Retain
    UpdateReplacePolicy: Retain
    Properties:
      LogGroupName: /aws/lambda/platform-hoop-verify
      RetentionInDays: 365
      KmsKeyId: !If
        - UseDefaultLogsKey
        - !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:kms:${AWS::Region}:${AWS::AccountId}:alias/platform-logs'
        - !Ref LogsKeyArn

  VerifyFunction:
    Type: AWS::Lambda::Function
    DependsOn: VerifyLogGroup
    Properties:
      FunctionName: platform-hoop-verify
      Runtime: python3.12
      Handler: cycle.handler
      Role: !GetAtt SchedulerRole.Arn
      Timeout: 300
      MemorySize: 256
      Code:
        S3Bucket: !Ref ArtifactBucket
        S3Key: !Ref ArtifactKey
      Environment:
        Variables:
          HOOP_ACCOUNT_TIER: !Ref AccountTier
          HOOP_ACCOUNT_KIND: !Ref AccountKind
          HOOP_MANIFEST_PARAM: !Ref ManifestParam
          HOOP_STATE_PARAM: !Ref StateParam
          ALERT_BUS_NAME: !Ref AlertBusName
          HOOP_EXERCISE_ACCOUNT_ID: !Ref ExerciseAccountId

  # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # The evaluation schedule
  # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # Fires regardless of the window and asks the scheduler what the window
  # implies. That is why there is one rule rather than a pair of cron rules at
  # the window's edges: a pair would drift out of step with a HOOP edited in
  # the registry, and an environment whose HOOP changed would keep coming up
  # at the old time with nothing reporting why.

  EvaluationSchedule:
    Type: AWS::Events::Rule
    Properties:
      Name: platform-hoop-evaluate
      Description: >-
        Evaluate this environment's HOOP window and turn down or up
        accordingly. Deliberately not two cron rules at the window edges — the
        window is data and this asks it every time.
      ScheduleExpression: !Ref ScheduleExpression
      State: ENABLED
      Targets:
        - Id: scheduler
          Arn: !GetAtt SchedulerFunction.Arn
          Input: !Sub '{"account_id": "${AccountId}", "hoop": ${HoopConfig}}'

  EvaluationPermission:
    Type: AWS::Lambda::Permission
    Properties:
      FunctionName: !GetAtt SchedulerFunction.Arn
      Action: lambda:InvokeFunction
      Principal: events.amazonaws.com
      SourceArn: !GetAtt EvaluationSchedule.Arn

Outputs:

  SchedulerFunctionName:
    Description: Turndown and turnup. Manual invocation uses this same function.
    Value: !Ref SchedulerFunction

  VerifyFunctionName:
    Description: Verifies a cycle and routes a failure.
    Value: !Ref VerifyFunction

  ExerciseMode:
    Description: Whether this deployment may cycle a platform-owned account.
    Value: !If [IsExercise, !Ref ExerciseAccountId, 'no']

redaction_check_exemptions.reason: CLAUDE.md: group and permission set NAMES are not personal data and live in the repository, so they appear here legitimately. Everything else in the personal-data files is treated as personal by default.
